papers.abstract: Generated videos often lose geometric consistency under camera motion: structures warp under viewpoint change, parallax becomes inconsistent, and smooth camera movement may collapse into shot-like transitions. We argue that this failure is largely a data problem. In web-scale video corpora, most visible motion comes from dynamic objects captured by static or weakly moving cameras, leaving only sparse supervision for viewpoint-induced appearance changes. To address this, we propose Video Geometry Corrector (VGC), a post-hoc video-to-video model trained on synthetic paired supervision. Starting from real videos with diverse camera motion and pose annotations, we construct VG-Pairs with a synthetic paired-supervision data generation pipeline. Each video clip is treated as a geometry-consistent target and paired with a distorted counterpart synthesized by a pretrained image-to-video inpainting model using trajectory-adaptive keyframes. VGC learns to map the distorted input to the geometry-consistent target without modifying the source generator, and uses optical flow as an auxiliary cue to help disentangle camera motion from object motion. Experiments on pose-conditioned and prompt-driven benchmarks show that VGC improves geometric consistency across multiple source generators, and scaling to a larger backbone further extends the framework toward more general video refinement.
authors: Weijie Lyu, Tiancheng Shen, Jason Li, Yujing Wang, Xiaoyuan Wang, Haobo Yuan, Yizhou Zhao, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Generated videos often warp structures, produce inconsistent parallax, or collapse smooth camera motion into shot-like transitions.
The paper attributes this largely to limited viewpoint-change supervision in web-scale video data.
VGC is trained on synthetic distorted/geometry-consistent video pairs created from real videos with camera-motion and pose annotations.
It refines outputs without modifying the source video generator and uses optical flow to separate camera motion from object motion.
Experiments across pose-conditioned and prompt-driven benchmarks show improved geometric consistency across multiple generators; larger backbones extend refinement capability.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Video Geometry Corrector (VGC). Starting from a real video with diverse camera motion, we select trajectory-adaptive keyframes and use them to condition an image-to-video inpainting model, which produces a geometry-distorted video that serves as the training input. We then train VGC to map this distorted input to the geometry-consistent target video with a reconstruction loss. Optical flow is computed from the distorted video and used as an additional conditioning signal for VGC, providing motion cues that help disentangle camera motion from scene dynamics. The 3D reconstruction is shown here only for visualization and is not used in the pipeline.

Figure 2: Effect of adaptive keyframe selection. The red arrows indicate a constant 3D direction while the camera is moving. For clips with large, nonlinear camera motion, conditioning the image-to-video model only on the first and last frames often produces a shortcut trajectory that deviates substantially from the ground-truth path (top; about 45◦ rotation versus about 225◦ in the ground truth). Our adaptive keyframe selection inserts intermediate keyframes, generates shorter segments conditioned on their boundary keyframes, and stitches them together. This produces geometry-distorted videos that remain close to the target camera trajectory and are therefore suitable as paired training data (middle), compared with the ground-truth supervision video (bottom).

Figure 7: General video refinement results. VGC corrects several geometric failures produced by the baseline models. In scene 1, HunyuanVideo [3] changes the cabinet into a glass door, while VGC restores the correct scene structure and camera motion, placing the door on the right side of the cabinet. In scene 2, HunyuanVideo generates a camera trajectory that passes through the wrong side of the doorway, whereas VGC recovers a plausible path. In scenes 3 and 4, VGC restores a consistent appearance and recovers fine geometric structure, such as the wooden supports. In the dynamic scenes, VGC better preserves identity and motion continuity: in scene 5, it maintains the same man in the leather jacket across frames and recovers a plausible motion trajectory, whereas the Wan baseline fails to infer coherent human motion; in scene 6, it restores the missing cyclist produced by CogVideoX [2]. The green boxes further show that VGC enhances local detail while remaining more faithful to the source video than SeedVR2 [20] and VEnhancer [15]. Please zoom in for details.

Figure 5: Visual results on DL3DV [24]. The first two rows show image-to-video results. In the baseline CogVideoX [2] outputs, the streetlight is duplicated, while VideoGPA [16] produces a distorted and tilted streetlight (red boxes). VGC corrects these geometric errors and restores a more plausible structure. The last row shows a text-to-video example, where VGC better preserves the original appearance of the sculpture, while VideoGPA changes its structure and other scene details.

Figure 6: Comparison of model sizes. In static scenes (top), both VGC 1.3B and 14B correct geometric distortions produced by the baseline model that SeedVR2 [20] and VEnhancer [15] fail to restore (red boxes). The 14B model further improves the geometry of moving humans and objects in dynamic scenes (bottom).

Figure 4: Visual results on RealEstate10K [27]. DFoT [28] and GF + REPA [10, 29] produce inconsistent lighting across frames, while GF [10] generates an incomplete sofa structure (red box). VGC restores more consistent lighting and more coherent scene geometry.

Table 3: General video refinement results on SpatialVID [25]. We compare VGC with general video refinement and enhancement methods [20, 15] on dynamic videos generated by CogVideoX [2], HunyuanVideo [3], and Wan [4]. Although VGC is designed for geometry correction under camera motion rather than generic enhancement, it achieves competitive performance across multiple perceptual and temporal metrics, and is particularly strong in dynamic degree, imaging quality, and DOVER [32]. These results suggest that the proposed correction framework extends beyond static-scene geometry and remains effective in more general settings.

Table 2: Quantitative results on DL3DV [24]. We evaluate VGC on three CogVideoX [2] source generators in both text-to-video and image-to-video settings. VGC consistently improves PSNR, SSIM, and MSE over the corresponding baselines, and further improves VideoGPA [16] when applied as a post-hoc corrector. These results show that VGC transfers across different generation settings and can be flexibly combined with other geometry-aware refinement methods.

Table 1: Quantitative results on RealEstate10K [27]. VGC achieves the strongest PSNR, SSIM, and revisit error (RVE) among the direct baselines. When applied as a post-hoc corrector to Geometry Forcing (GF) [10] and GF + REPA [10, 29], it further improves their performance, showing that it can be flexibly combined with geometry-aware generators. Comparing VGC with and without optical flow shows that flow yields modest gains in image quality while maintaining similar longrange geometric consistency.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a post-hoc video-to-video model to correct geometric consistency in generated videos, relevant to video generation and refinement.
papers.title: Learning to Correct Geometry in Generated Videos
papers.tldr: VGC post-processes generated videos to correct geometry and improve consistency under camera motion using synthetic paired supervision and optical-flow cues.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space diffusion models have recently re-emerged as a compelling alternative to latent diffusion, avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder. JiT shows that a vanilla diffusion transformer can generate directly in pixel space by replacing the commonly used velocity prediction ($\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction) with clean image prediction ($\boldsymbol{x_0}$-prediction). In this work, we revisit this choice and introduce MFlow, an adaptive parameterization that learns to interpolate between $\boldsymbol{x_0}$- and $\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction across principal directions of the data, learned end-to-end with diffusion training. We find that the preferred parameterization varies systematically with the data representation and model capacity -- notably, increasing model capacity shifts preference toward velocity prediction. We evaluate MFlow across ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation, demonstrating competitive or improved generative performance across diverse settings. In addition, we find that vanilla pixel diffusion transformers, irrespective of parameterization, retain a persistent high-frequency deficit relative to real images. To address this, we introduce ConvRefiner, a lightweight convolutional module trained post-hoc with an adversarial loss while keeping the diffusion backbone frozen. With only a small amount of additional training, ConvRefiner restores the high-frequency statistics of generated images while preserving FID. Project webpage: https://soumik-kanad.github.io/mflow-diffusion/.
authors: Soumik Mukhopadhyay, Long Mai, Abhinav Shrivastava, Aniruddha Mahapatra
bullets: Pixel diffusion avoids the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder, but its prediction parameterization strongly affects performance.
MFlow learns the preferred interpolation between x₀- and u-prediction across data principal directions during diffusion training.
The preferred parameterization depends on data representation and model capacity; larger models favor velocity prediction more strongly.
Experiments on ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation show competitive or improved generative performance across settings.
Pixel diffusion transformers exhibit a persistent high-frequency deficit; post-hoc ConvRefiner addresses it with lightweight adversarial training while freezing the backbone and preserving FID.

Figure 13: Leading modes of the uncentered patch-PCA basis. We reshape the first 64 eigenvectors of the 16 × 16 × 3 patch-PCA basis into RGB patches; the value λ denotes the variance of each direction. The leading ordering interleaves patch-global or very low-frequency modes with spatially varying modes. In particular, PC0 is dominated by low-frequency patch-level tone, PC1 is an approximately uniform chromatic mode, PC2–PC3 encode spatial gradients, and PC4 returns to an approximately uniform chromatic mode. Eigenvector signs are arbitrary, so the interpretation is based on spatial structure rather than the displayed color polarity.

(left) We see improved details in the leaf veins in the generated image. (right) We also note the average power gain in the high-frequency (0.5–0.7) region. We see overall improvement in texture details comparable to real image spectrum.

We also show the visual improvements – we see that b4 adds additional texture details, while b8 sometimes overshoots in texture.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes adaptive parameterization and a conv refiner for pixel-space diffusion transformers, with evaluations on video generation among other settings.
papers.title: Rethinking the design space of Vanilla Pixel Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: MFlow adaptively combines clean-image and velocity prediction for pixel-space diffusion transformers, while ConvRefiner restores missing high-frequency detail without degrading FID.

papers.abstract: Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints. Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials. Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower. Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or MuJoCo's signed-distance collision. Videos and interactive simulations are at https://younghyopark.me/blind-proprioceptive-assembly/.
authors: Antonia Bronars, Younghyo Park, Kushal Kedia, Pulkit Agrawal
bullets: Policies use only short histories of joint positions, velocities, and actions—without vision, force, torque, or tactile sensing.
Reinforcement learning in simulation teaches peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading under randomized parts, grasps, and contacts.
The peg-insertion policy transfers zero-shot to hardware and succeeds on 73% of trials across different peg shapes and sizes.
In simulation, blind policies generalize better to unseen part shapes and sizes than matched visual policies, but may operate more slowly.
An open-source procedural generator creates accurate, clearance-preserving assembly environments from exact convex pieces for MuJoCo.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Speed against accuracy for a 16 mm round peg with 100 µm clearance, (a) on CPU, one environment on one thread, and (b) on GPU, per environment step across 256 MuJoCo Warp worlds, with the error also measured on Warp. Each line is one method’s Pareto front over all its settings; lower left is better, and hollow markers fill the clearance (dotted line). (c) The peg, centered and aligned, dropped from 1 mm above each method’s default plate and shown 0.2 s later.

Figure 7: Policy Architecture. A temporal convolution compresses the last H = 30 proprioceptive observations ot (joint positions q and velocities q̇, gripper pose x and twist ẋ, and the previous action at−1) into a latent zt, and an MLP maps zt and the current observation ot to joint targets qd for a joint impedance controller. During training, we provide contact supervision from privileged simulator state. A contact decoder (amber) predicts the contact state (ĉt) from zt. Its cross-entropy Lcontact with the simulator’s labels ct (left, near half of the fixture cut away) trains the encoder, but ĉt never reaches the policy.

Figure 10: The blind policies’ joint histories encode the task’s mode, in simulation and in the real world. A linear probe fitted only in simulation reads the mode from each policy’s history latent. Each matrix gives its confusions (%); beside it, one start state is decoded at every step (T: true mode, D: decoded). On all three tasks, the probe cleanly separates modes that call for different actions, such as lifted, engaged, and stuck. (a) On the robot, it decodes the same sequence of peg insertion modes as in simulation.

Figure 2: Peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. (a–c) A start of each task, faded, and the same grasp at success: the peg seated in its hole, the gear seated on its shaft in mesh with both anchor gears, and the nut turned until its thread has caught. (d–f) Stadium pegs, gear sets, and nuts and bolts generated by mjfit and used for training, to scale.

Figure 11: Proprioceptive policies remain more robust to geometric variation. Success of the blind and visual policies (both with a 30-step history) on each task, in distribution (left of the dashed line) and on unseen parts, each widening one object property beyond its training range while the others stay within theirs.
Figure 1: Blind insertion. A policy trained only in simulation inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in the real world using only its joint encoders and previous actions.

Figure 12: Real-world results of the blind policy, with no fine-tuning, beside the same policy in simulation on the same peg (2,048 episodes). Error bars are 95% Wilson intervals. Details in Appendix C.

Figure 9: Proprioception guides efficient search without vision. Because the blind policy must search through contact, it follows a less direct path and seats later than the visual policy (a, b). Nonetheless, it travels far less (c) than an optimistic scripted spiral search baseline (Chhatpar & Branicky, 2001).

Figure 8: Proprioception alone is enough to learn all three tasks. Blind policies, which sense only their own joints, reach the same near-perfect training success as visual policies with a wrist camera. Lines are the mean of two training seeds.

papers.selection_reason: RL-based blind proprioceptive assembly policies with sim-to-real transfer.
papers.title: Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
papers.tldr: Proprioception alone can support precise, vision-free assembly across varied parts, with simulated policies transferring to real peg insertion.

papers.abstract: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.
authors: Xinhao Liu, Yunsheng Tian, Yuheng Qiu, Pieter Abbeel, Xi Chen, Guanya Shi, Chen Feng
bullets: Fine-tuned VLM navigation policies often fail to recognize visible goals or estimate their distance.
The proposed approach explicitly grounds the navigation goal to address these failures.
It substantially improves success and achieves state-of-the-art results across six benchmarks in three scene collections.
The authors correct annotation defects and find that, with ground-truth grounding, the policy nearly matches its demonstration-generating expert.
The remaining performance gap is attributed primarily to perception, especially goal grounding.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses object-goal navigation by explicit goal grounding in a VLM-based policy, a core robot navigation and goal-conditioned task.
papers.title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
papers.tldr: StopWatch identifies goal grounding—not exploration or policy learning—as the main bottleneck in VLM-based object-goal navigation and improves navigation by explicitly grounding the goal.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.
authors: Jianyuan Zhong, Chenwei Wu, Zhaochen Yu, Xixian Jiang, Xuewei Li, Hao Xiao, Xilin Dai, Junyang Wang, Jiaru Zou, Zhiqing Cui, Boyuan Zheng, Jing Xiong, Zhen Zhang, Qiang Gao, Michael Morley, Luis Nakayama, Qiang Xu, Liyue Shen, Tao Gui, Leo Anthony Celi, James Zou, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
bullets: Defines valuable, testable hypotheses as evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties paired with feasible investigations, decision criteria, and alternatives.
Uses multi-agent evolutionary search to build hypothesis trees and compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks.
Recursively learns through credit assignment, workflow replay, and rediscovery of improved strategies for new investigations.
Introduces DFM-Bench to evaluate hypothesis quality and cumulative progress across hypotheses, revisions, development paths, and research runs.

Across four life-science domains, hypothesis quality improved from 4.86 to 5.39 after two self-improvement rounds; expert evaluations and post-cutoff correspondence also favored DiscoveryRSI in the reported comparisons.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | DiscoveryRSI couples multi-agent hypothesis development with recursive self-improvement. (a) Within an episode, a Lead coordinates Generation and Evolution; candidate hypothesis versions are critiqued and progress is recorded. Selected hypotheses are compiled into Harbor tasks, with linked evidence, data, drafts, artifacts, assessments, contributions, and execution records. (b) Research trees carry hypotheses across RSI rounds: the recorded state 𝐻𝑘 enters RSI, which produces updated parameters (𝜃𝑘+1, 𝜓𝑘+1) and fresh questions for rediscovery. papers.selection_reason: Introduces DiscoveryRSI, a multi-agent framework for scientific hypothesis discovery. It demonstrates recursive learning and self-improvement strategies for LLM-based research agents.
papers.title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
papers.tldr: DiscoveryRSI recursively improves scientific hypothesis generation by evolving evidence-grounded research plans and learning from their outcomes, producing higher-quality hypotheses and stronger alignment with later research.

papers.abstract: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.
authors: Joshua Williamson, Niall Jeffrey, Lorne Whiteway
bullets: Targets spherical physical-science datasets with no preferred position or orientation, where ignoring symmetry can require costly simulations.
Implements a gauge-equivariant architecture on HEALPix using steerable filters, parallel transport, and spin-weighted features.
Provides provably exact SO(3) equivariance under a band-limit, with full-network invariance errors at the percent level or lower.
Achieves strong benchmark performance in dense gradient regression, competitive CMB foreground removal and denoising, and tighter cosmological-lensing SBI posteriors at matched simulation counts.
Scope: equivariance and exactness depend on the band-limit, while full-network invariance is controlled by hyperparameters.

The poor results from models not optimised for spherical data (especially the Planar CNN) given a fixed simulation budget forces a user to rely on imperfect simulators to increase the simulation count – our method avoids this by including a spherical symmetry as inductive bias.

papers.selection_reason: Develops an SO(3)-equivariant CNN for spherical data, explicitly incorporating geometric symmetry to avoid relearning invariance, directly relevant to spatial intelligence and geometric reasoning.
papers.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
papers.tldr: An SO(3)-equivariant CNN for spherical data encodes rotational symmetry exactly, reducing the need to learn it from simulations and improving scientific inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.
authors: Chiatzen Wang, Bill Xu, Haochen Gu, Hongyang Zhang
bullets: Lossless verification preserves output distributions, making accepted tokens per round a useful efficiency proxy; relaxed verification does not.
Across twelve target–drafter pairs, the most relaxed settings accepted 1.34× more tokens per round but produced 1.54× longer completions on average.
Extra accepted tokens often had low target-model probability and contributed to length inflation, especially by extending reasoning traces.
Rules that reduced verifier rounds typically caused substantial accuracy drops, sometimes because continued reasoning exhausted the output budget.
Completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and accuracy should be reported alongside acceptance rates.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the efficiency of speculative decoding, specifically identifying 'length inflation' in lossy verification. This provides important empirical findings regarding LLM decoding speed and verification mechanisms.
papers.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Relaxed speculative decoding may accept more tokens per round but often generates much longer completions, undermining its apparent speed gains and sometimes reducing accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables language-model agents to personalize future interactions, but a finite memory bank cannot preserve every extracted fact. Existing memory gating policies are typically shared across users and therefore fail to account for user-specific patterns of future reuse. In this paper, we study memory gating at the fact level. We first propose a retrieval-based labeling strategy that labels each fact by whether it is later retrieved and incorporated into responses. We then formulate online memory gating as contextual apple tasting with delayed one-sided feedback, and propose Warm-Start UCB, which combines offline learning from existing data with online adaptation to the current user. Our theoretical analysis establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(T\epsilon \wedge d\sqrt{T})$ when the delay window is at most $O(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the total number of rounds, $\epsilon$ is the initialization error, $d$ is the dimension of the feature map, and $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides constant and poly-logarithmic factors. The results of our experiment demonstrate that our method outperforms all baselines under different memory budgets and history lengths, establishing it as a promising personalized memory gating policy.
authors: Kaixuan Ji, Zixiang Chen, Wenting Zhao, Cheng Qian, Heng Wang, Weizhi Zhang, Jielin Qiu, Liangwei Yang, Quanquan Gu, Silvio Savarese, Shelby Heinecke, Huan Wang
bullets: Targets fact-level memory gating under finite memory capacity, where shared policies overlook user-specific reuse patterns.
Labels facts based on whether they are later retrieved and used in responses.
Models online gating as contextual apple tasting with delayed one-sided feedback.
Combines offline initialization with online adaptation to the current user through Warm-Start UCB.
Experiments report better performance than all baselines across memory budgets and history lengths.],

papers.abstract: While deriving text embeddings directly from frozen LLMs has emerged as a promising direction, existing methods focus almost exclusively on English, leaving multilingual settings largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of multilingual training-free text embeddings in LLMs. Our analysis reveals a language-conditioned embedding geometry in which semantically equivalent sentences remain misaligned across languages. We hypothesize that language-specific variation can be disentangled from semantic content to improve embedding quality. To this end, we propose Paired-Residual Subspace Removal (PRSR), a training-free inference-time intervention that steers LLM representations toward a more language-invariant semantic space. PRSR first constructs paired residuals from multilingual parallel sentences to capture language-specific deviations. It then estimates layer-wise low-rank subspaces from these residuals and suppresses the corresponding components in the last-token hidden states. We conduct more than 200 monolingual evaluations across 18 languages using MTEB and MMTEB, along with cross-lingual bitext mining between English and over 200 other languages. Empirical results demonstrate that PRSR consistently improves the performance of existing training-free baselines in both monolingual and cross-lingual settings across different LLMs.
authors: Ailiang Lin, Zhuoyun Li, Yusong Wang, Keyu Mao, Kotaro Funakoshi, Manabu Okumura
bullets: Identifies language-conditioned embedding geometry that misaligns semantically equivalent sentences across languages.
Uses parallel multilingual sentences to construct paired residuals capturing language-specific variation.
Estimates layer-wise low-rank residual subspaces and suppresses them in last-token representations at inference time.
Evaluated across 18 languages with MTEB/MMTEB and in English-to-200+ language bitext mining.
Consistently improves existing training-free baselines across monolingual and cross-lingual tasks and multiple LLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of PRSR. (a) Paired-residual subspace construction. At each selected layer, we first construct paired residuals by subtracting the group mean from the last-token representations of parallel sentences. We then stack the residuals across groups and languages, and apply SVD to estimate a low-rank language-sensitive subspace. (b) Inference-time intervention. We remove the projections of last-token hidden states onto these subspaces at the corresponding layers of the frozen LLM, steering representations toward a more language-invariant semantic space.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Paired-Residual Subspace Removal (PRSR), a training-free inference-time intervention to improve multilingual text embeddings by removing language-specific variation. This is a direct technical contribution to LLM representation learning and multilingual capabilities.
papers.title: Steering beyond Language: Improving Multilingual Training-Free Text Embeddings via Paired-Residual Subspace Removal
papers.tldr: PRSR improves multilingual, training-free text embeddings by removing language-specific representation components from frozen LLMs.

papers.abstract: Video world models that generate and explore environments at scale need a persistent 3D memory of what they have produced. Plane primitives offer a natural candidate: a compact set of oriented planes captures the dominant structural elements (e.g., walls, floors, facades) of indoor and outdoor scenes, while requiring only 7 parameters per primitive. We present PPMem, a video world model that adopts plane primitives as its persistent 3D memory. PPMem augments a video diffusion transformer with a planar prediction head and a Depth Token Fusion (DTF) module: each autoregressive chunk jointly produces RGB video and planar geometry, which merges into a persistent plane memory that conditions subsequent chunks via rendered depth. The resulting memory is three orders of magnitude more compact than per-pixel point clouds (~100K primitives, 5MB for a full scene), geometrically explicit (metric depth, normals, exportable surfaces), cross-view consistent (jointly predicted by the shared backbone), and adaptive (refined by the merging procedure as generation proceeds). On DL3DV and RealEstate10K, PPMem outperforms prior 3D-grounded world models in video quality while jointly producing metric-scale depth, surface normals, and exportable planar geometry, sustaining coherence across hundreds of frames under large viewpoint changes. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/ppmem.
authors: Yuze He, Bin Tan, Zelin Gao, Yujun Shen, Yong-Jin Liu, Nan Xue, Yinghao Xu
bullets: Uses oriented plane primitives to represent dominant scene structure with a compact persistent memory.
Adds a planar prediction head and Depth Token Fusion to jointly generate RGB video and geometry in each autoregressive chunk.
Merges predicted planes over time and conditions future chunks through rendered depth, enabling adaptive cross-view consistency.
Produces metric-scale depth, surface normals, and exportable planar geometry alongside video.
On DL3DV and RealEstate10K, reports improved video quality over prior 3D-grounded world models and coherence across hundreds of frames under large viewpoint changes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: PPMem architecture overview. The Wan DiT receives noisy video latents channelconcatenated with projected source-view RGB/masks and partial depth rendered from the plane pool; context frames are prepended temporally. The DiT produces two token streams: video tokens decoded by the Wan VAE into RGB outputs, and geometry tokens adapted by geometry LoRA and fused with partial depth tokens via a ViT-based Depth Token Fusion module. The fused tokens are decoded into per-frame plane primitives, which merge into the persistent plane pool. The pool is rendered at the next chunk’s target cameras and fed back as conditioning.

Figure 4: Qualitative long-context comparison. PPMem preserves scene structure and color consistency across the full sequence. VMem collapses early under large viewpoint change; SPMem grows vague and drifts; Gen3C and Voyager lose structural alignment as the viewpoint diverges.

Figure 1: Given a single input image and a camera trajectory, PPMem autoregressively generates video while accumulating a persistent plane-based 3D memory. We show two DL3DV scenes (indoor, outdoor) with generated frames at selected indices. Insets visualize the plane pool at each frame, colored by the current view frustum. The plane geometry grows to cover the full explored scene, serving as persistent spatial memory for subsequent generation.

Figure 5: Depth quality analysis. (a) Per-frame depth metrics (AbsRel ↓, δ<1.25 ↑) on DL3DV over 121 frames. PPMem maintains consistently lower depth error than Voyager, the only other baseline with joint depth output. (b) We scale the input depth conditioning by a known factor and measure the predicted/GT depth ratio. Concat + DTF (ours) tracks input scale faithfully (1.00± 0.01 at scale 1.0, mean ± s.e. over 56 scenes), while channel concatenation alone exhibits compressed response at extreme scales. Measured as deviation from the identity mapping over the full scale range, DTF also stays closer to it (natural-log RMSE 0.273 vs. 0.320 for concatenation alone; 0.131 vs. 0.293 with scale augmentation).

Figure 3: Perceptual similarity vs. frame index on DL3DV long-context generation (∼350 frames). Left: CLIP similarity. Right: DINOv2 similarity. PPMem (blue) maintains the highest perceptual fidelity across the full generation. VMem collapses early; Gen3C and SPMem degrade steadily; the gap widens with frame count, especially on DINOv2.
Table 5: Feature decoder and loss component ablations. Top: decoder architecture (all else fixed). Bottom: loss removal (full model as baseline).

Table 2: Short-context comparison on DL3DV and RealEstate10K. We report two frame budgets: N=49 (native chunk size for Voyager and SPMem; VMem uses 48) and N=121 (Gen3C native chunk). At N=49 most baselines are single-chunk; at N=121 Voyager, VMem, and SPMem all require autoregressive looping.

Table 3: 3D representation and prediction ablation. We compare our joint plane pool against three inference-only alternatives (same checkpoint, no retraining): a same-model rollout without persistent memory, Gen3C-style per-frame MoGe-2 point cloud memory, and post-hoc standalone Plana3R reconstruction.

Table 1: Properties of 3D representations for cross-chunk video memory. We compare along four aspects: whether geometry is predicted internally by the generation model or externally, whether predictions are cross-view consistent, the number of persistent 3D primitives, and whether the representation captures structured surfaces. Primitive counts are estimates at ∼400 frames, 576×1024.
Table 4: Depth conditioning mechanism ablation. All variants share the same backbone and training data, varying only the depth conditioning mechanism.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a video world model with persistent planar 3D memory and depth token fusion, directly addressing long-horizon world prediction.
papers.title: Persistent Planar Memory for Video World Models
papers.tldr: PPMem gives video world models a compact, persistent plane-based 3D memory to maintain coherent, geometrically grounded generation over long sequences and changing viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) remain a major source of preventable morbidity and mortality in healthcare settings. Proper execution of the central line dressing change (CLDC) procedure is essential for infection prevention, yet current approaches to competency assessment rely primarily on manual ob- servation by clinical educators, making evaluation time-intensive, difficult to scale, and limited in consistency and granularity. These challenges highlight the need for AI-assisted skill evaluation methods that can support more objective, reproducible, and scalable assessment of clinical performance. However, progress in this area has been constrained by the lack of broad-scale, clinically grounded datasets for developing and evaluating such methods. In this work, we present the collection process of a large-scale video dataset for CLDC skill evaluation, comprising 365 recordings of registered nurses collected during the 2026 annual competency exam at Houston Methodist Hospital. Each video is paired with subtask-level temporal annotations and clinical performance assessments spanning 17 subtasks of the procedure. We describe the data collection and curation pipeline, including pilot testing of record- ing configurations, annotation protocol design, and post-collection processing. We further establish the feasibility of video-based skill assessment through benchmark experiments with spatiotemporal deep learning models. This dataset provides a foundation for future research on automated clinical skill assessment, feedback generation, and AI-assisted training in nursing education.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. Under such workloads, we observe that existing draft models suffer from up to an 80% degradation in acceptance length, while maintaining their historical KV cache introduces substantial system overhead. In this paper, we identify the growing historical context as a common source of both problems and introduce DLite, a history-free speculative decoding framework for agentic AI. DLite directly reuses contextual hidden states from the target model and performs local speculative prediction without explicitly maintaining the historical context, transforming an increasingly complex modeling problem into local simple prediction problem. A lightweight sequential head further restores intra-block causal dependencies with low overhead. To effectively train this heterogeneous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strategy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2-6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models (VDMs) trained on internet-scale data encode a rich prior on appearance, motion, and physics that is difficult to replicate with explicit 3D rendering and costly 3D data capture. We introduce Video Diffusion Avatars (VDAs), a method that creates photo-realistic, multi-view consistent avatars from a single image by fine-tuning a VDM for precise control over camera viewpoint, facial expression, and upper-body pose. Departing from 3D morphable models (3DMMs), VDAs use a learned expression space that lifts the expressiveness ceiling of 3DMMs, e.g., for the tongue and mouth interior. However, learned expression codes exhibit heavy viewpoint bias, as our DISTRACT benchmark reveals. We show that this bias can be removed through disentanglement, enabling their use as driving signals for multi-view consistent avatars. Camera and upper-body pose are controlled jointly via proxy-mesh renderings, giving independent control over expression, pose, and viewpoint. A camera-triplet training strategy makes the approach efficient: our models train for 34 hours on a single A100 using only public multi-view data. VDAs outperform state-of-the-art single-image 3D avatars on novel-view reenactment, reducing face LPIPS by 29% and improving perceptual quality (JOD) by 66% on BecomingLit. A static 3DGS reconstruction probe further confirms that our generations are the most multi-view consistent. Built on a video prior, VDAs produce effects beyond the reach of explicit renderers, including physically plausible hair dynamics, shadows, reflections, and refractions.

papers.abstract: Progress estimators play an essential role in providing dense reward signals for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation, but accurately assessing task progress can be much challenging. Existing methods heavily rely on expert data and naively assume that all actions within a demonstration contribute to task success. This assumption often breaks down in real-world scenarios, especially in high-precision manipulation, where subtle geometric errors can lead to task failure. Therefore, these methods can erroneously interpret human mistakes as meaningful progress, further corrupting progress learning. We argue that a key limitation is the lack of a global prior regarding task evaluation criteria, which is crucial for distinguishing meaningful progress from human mistakes. To this end, we propose PRIME, a novel progress estimator capable of learning precise progress estimation from imprecise demonstrations by aggregating experience across trajectories. PRIME constructs a weighted graph over observed states, connecting states across trajectories based on spatial proximity and visual consistency. Edge weights encode spatial distances as transition costs, and shortest-path search approximates the geodesic distance to success. Changes in this distance naturally distinguish advancement, stagnation, and setbacks without assuming monotonic progress over time. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real world on precise manipulation tasks show that PRIME is consistently effective across diverse tasks, and robust to data with varying degrees of suboptimality. Notably, the advantage of PRIME gets more pronounced in higher-precision scenarios, yielding up to a \(5\times\) improvement in policy success rate over the SFT baselines on charger insertion.
authors: Huanqian Wang, Boshi Tang, Botong Xiao, Jie Zhang, Yang Yue, Danhua Tao, Shiji Song, Gao Huang
bullets: Existing progress estimators may treat every demonstrated action as meaningful progress, allowing human errors to corrupt learning.
PRIME builds a weighted graph connecting visually and spatially similar states across trajectories.
Shortest-path distances to successful states provide a global progress signal without assuming progress is always monotonic.
Experiments in simulation and the real world show robustness across precise manipulation tasks and varying demonstration quality.
On charger insertion, PRIME improves policy success by up to 5× over SFT baselines, with larger benefits at higher precision.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: An overview of PRIME. (a): Graph construction. Each demonstration timestep is represented by a graph node which comprises multi-view observations and the corresponding robot configuration. (b): Edge establishment. Cross-trajectory edges are established through multi-view visual consistency and configuration proximity, with weights reflecting pose and gripper-state differences. (c): Shortest-path distance as progress for RL. The graph G defines the remaining distance to task completion as the weighted shortest-path distance from the current node to the goal. This distance serves as a measure of task progress.

Fig. 2: Quantitative success rate comparison and qualitative illustration of progress estimation. (Left) Success rates of different methods across three real-world tasks: peg-in-hole, peg-in-hole (Hard) and charger insertion. (Right) Qualitative illustration of progress estimation on Peg-Hard task. PRIME reflects partial advancements during an undershoot, maintains a constant estimation during idling, and appropriately penalizes the progress when a drift occurs. (Bottom) Correspondence between suboptimal behaviors and progress estimation of PRIME. Our method accurately identifies different types of suboptimal behavior, and assigns progress estimation accordingly.

Fig. 4: Evaluation on various robotic trajectories. We compare our method against baselines across three scenarios. (1) Successful Execution: For a clean trajectory with minor pauses, PRIME provides a smooth, monotonic progress estimate. (2) Suboptimal Execution: When a human collector makes a mistake and lifts the cylinder upward to adjust, PRIME captures this setback with a local decrease in progress (orange band). (3) Failure Detection: When the cylinder is misplaced, PRIME reflects a sharp drop in progress (red band) as the trajectory drifts toward failure. For visualization, we normalize our distance predictions as 1 − d(st)

Fig. 1: Overview of suboptimal behaviors and their impact on policy training. (Top) Demonstrations for precision manipulation inevitably contain suboptimal behaviors, even after trajectory-level filtering. In peg-insertion, for example, removing successful yet low-quality trajectories improves the task success rate only from 50% to 66.7%, whereas our step-level filtering achieves a success rate of 100%. (Bottom) During data collection, human operators unavoidably introduce suboptimal behaviors such as drifting (unintended lateral deviation), overshooting (motion beyond the target), and idling (unnecessary pauses or inactivity). While prior works assume that all actions contribute equally to the final success, they fail to capture the real-time progress in the face of these behaviors.

papers.abstract: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.
authors: Koki Ryu, Hitomi Yanaka
bullets: Existing benchmarks conflate acoustic perception with semantic reasoning, obscuring the source of model failures.
VocalGrad evaluates temporal change direction through binary classification, minimizing reliance on language understanding.
State-of-the-art LALMs show a substantial human–model gap and perform near chance on the benchmark.
Linear probing identifies two failure modes: relevant information is either unused by the language-model head or becomes less linearly decodable across layers.
The benchmark exposes acoustic-representation limitations not visible from text outputs.

papers.abstract: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.
authors: Hyunseo Kim, Suil Choe, Sukkyoung So, Daeyeon Yi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating structured product listings as free-form text with implicit, non-reusable strategies.
Uses an Editor, Reflector, Moderator, and Curator to apply, update, filter, and commit optimization behaviors.
Stores successful strategies in a persistent handbook while deactivating consistently harmful behaviors.
Experiments find structured, feedback-evolved behaviors improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk over monolithic prompt optimization.
Learned behaviors transfer to unseen product categories, supporting interpretable and reusable optimization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the GLOBE framework. Each iteration deploys the active handbook Hn over a batch of K query-product pairs: the editor rewrites the target listing and the ranker returns episode-level rank feedback. The Reflector then proposes behavior additions or modifications, the Moderator removes redundant proposals, and the Curator commits the survivors into Hn+1, which replaces Hn as the handbook deployed over the next batch. Repeating this deployment-and-evolution cycle accumulates episodic feedback into persistent editing knowledge.

Figure 1: Comparison between monolithic prompt optimization and GLOBE’s structured handbook optimization. This is the prompt-level analogue of GLOBE’s handbook evolution: the optimization knowledge is carried entirely by a single free-form instruction rather than by structured, field-scoped behaviors.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.
authors: Vinay Saji Mathew, Soundar Kumara, Gretta Kellogg, William K. M. Lai
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of diffusion-based all-atom protein structure prediction.
Uses a geometric noise schedule and multistep consistency training for few-step distillation.
Adds physical steering and target-free candidate selection to reduce geometric defects.
Evaluates AF3-Blitz and Boltz-2-Blitz under a common protocol covering structure, interfaces, ligand placement, and stereochemistry.
AF3-Blitz outperforms evaluated few-step baselines and exceeds its teacher on several accuracy metrics.

papers.abstract: Planning while moving faces an historical trade-off between deliberation and reactivity. A planner running concurrently with execution needs time to compute, so the robot must commit to an open-loop action chunk for that duration: a longer commitment buys a better plan at the cost of feedback frequency. Existing controllers fix this action commitment, and consequently the computation budget, before deployment. However, the optimal computation time is highly state-dependent (due to factors such as unmodeled dynamics, safety constraints, and marginal optimisation gains), i.e. dynamic, therefore offline static tuning risks leaving systems blind during critical maneuvers or unable to find global effective solutions. We cast the identification of the optimal computation budget as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) in which a single decision defines both the robot action commitments and the time allocated to the solver. To solve this, we train a reinforcement-learning policy conditioned on the current state, the executing plan, and inexpensive planner statistics. Across ground-robot navigation, agile quadrotor flight, and contact-rich manipulation, the learned policy changes its budget with the demands of the scenario, discovering efficient reasoning patterns that outperform fixed-budget baselines. https://lorenzomagnino.github.io/learning-robot-metareasoning-review/
authors: Lorenzo Magnino, Antonio Marino, Michael Amir, Daigo Shishika, Amanda Prorok
bullets: Fixed computation budgets force a trade-off between better plans and frequent feedback.
The optimal planning time varies with state, safety constraints, dynamics, and expected optimization gains.
The approach formulates budget selection as a semi-Markov decision process.
An RL policy uses the current state, executing plan, and inexpensive planner statistics to select both action duration and solver time.
Experiments span ground navigation, agile quadrotor flight, and contact-rich manipulation, where adaptive budgets outperform fixed-budget baselines.

This lets the robot decide how much to deliberate under environmental uncertainty and temporal constraints. The new plan takes over, the state and statistics are refreshed, and the loop repeats.

papers.abstract: A 3D asset admits multiple valid part decompositions, while semantics-aware segmentation should reflect both the desired granularity and the parts a user wants to extract. Ideally, a practical segmentation model should strive for a simple principle: what you ask for is what you get. However, realizing this goal is hindered by two core obstacles: the lack of multi-granularity training data and the absence of a holistic control mechanism. We propose FLEXPART, a unified framework for text-controlled 3D mesh segmentation. To establish flexible control, we introduce a holistic control prompt comprising semantic part names with location and shape clauses. To support this mechanism, we utilize an automated Vision-Language Model (VLM) pipeline to construct a large-scale dataset of multi-granularity partitions and their corresponding prompts. Driven by this data, FLEXPART generates a view-independent part-identity field in native 3D space, directly assigning discrete part IDs to mesh faces. To compel the model to respect semantic conditions rather than rely on geometric priors, we train the model using randomized background dropping. Furthermore, an inference-time VLM planner can automatically complete descriptive clauses from 2D renderings, allowing users to simply name the desired parts in ordinary words. FLEXPART with planner-completed prompts outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 15% in mIoU, even when that baseline receives ground-truth guidance. On our held-out FLEXPARTBENCH, FLEXPART leads at each granularity and improves average mIoU by 22% over the strongest baseline. With only the requested part names supplied by the user, it also improves IoU by 35% over the strongest click-driven baseline on selective segmentation.
authors: Yiqun Zhao, Jiachen Xu, Yihao Zhi, Yunfei Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Xintong Han, Chunchao Guo, Shenghua Gao
bullets: Addresses the lack of multi-granularity data and holistic control in semantics-aware 3D part segmentation.
Uses prompts containing part names plus location and shape descriptions to control segmentation.
Builds a large-scale multi-granularity dataset with an automated VLM pipeline.
Predicts discrete part IDs directly on mesh faces and uses randomized background dropping to emphasize semantic cues.

An inference-time VLM planner can complete descriptive clauses from renderings, enabling ordinary-word part requests; the method reports gains over evaluated baselines across granularities and selective segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Granularity control on FLEXPARTBENCH. For each method, panels show fine (large), coarse (top right), and medium (bottom right) granularities. Conversely, PartField and SAMPart3D are biased toward geometric boundaries over the requested semantic groupings, and Find3D suffers from severe surface fragmentation. Meanwhile, SegviGen struggles to follow the ground truth, since relying on a single reference map fails to resolve occlusions.

Figure 7. Generalization to generated assets. Four Hunyuan3D 3.1 meshes. Although these AI-generated meshes lack well-defined geometric boundaries, our method generalizes robustly by following semantic instructions rather than relying on rigid geometric priors.

Its decoder can be queried at any 3D coordinate, with two cross-attention modules for geometry (SDF) and a discrete, binary-encoded part ID. Face-centre queries produce the mesh labels. Right: a text-conditioned DiT generates the field’s latent representation from the geometry latent (green) and encoded text tokens. A full decomposition (blue) and a selective input (red) differ only in the control prompts, and in the selective case an explicit background item absorbs parts that belong to the background. Each part item is visualized in the color corresponding to the input prompts.

CubePart allocates and generates an independent latent geometry for each requested item, whereas our method retains the input surface and predicts its face labels. The displayed cases illustrate the resulting differences in partition and surface preservation. Top: At the fine level, CubePart fails to generate the waist, leaving the chest and pelvis disconnected; in contrast, our method continuously labels the original surface. Middle: The coarse prompt requests both arms and both legs as separate items, but CubePart erroneously merges them (purple). Our method correctly separates the arms (green) and legs (grey). At the fine level, CubePart generates the right hand as fragmented specks. Bottom: CubePart handles the coarse request successfully but its fine-grained output (armour plates, brackets, hoses) becomes a cloud of fragments. Our method instead assigns labels on the unchanged input surface, yielding a complete partition without post-processing.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on PartObjaverse-Tiny. Left of the divider, -GT denotes ground-truth conditions (our annotated prompt; SegviGen’s rendered guidance map), and -Auto denotes automatic conditions (our planner-completed names; SegviGen’s predicted map). Right of the divider, baselines use their native inputs. As shown, baselines suffer from missing occluded parts (SegviGen), over-segmenting along geometric seams (PartField, P3-SAM, SAMPart3D), or imprecise boundaries (Find3D). FLEXPART avoids these issues, effectively following the semantic intent from GT.

papers.abstract: End-to-end visual generation with pixel-space loss has recently achieved competitive performance without the need for learned image tokenizers. In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced "lily"), a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 $\to$ 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at https://suchiragarwal.com/lilie.
authors: Suchir Agarwal, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Ziyu Chen, Kyle Sargent, Juan Carlos Niebles, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Motivation: Pixel loss may provide a poorer training signal than supervision aligned with image semantics and language.
Method: Train an invertible normalizing-flow image encoder jointly with a vision-language model to recover captions from noised features.
Application: Use the encoder to define a language-informed loss for JiT text-to-image models.
Result: On GPIC, LILIE loss reduces gFD from 66.84 to 53.01 versus a pixel-only baseline.
Scope: The approach is evaluated on the GPIC dataset; broader applicability is not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: While data collection for model training is relatively easy, curating high-quality datasets from large collections is inherently challenging. Coreset estimation methods address this problem by identifying the best data subsets to train models on. However, existing approaches often require proxy model training, extensive annotations, or task-specific tailoring. Unsupervised alternatives typically exploit geometric properties in foundation model feature spaces, but are limited to pairwise image-to-image comparisons or comparisons against a fixed subset. We introduce CoreDNA, an unsupervised, task-agnostic coreset estimation approach that pools neuron activations from vision foundation models into per-image and per-dataset distributions. By comparing each image's distribution to the dataset-level distribution, CoreDNA can capture both low-level visual structure and high-level semantic information across layers. We find that high-quality samples concentrate in the tails of the last layer's activation statistics, which we validate by relating them to training-based coreset methods. Building on these findings, we develop a computationally efficient selection mechanism to construct task-agnostic, high-quality coresets for selective annotation and model training. Across image classification, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and imitation learning for end-to-end driving and mobile manipulation, CoreDNA matches or outperforms the state of the art, demonstrating unprecedented generalization across perception and action tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of compact activation-based representations for data selection.
authors: Julia Hindel, Benjamin Ramtoula, Kyuhwan Yeon, Nick Heppert, Paul Newman, Daniele De Martini, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses the challenge of curating large datasets without extensive annotations, proxy training, or task-specific design.
Pools neuron activations from vision foundation models into per-image and dataset-level distributions across layers.
Finds that valuable samples tend to lie in the tails of final-layer activation statistics.
Provides an efficient coreset selection method for annotation and model-training subset construction.

papers.abstract: Obstacle avoidance for autonomous quadrotors in cluttered environments remains challenging, especially when both dense static obstacles and moving obstacles are present. Existing methods are often tailored to either static or dynamic settings, which always limit their adaptability across diverse environments. This paper presents TransNav, a transformer-based end-to-end navigation method for quadrotor obstacle avoidance in both static and dynamic environments. TransNav employs a patch-based point-cloud encoding scheme that combines local feature extraction with global contextual modeling, enabling compact yet informative environment representation. The method integrates perception and navigation in a single architecture and directly predicts a finite-horizon action sequence, from which the first action is executed. Moreover, we develop an unsupervised learning strategy by incorporating a lightweight point-mass dynamics model, which directly optimizes trajectory-level costs over the predicted sequence through numerical gradient propagation. Thus, the policy can be efficiently trained without expert demonstrations. Simulation and real-world experiments show that the proposed method achieves strong performance in dense static environments and competitive obstacle-avoidance capability in dynamic scenarios, while maintaining low inference cost for onboard deployment.
authors: Jianghan Zhu, Zhuo Li, Yanjun Zhang, Jian Sun
bullets: Targets the challenge of handling dense static and dynamic obstacles within one navigation method.
Uses patch-based point-cloud encoding to combine local geometric features with global environmental context.
Predicts a finite-horizon action sequence and executes its first action for closed-loop control.
Trains unsupervised with a lightweight point-mass dynamics model and trajectory-level cost optimization.
Simulation and real-world tests show strong static-environment performance, competitive dynamic avoidance, and low onboard inference cost.

papers.abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.
authors: Dominic Maggio, Lorenzo Shaikewitz, Aryan Naveen, Kris Hauser, Luca Carlone
bullets: Addresses the gap between foundation-model-based 3D mapping and complete robot autonomy pipelines.
Integrates FOUND-IT with a mobile manipulator using a single uncalibrated camera.
Supports object change detection, multiple mapping sessions, navigable-path reasoning, and grasping for scene rearrangement.
Reports rigorous on-robot experiments assessing the system’s effectiveness and limitations.
The scope is constrained by the limitations of monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction.

papers.abstract: Latent world models learn action-conditioned state transitions in a compact representation space, providing a predictive model for visual planning and control. However, planning with these models typically requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences. We propose to replace this online search with a goal-conditioned inverse model that directly predicts actions from current and goal observations. A key challenge is that action prediction alone neither ensures that goal representations encode action-relevant information nor that predicted actions are consistent with the learned latent prediction model. We introduce Hindsight Inverse JEPA Planning (HIJP), a search-free framework that addresses both aspects during training. HIJP relabels future observations along offline trajectories as goals, providing action supervision across multiple temporal horizons. By retaining gradients through the goal representations, this supervision directly shapes the visual representation. HIJP further feeds predicted actions into the latent predictor model and aligns the resulting next-state representations with encoded successor observations, enforcing action-transition consistency. At inference time, the inverse dynamics model and latent predictor models are applied alternately to generate multi-step action sequences without online search. Across four visual control tasks, HIJP achieves 86.8% overall success and a 1.9-16.5x planning speedup over search-based planning.
authors: Guanchen Du, Jinhao Du, Yanpeng Sun, Shan Zhang, Na Zhao, Zechao Li
bullets: Latent world-model planning usually requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences.
HIJP uses future observations as hindsight goals to train an inverse model across multiple planning horizons.
Gradients through goal representations make visual features more action-relevant.
Predicted actions are checked against latent state transitions to enforce inverse-model/world-model consistency.
Across four visual control tasks, HIJP reaches 86.8% overall success and provides a 1.9–16.5× planning speedup over search-based methods.

papers.abstract: Dense assistance methods such as speculative decoding repeatedly verify draft tokens with a target model, keeping target computation coupled to generation. We study sparse collaborative decoding, where a draft model generates most tokens and a target model is invoked only for short corrective segments. The key problem is deciding when to call the target. We show that local uncertainty is a weak trigger: entropy, negative log-likelihood, logit margin, top-$k$ mass, and velocity features give near-chance failure prediction, with AUC 0.50-0.53. In contrast, aggregate trajectory-shape features over the draft confidence path reach AUC 0.86 using a lightweight logistic predictor trained only from draft correctness labels. This induces a trigger-timing tradeoff: early calls have more leverage but weaker evidence, while later calls have stronger evidence but less ability to redirect the trajectory. Used online, learned sparse collaborative decoding improves over the best open-loop schedule by +5.3 to +20.0 accuracy points across five GSM8K draft-target pairs. On MATH-500, it gains 7.0-13.5 points when early prediction and target competence align, but loses when either is weak. On StrategyQA, it improves over open-loop by 5.0-8.3 points, showing transfer beyond arithmetics.
authors: Amit Ranjan Trivedi, Sruthikesh Surineni, Kyong Ho Lee, Mohit Mittal, Steven Li, Rex Hill
bullets: Sparse decoding uses a draft model for most tokens and invokes the target only for short corrective segments.
Local uncertainty features are weak failure predictors (AUC 0.50–0.53), while aggregate confidence-trajectory features reach AUC 0.86.
A lightweight logistic predictor, trained only on draft correctness labels, learns when to trigger target-model intervention.
Online triggering improves over the best open-loop schedule by 5.3–20.0 accuracy points on five GSM8K pairs and transfers to MATH-500 and StrategyQA.
Performance depends on timing and alignment between early prediction quality and target-model competence; gains can disappear when either is weak.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Trajectory-triggered sparse collaborative decoding. A draft model generates most of the reasoning trajectory, while a stronger target model is invoked only at selected points. Figure 9: Target intervention behavior matters beyond target-only accuracy. Shorter target continuations are associated with better closed-loop accuracy. Stronger target-only models can degrade closed-loop performance when their continuations are long or overwrite the draft context.

Figure 10: Draft tuning for target followability. Left: layer-wise sensitivity on GSM8K, where gains concentrate in early-to-mid layers, suggesting stabilization near the target-to-draft handoff. Right: layer-wise sensitivity on SVAMP, where gains peak in middle layers, suggesting improved longer-horizon retention of injected trajectories.

Figure 3: Intervention leverage decreases with decoding position. We perturb the draft prefix at different token positions and measure whether the final decoded sequence changes. Single-token and eight-token perturbations are most influential early and decay with position. Eight-token perturbations raise the absolute flip rate but preserve the same trend. This supports the trigger-timing tradeoff: early calls have greater influence but weaker evidence, while later calls have stronger evidence but less ability to redirect.

Figure 2: Time-frequency view of trajectory instability. Wavelet transforms of logit-margin-derived signals show elevated mid-frequency oscillations for incorrect trajectories, consistent with unresolved competition between reasoning paths before commitment.
