papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling. Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-$alpha$ further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM also outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High. On three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for $pi_{0.5}$ and 25% for Fast-WAM.

papers.abstract: Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order, handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in 19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program, model its memory exactly from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in all our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse "trap" lower bounds, each computable with $O(n^2)$ minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out wrapper graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. So most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even at treewidth two, encodes knapsack exactly on series-parallel graphs, and is solvable exactly on bounded treewidth. It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers the peak by 5.2-6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.
authors: Ivan Fomin, Ivan Koryabkin, Boris Sheludko
bullets: Compiler regeneration often fails to realize predicted memory savings and can worsen memory use or alter GPU results.
Profiling generated code and reordering its statements exactly matches modeled peak memory and preserves bitwise-identical outputs on CPU.
Forward and reverse minimum-cut bounds certify optimal schedules for most tested graphs, including all studied microcontroller-class models.
Branching networks benefit most from reordering; compiled training saves up to 7.6%, while DeepLabV3 improves by 10.0%.
Selective recomputation is strongly NP-hard under fixed caps, but reduces peak memory by 5.2–6.1% on ReDimNet with under 0.4% extra MACs.

papers.selection_reason: Exact peak-memory scheduling and recomputation limits for inference directly target memory-efficient AI.
papers.title: Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust: Exact Realization, Certified Optimality, and the Limits of Recomputation for Inference
papers.tldr: The paper presents a reliable, certifiably optimal operator-ordering approach for reducing inference peak memory, while showing when recomputation is useful or computationally hard.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing inference-time visual token pruning methods often irreversibly remove low-ranked tokens, although the set of visual tokens receiving high query-conditioned attention can change across decoder depth. Recoverable routing preserves skipped tokens for later reconsideration, but re-admits them with stale representations after bypassing intermediate transformations. We further find that replacing stale re-admitted states with their current-depth oracle states from a full-token reference trajectory substantially improves grounding performance. We therefore propose CatchUp, a training-free framework for depth-aware visual-token re-admission. CatchUp repeatedly re-evaluates query-conditioned visual relevance, processes only selected visual tokens through each decoder interval, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission. Upon re-admission, CatchUp approximates missed representation evolution using reference-to-current transition signals from semantically and spatially related visual tokens. Across three referring-expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention in both benchmark groups at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets. At a 64-token budget with 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, CatchUp retains 92.17% of the full model's performance on average across six multimodal benchmarks while reducing end-to-end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp
authors: Eunju Park, Uiwon Hwang
bullets: Problem: Irreversible visual-token pruning can discard tokens that become relevant later, while recoverable routing may re-admit them with stale representations.
Method: Re-evaluates query-conditioned token relevance at each decoder interval, processes only selected tokens, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission.
Key idea: Uses transition signals from semantically and spatially related tokens to approximate the representation evolution missed by skipped tokens.
Results: Across three grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets.
At 64 tokens, it uses 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, retains 92.17% of full-model performance on average, and reduces end-to-end latency by 8.0%.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free depth-aware visual token re-admission for efficient LVLMs; directly targets token pruning/eviction and MLLM efficiency.
papers.title: CatchUp: Depth-Aware Re-Admission of Visual Tokens for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: CatchUp is a training-free method that efficiently prunes and later re-admits visual tokens across decoder depth while approximating their updated representations, preserving LVLM performance with lower latency.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.
authors: Yong Wang, Boyu Shen, Xinwei Zhang, Yizheng Li, Keyuan Luo
bullets: VLA models struggle with long-horizon tasks because limited temporal context hinders the accumulation and reuse of experience.
It proposes a taxonomy based on memory scope and persistence, covering five established paradigms and one emerging frontier.
Representative systems are compared by memory characteristics, architectural complexity, and open-source maturity.
The survey identifies a trade-off: greater architectural complexity generally corresponds to lower open-source maturity.
Key open challenges include efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolution.

papers.tldr: This survey organizes memory mechanisms for long-horizon robotics VLA models and highlights the trade-offs and challenges involved in building lifelong embodied agents.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. BM25 retrieval supplies local context; subsequent passes expose intermediate drafts, missing-information markers, follow-up queries, and optional claim--evidence mappings. These artifacts inform retrieval, revision, clarification, or abstention decisions. We examine the architecture through qualitative, trace-based case studies in two fully synthetic settings: emergency medical services and Munich-Sim, an emergency-operations simulation. Local prototype runs on an Apple M4-family laptop with 128 GB memory illustrate source-labeled documentation, explicit gap marking, and structured dispatch-style outputs. The traces also reveal provenance-assignment errors, incomplete evidence coverage, and unsafe assumptions that remain possible despite prompting constraints. These cases demonstrate report-level inspectability and local execution, not comparative superiority, hallucination reduction, clinical validity, or operational safety. The architecture separates retrieval and control from the model interface, but behavior across different models remains to be evaluated. SRCoT is a research proof of concept requiring human review, with its principal contribution lying in an inspectable control procedure rather than a new model.
authors: Fabian Broszio, Michael Hoffmann, Adrian Paschke
bullets: Addresses unsupported or operationally conflicting LLM outputs.
Separates environment state, persistent knowledge, experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores.
Uses BM25 retrieval and reflective passes to identify gaps, generate follow-up queries, map claims to evidence, and choose revision, clarification, or abstention.
Qualitative trace-based case studies in synthetic emergency-services settings show inspectable source labeling, gap marking, and structured outputs.
Traces still reveal provenance errors, incomplete evidence, and unsafe assumptions; comparative effectiveness and safety remain unevaluated.

papers.title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs
papers.tldr: SRCoT is a local, inspectable Retrieve–Reflect–Revise pipeline that uses provenance-labeled evidence to guide LLM generation, while still requiring human review.

papers.abstract: Native language identification (NLI) infers a non-native speaker's first language (L1) from their second language (L2) production. We investigate a token probability approach that scores each text sample as a continuation of a prompt prefix specifying a candidate L1, then predicts the candidate with the highest score. We evaluate our approach using Llama 3.1 8B and 70B on three datasets: TOEFL9, Write and Improve 2024, and BULATS-L1. We compare its performance with previous prompting-based classification approaches. Token-probability scoring substantially improves on direct classification, particularly with the 8B model, while the 70B model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all datasets. Our results indicate that pretrained LLMs' token probabilities contain information useful for distinguishing L1 backgrounds from L2 English production.
authors: Ahmet Yavuz Uluslu, Mark Gales, Kate Knill, Gerold Schneider
bullets: Frames NLI as choosing the candidate L1 with the highest token-probability score.
Evaluates Llama 3.1 8B and 70B on TOEFL9, Write and Improve 2024, and BULATS-L1.
Token-probability scoring substantially outperforms direct prompting-based classification, especially with the 8B model.
The 70B model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three datasets.
Findings suggest LLM token probabilities encode information about L1 backgrounds in L2 English.

papers.abstract: Spatial context prediction requires visual grounding and spatial reasoning to identify vacant regions relative to objects in a scene. Spatial relationships and physical constraints remain challenging for large vision-language models (VLMs). Recursive reasoning has demonstrated strong performance on discrete and abstract reasoning tasks, motivating its use for improving spatial context prediction in natural images. Weight sharing enables higher accuracy with a small trainable parameter count. We introduce Spatial-TRM, a compact recursive model with frozen vision-language features, a convex region decoder, and just 11.2M trainable parameters. This weight-tied reasoner supports six spatial relationships, three reference frames, and open-vocabulary anchor objects. On the RoboSpatial-Home benchmark, Spatial-TRM achieves 29.51% context accuracy, a gain of 9.02 percentage points (44.0% relative) over a separately trained single-step model with the same parameter count. Including the frozen encoders, the model has 877.8M total parameters, approximately $15\times$ fewer than the reported 13B size of RoboPoint. These results show that repeated refinement improves spatial context prediction from pretrained vision-language features at a fixed trainable parameter count on this benchmark.
authors: Wajeeha Tahir, Anna Tegon, Lionnus Kesting, Gamze \.Islamo\u{g}lu, Krist\'of Karacs, Luca Benini, Thorir Mar Ingolfsson
bullets: Targets spatial context prediction: identifying vacant regions relative to objects while handling spatial relationships and physical constraints.
Combines frozen vision-language features, a convex region decoder, and a compact 11.2M-parameter recursive reasoner.
Supports six spatial relationships, three reference frames, and open-vocabulary anchor objects.
Reaches 29.51% context accuracy on RoboSpatial-Home, improving by 9.02 percentage points over a same-size single-step model.
The reported gains are demonstrated on RoboSpatial-Home and do not establish broader generalization beyond this benchmark.

papers.abstract: Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse, viewpoint-dependent observations. When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering approach or verification actions. We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence (FCP). We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and revises each candidate through Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states. The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate: rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90--6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.
authors: Kaibo Yang, Xingyu Wu, Enze Zhu, Yajie Chai, Xuyang Li, Jiahui Cui, Xiaoxuan Liu, Lei Wang, Zhan Chen
bullets: Addresses false candidate persistence, where disproven targets continue triggering approach or verification actions.
Associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and tracks Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states.
Binds waypoints to their source candidates so rejecting a candidate invalidates stale goals; conservative reactivation handles temporary occlusion.
Across benchmark splits, improves success rate by 2.90–6.31 points while reducing behavioral FCP and post-contradiction travel.
Real-world DJI scenarios show improved task success and behavioral reliability with a low false-rejection rate.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through cooperation. Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills. CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded execution parameters. Physical verification evaluates each executed transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors. Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end success. Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and contact stability. These results support executable coordination as a practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under shared physical constraints.
authors: Zicheng Liu, Haochen Wu, Jiawei He, Suyun Zhao, Huan Yang, Cheng Chi, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses the gap between high-level multi-robot planning and adapting coordination when physical execution deviates from intent.
Represents coordination as code over fixed motor skills, including motion primitives, objectives, temporary roles, and bounded parameters.
Uses verifier-guided evolution: failed transitions trigger revision from an accepted checkpoint, while verified experience informs later decisions.

In simulations with two Unitree G1 robots transporting a payload through constrained corridors, all tested multimodal backbones achieved some end-to-end successes, completing 8 of 15 base runs overall.
The approach remains limited by motion precision and contact stability.

papers.abstract: Recent diffusion models have advanced image-conditioned video generation, but their accessibility raises risks of unauthorized manipulation. Image immunization has emerged as a promising defense for Image-to-Video (I2V) protection, yet existing methods often rely on degrading visual quality or temporal coherence. In this work, we revisit I2V immunization as reducing source-content preservation, shifting the focus from output degradation to weakening source-conditioned content propagation. To this end, we propose I2V-DETACH, an image immunization method that prevents unauthorized I2V generation through source grounding detachment. I2V models preserve source content by propagating source-image cues into video latents during denoising. Accordingly, I2V-DETACH disrupts this process in two complementary ways: it suppresses source-video grounding to reduce source cue propagation, and strengthens intra-video interactions to shift denoising toward video-side dynamics with reduced reliance on the source image. To obtain informative optimization signals, we initialize auxiliary video latents with source-oriented states that remain within the source-conditioned generation regime while deviating from source-preserving trajectories. Extensive experiments across diverse diffusion architectures show that I2V-DETACH substantially reduces source-content preservation, improves over prior immunization methods, and exhibits strong black-box transferability.
authors: Chanhui Lee, Yeonghwan Song, Yewon Kang, Jeany Son
bullets: Targets source-content preservation, avoiding reliance on visual-quality or temporal-coherence degradation.
Suppresses source–video grounding to weaken propagation of image cues into video latents.
Strengthens intra-video interactions so denoising relies more on video dynamics than the source image.
Uses source-oriented auxiliary video latents to generate informative optimization signals.
Experiments across diverse diffusion architectures show reduced source preservation, improvement over prior immunization methods, and strong black-box transferability.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer questions about whole images well, yet they still struggle with fine-grained region understanding. A key reason is that text-only supervision never specifies which regions support an answer. To close this gap, we present Xiaomi-Lens-0, a 4B MLLM built on Qwen3.5 that predicts masks from its own visual representations. Specifically, a lightweight decoder combines vision-encoder patch features with visual latents, the language model's mask-token states, so mask supervision reaches the shared backbone without an additional segmentation encoder. Because each latent decodes to a mask, the model can interleave reasoning with region-specific latents and thus think with visual latents, while grounded reasoning traces supervise the regions it visits during chain-of-thought. As a result, across all eight RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg splits, Xiaomi-Lens-0 gains 5.6 points on average over Qwen3.5 in referring comprehension and achieves the highest segmentation cIoU among compared models. Moreover, it surpasses Qwen3.5 across all perception benchmarks. Homepage: \href{https://seerray-lab.github.io/Xiaomi-Lens-0}{this https URL}
authors: Pei Fu, Yike Liu, Yue Sun, Hanmo Wang, Xiuwen Xi, Ruoceng Zhang, Shaojie Zhang, Chao Jiang, Hang Li, Bingrui Liu, Zhenbo Luo, Heng Qu, Changjian Xu, Ming Xu, Jian Luan
bullets: Addresses the gap between strong whole-image question answering and weak region-level understanding caused by insufficient region-grounded supervision.
Uses a lightweight decoder that combines vision patch features, visual latents, and mask-token states to predict region masks without a separate segmentation encoder.
Supports region-specific visual latents and grounded reasoning traces, allowing reasoning to reference and supervise the regions it visits.
Improves referring comprehension by an average of 5.6 points over Qwen3.5 across eight RefCOCO-family splits and achieves the highest reported segmentation cIoU among compared models.

papers.abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods detect reasoning faithfulness from model outputs or static activations, but are limited in explaining how unfaithfulness develops during generation. We introduce VERITAS to verbalise the model's computation: how different reasoning anchors emerge, transfer across layers, and surface in the output. VERITAS adopts the layer-wise Jacobian projection to produce a verbalised account of the model's internal reasoning evolution at each generated CoT token. By training a classifier on the extracted features along the traces, we show that these structured features provide insightful perspectives on how and where reasoning diverges toward unfaithfulness. Experiments on four datasets from FaithCoT-Bench and BonaFide show that VERITAS achieves a significant performance gain over LLM-as-Judge, with a 28.4% gain in balanced accuracy, and an average improvement of 16.0% over activation probing. Further analysis shows VERITAS can be generalised to different datasets and model architectures. Our work shows that verbalising model computation provides a richer and more interpretable lens on CoT faithfulness, moving beyond detection toward a mechanistic understanding of how reasoning fails.
authors: Yujing Wang, Yulan He, Wenya Wang, Hanqi Yan
bullets: Addresses the limited interpretability of CoT faithfulness methods based on outputs or static activations.

Across four FaithCoT-Bench and BonaFide datasets, improves balanced accuracy by 28.4% over LLM-as-Judge and 16.0% on average over activation probing.
Generalises across datasets and model architectures, supporting mechanistic analysis of reasoning failures.

papers.abstract: We present LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300, a policy that combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a learned binary state-reward scorer. At inference, the policy samples four action chunks, predicts the future latent features and robot state for each, and executes the candidate with the highest predicted-state reward logit. Predictions therefore influence the actions sent to the environment. The evaluated system uses a 16-step prediction horizon and keeps all three components frozen during evaluation. In the local evaluation on 50 RoboCasa 1.0.1 tasks in the pretrain kitchen split, with 50 episodes per task, the system records 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) in the historical self-trained GR00T-N1.5 baseline. The observed difference is 26 successes, or 1.04 percentage points. The atomic group improves from 141/900 to 150/900. Separately, the RoboCasa maintainers re-evaluated the submission and reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%) across 50 tasks, with leaderboard rates of 48.3%, 16.3%, and 3.1% for Atomic-Seen, Composite-Seen, and Composite-Unseen. The local and official results are reported separately; their difference is not attributed to a model improvement. Recorded local audits identify 212,700 changed environment-input chunks, including 28,223 in atomic tasks. We describe the actual training stages, implemented inference mechanism, evaluation provenance, and public reproduction entrypoints. These results document an active prediction-and-selection system and a positive historical difference.

papers.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.
authors: Guodong Du, Wanyu Lin
bullets: Addresses fragmented training data, multi-task interference, and conflicts caused by conventional model merging in VLA models.
Uses a nested hypernetwork conditioned on the target task to generate adaptive action-expert parameters alongside a frozen base VLA.
Stores task-specific compressed VLM residuals separately for flexible skill reuse and storage efficiency.
Across MetaWorld, ManiSkill, and CALVIN, it outperforms the strongest merging baseline by 41 percentage points on average.
Matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 percentage point on ManiSkill and substantially narrows the gap on CALVIN.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Architecture of the nested hypernetwork Gϕ. Patches are addressed by (ptype, layer, patch_h, patch_w) and mapped to four per-task patch embeddings (patch path). The task id m is mapped to a task embedding and processed by a lightweight task encoder (2D convolutions plus average pooling) into a single task feature ftask. ftask is broadcast across all patches and concatenated with the patch embeddings, then passed through a shared FC trunk augmented with a per-task low-rank LoRA path (LoRA path). The trunk output is decoded by a multihead output module that allocates one fully-connected projection per task (multi-head path) into a flat patch prediction. The precomputed action-expert mask MA m and global rescale α produce τ̂Am = α · Gϕ(m)⊙MA m; the compressed VLM update is retained separately.

Figure 2: NestedVLA pipeline. (1) Skill acquisition: each task is fine-tuned independently from the same base Θ0 and the resulting task vector τm is compressed into a sparse skill zm = α · τm ⊙Mm via drop-and-rescale. (2) Skill consolidation: a single nested hypernetwork Gϕ is trained against the action-expert portions of {zm} with a multi-task masked MSE loss. (3) Skill generation: at inference, querying Gϕ with task id m generates the action-expert update; the corresponding compressed VLM update is retrieved and both compose with the frozen base.

Figure 1: Motivation and overview of NestedVLA. (a) Model merging combines independently fine-tuned VLA weights into a shared model, where incompatible updates can impair the source tasks. (b) NestedVLA retains a compressed task-specific VLM update and uses an embedded taskconditioned hypernetwork to generate the action-expert update. Both updates are applied to a shared base to materialize the selected VLA.

papers.abstract: LLM-agent memory selection often uses retrieval rankings based on record relevance or individual influence. Such rankings cannot identify sufficient subsets under redundant or jointly necessary evidence. We study per-decision memory sufficiency: selecting a small subset that preserves full-memory behavior. To separate search error from model error, we introduce JointCoreBench, a benchmark with nine interaction families, six workflow domains, natural-language decisions, and exact sufficient-set oracles, and JointCore, a relevance cost-ordered group-deletion baseline that tests blocks before individual records. On 6,912 exact conditions, cost-ordered JointCore recovers a minimum-cost sufficient set in 100.0% of cases, reduces subset evaluations from 30.00 to 11.13 (62.9%), and achieves 87.8% active-memory savings. Across four 12B-70B model families and 432 tasks per model, its unweighted mean is 10.28 versus 16.00 model queries and 50.6% versus 43.1% minimum-cost recovery relative to cost aware singleton deletion. Both methods preserve full-memory behavior under the deterministic primary interface. Tests with physical deletion, UNKNOWN masks, PENDING sentinels, counterfactual values, and alternative labels identify interface dependent behavior. JointCore is an efficient benchmark baseline; the study does not establish deployment-ready memory compression.
authors: BHVSP Subrahmanyam, Neeraj Choudhary
bullets: Marginal relevance and individual influence miss redundant or jointly necessary evidence needed for per-decision memory sufficiency.
JointCoreBench provides exact sufficient-set oracles across nine interaction families, six workflow domains, and 6,912 exact conditions.
JointCore tests relevance-ordered blocks before individual records, recovering minimum-cost sufficient sets in 100.0% of benchmark cases.
It reduces subset evaluations by 62.9% and achieves 87.8% active-memory savings on the benchmark.
Across four model families, JointCore averages 10.28 queries and 50.6% minimum-cost recovery, but results depend on the memory interface and do not establish deployment readiness.

papers.abstract: Candidate-based end-to-end driving planners reason over a finite set of trajectory hypotheses. However, for sparse planners, a limited candidate set may provide insufficient support for scene-relevant maneuvers, while fixed downstream candidate budgets do not account for prediction uncertainty. To address these challenges, we introduce Expand-and-Prune, a test-time framework that jointly adapts candidate support and capacity without updating learned parameters. The framework expands the native candidate set using semantic driving intent and temporally propagated predictions and then uses uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores to adaptively prune the resulting candidates. Across four heterogeneous candidate-based planners and four benchmarks, Expand-and-Prune consistently improves planning performance. It achieves state-of-the-art results on LangAuto, increasing the Driving Score from 68.2 to 75.9, while providing further improvement on Bench2Drive, Fail2Drive, and NAVSIMv2, with particularly strong improvements in out-of-distribution scenarios. Moreover, in its full instantiation, 72.5% of selected trajectories originate from the newly introduced intent-guided or temporal candidates, confirming that candidate-space expansion provides useful hypotheses beyond those generated natively by the planner. The code is available at https://github.com/iis-esslingen/Expand-and-Prune.
authors: Fabian Schmidt, Karol Fedurko, Markus Enzweiler, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses sparse candidate sets and fixed candidate budgets that may miss relevant maneuvers or ignore prediction uncertainty.
Expands candidates using semantic driving intent and temporally propagated predictions.
Adaptively prunes candidates based on uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores.
Improves planning across four planners and four benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in out-of-distribution scenarios.
On LangAuto, raises Driving Score from 68.2 to 75.9; 72.5% of selected trajectories come from newly added candidates in the full method.

papers.abstract: A common way to make language models and agents more accurate is to spend more compute at inference time: generate many candidate solutions and submit the one a verifier prefers. Success then requires that some candidate is correct and that the verifier picks it. The first grows predictably with the number of samples; the second does not, because real verifiers (unit tests, majority votes, LLM judges, reward models) accept wrong answers, reject right ones, and make correlated mistakes. With a fixed budget, a practitioner must decide how many samples to draw, which models to draw them from, and how much to spend on verification, and today these choices are made by rules of thumb. We introduce SPLIT, which makes them from a small labelled pilot. It rests on an exact formula for the probability of submitting a correct answer under accept/reject and top-score selection that accounts for varying task difficulty, blind spots shared across models, and correlated repeated verifier calls. SPLIT fits the formula by empirical Bayes and uses it to plan budgets on unseen tasks. Across seven benchmarks spanning math, science QA, code and software-engineering agents, 26 models, 175 agent systems and six kinds of real verifiers, all from public releases, SPLIT lands within 0.02-0.8 percentage points of the best allocation in hindsight, while every fixed rule we test loses at least 2.5 points in some setting. Regret depends only on how well SPLIT ranks configurations, and it stays near-optimal under compute, price and latency costs and online. The formula also explains when asking more LLM judges lowers precision. As a forecaster far beyond the pilot, SPLIT beats power-law fitting when the verifier caps success, and we report where it loses.
authors: Srinivasan Iyengar
bullets: Test-time accuracy depends on both generating a correct candidate and having the verifier select it; real verifiers can make correlated false accepts and rejects.
SPLIT fits an exact success-probability formula with empirical Bayes, modeling task difficulty, shared model blind spots, and repeated-verifier correlations.
It plans sample counts, model mixtures, and verification effort for unseen tasks under compute, price, latency, and online constraints.
Across seven benchmarks, SPLIT came within 0.02–0.8 percentage points of the hindsight-best allocation; fixed rules lost at least 2.5 points in some settings.
The analysis identifies when additional LLM judging reduces precision and when SPLIT loses as a long-range forecaster.

papers.selection_reason: Optimal allocation of test-time compute under imperfect verifiers is a meaningful efficiency contribution for LLM inference.
papers.title: Sample, Mix, or Verify? Allocating Test-Time Compute under Imperfect Verifiers
papers.tldr: SPLIT uses a small labelled pilot to allocate test-time sampling and verification compute effectively despite imperfect, correlated verifiers.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing high-quality, renderable 3D scenes from long videos is essential for robotic perception and embodied intelligence. Many feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction methods rapidly predict 3D scenes from a small set of images, but extending them to longer sequences presents two bottlenecks: jointly processing all views increases GPU memory requirements, while accumulating pixel-aligned predictions redundantly represents the same surfaces and increases storage and rendering costs. We present LonGaussian, a streaming feed-forward framework that reconstructs compact, globally renderable Gaussian scenes from long image sequences with known intrinsics and unknown camera poses. Built on a pretrained streaming 3D reconstruction backbone, LonGaussian decodes long-context geometric features into dense Gaussians. Within each chunk, multi-frame point tracks link repeated observations of the same surface and guide a learned merger to consolidate the corresponding Gaussian predictions. Rendered-depth consistency filtering further suppresses Gaussians from other chunks that incorrectly occlude locally reconstructed surfaces. On DL3DV and RealEstate10K benchmarks, LonGaussian improves novel-view rendering quality while using substantially fewer Gaussians than the evaluated feed-forward baselines.
authors: Zhoufeng Xie, Guanjun Wu, Shuai Zhang, Xinggang Wang, Wenyu Liu
bullets: Addresses memory growth and redundant Gaussian storage in long-context feed-forward 3D reconstruction.
Uses a pretrained streaming reconstruction backbone to decode geometric features into dense Gaussians from images with known intrinsics and unknown poses.
Links repeated surface observations within each chunk using multi-frame point tracks to guide learned Gaussian merging.
Applies rendered-depth consistency filtering to remove Gaussians that incorrectly occlude locally reconstructed surfaces.
On DL3DV and RealEstate10K, improves novel-view rendering quality with substantially fewer Gaussians than evaluated feed-forward baselines.

papers.abstract: Small-to-large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. We present a systematic evaluation of confidence-based routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 model, dataset, language, and scale configurations and 42,288 predictions. We compare global confidence routing with random routing, equal-quota confidence routing, and an oracle upper bound. Confidence identifies beneficial escalations on the Belebele reading comprehension and SIB-200 topic classification datasets, with mean correction-detection AUCs of 0.612 and 0.705. At 50% escalation, it improves over random routing by 1.40--4.67 percentage points on Belebele and 2.54--5.63 points on SIB-200. In contrast, the mean AUC on the MMLU-ProX-Lite knowledge and reasoning dataset is only 0.510, and routing provides no consistent improvement over random selection because small models often remain highly confident while incorrect. Global confidence routing also creates language escalation gaps up to 30.33 percentage points, whereas equal-quota routing removes this disparity with little aggregate accuracy cost. These results show that confidence routing is task-dependent and can allocate computation unevenly across languages. Code is available at https://github.com/sabbir5622r/multilingual-llm-routing
authors: Md Sabbir Hossen, Anichur Rahman, Pabon Shaha, Airin Afroj Aishi, Andrew H. Sung, Md Shohel Rana
bullets: Evaluates routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 configurations and 42,288 predictions.
Confidence successfully identifies inputs benefiting from escalation on Belebele and SIB-200, outperforming random routing at 50% escalation.
Routing is ineffective on MMLU-ProX-Lite because small models can be confidently wrong.
Global confidence routing produces language escalation gaps of up to 30.33 percentage points.
Equal-quota routing removes language disparities with little aggregate accuracy cost.

papers.abstract: Relational out-of-distribution errors are easy to describe and hard to evaluate cleanly. An image may be natural, a caption may be fluent, and all mentioned objects may be common, yet the caption may describe the wrong relation in the image. Many evaluations intended to test this behavior can be solved without checking the pairing at all, because negatives differ in caption style, template, length, object frequency, or image statistics. We propose counterfactual pairing cycles, a blocked evaluation primitive that reuses the same two images and the same two captions on both sides of the comparison, changing only which image is paired with which caption. This makes image-only, text-only, and additive component shortcuts cancel exactly in finite samples. The same contrast also gives a training loss for relational outlier exposure and a diagnostic for bilinear vision-language scores. Across synthetic controls, GQA, and COCO, cycles separate coarse image-caption matching from directional role-binding failures, while also identifying geometric size relations that remain strongly visible in global features. In a shortcut-contaminated COCO outlier-exposure stress test, a model selected by a near-perfect shortcut validation AUROC retains substantial relational signal but remains below cycle training on exact cycles; cycle training improves CycleAcc from 0.882 to 0.927. The main lesson is simple: to test whether a model understands a pairing, the benchmark should keep the parts fixed, change the pairing, and ask only about coupling. The official implementation is available online.
authors: Yibo Zhou, Yirong Xiang
bullets: Existing relational OOD evaluations can be solved through image-only, text-only, or additive shortcuts.
The proposed blocked cycles reuse two images and two captions, changing only the image–caption assignment so these shortcuts cancel.
The same contrast supports a training loss for relational outlier exposure and diagnoses bilinear vision-language scores.
Experiments on synthetic controls, GQA, and COCO separate coarse matching from directional role-binding failures and reveal persistent global-feature sensitivity to geometric size.
Cycle training improves CycleAcc from 0.882 to 0.927 in a shortcut-contaminated COCO stress test, though performance remains imperfect.

papers.abstract: Small differences between internal representations can shrink or grow as they pass through a Transformer layer, affecting how information is preserved and how sensitive the model is to perturbations. Yet it remains unclear when changes in attention weights can turn a representation difference that would otherwise shrink into one that grows. We develop a \textbf{Mixture-Gated Theory of Anisotropic Representation Dynamics} that separates self-attention into value transport, query gating, and key gating. Our analysis reveals how the geometry of attended representations constrains gating and how interactions between these mechanisms can reverse contraction induced by value transport. We formalize this phenomenon as gating-induced regime switching, where a representation difference contracts under fixed attention routing but expands under full attention. We derive a necessary and sufficient spectral criterion that certifies the existence or absence of switching and identifies switching directions without exhaustive search. Beyond existence, our theory characterizes maximum relative switching strength, certifies the severity of contraction that gating can overcome, and determines the largest dimension of a subspace in which every nonzero direction switches. Experiments across four Transformer architectures validate these predictions through analytical and finite-forward comparisons, revealing distinct and joint query--key gating mechanisms and nontrivial switching subspaces. Our results provide a mechanistic and spectral understanding of how attention routing can alter local representation dynamics.
authors: Nguyen Do, My T. Thai
bullets: Decomposes self-attention into value transport, query gating, and key gating to analyze anisotropic representation dynamics.
Defines gating-induced regime switching: differences that contract under fixed attention routing can expand under full attention.
Derives a necessary-and-sufficient spectral criterion for detecting switching and identifying switching directions without exhaustive search.
Also characterizes switching strength, the contraction gating can overcome, and subspaces where all nonzero directions switch.
Experiments across four Transformer architectures support the theory and reveal distinct, combined query–key gating effects.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Switching across architectures and depths. (a) Median normalized effective switching dimension across seven normalized depths and four Transformer architectures. Normalization uses the projected transport-contractive subspace. (b) Mechanism composition among sampled switching directions. (a) Analytic regime spheres: Two orthographic views (View A and B) of selected spherical slices across four Transformer architectures, colored by their predicted growth regimes. (b) Spatial adjacency graphs: Node sizes indicate regime proportions, and edges represent shared regime boundaries. NC: transport non-contractive; NS: contraction without switching; Q/K: query-/key-driven switching; E: either pathway sufficient; J: joint query–key required. Percentages are computed over all sampled sphere directions, rather than only switching directions as in Figure 6(b). Results characterize the selected slices, not the full representation space.

Figure 16: Mechanism composition among projected switching directions. Fractions are pooled over the sampled switching directions within each architecture. Query-only, key-only, joint query–key, and either-pathway-sufficient classes are disjoint under the specified counterfactual tests. Fractions are conditional on full-dynamics switching and are not ambient-space probabilities.

Figure 2: Geometric support and null directions of query gating. Centered attended representations span a subspace Ur, whose dimension may be substantially smaller than the ambient representation dimension. The transformed subspace WQKUr determines which query perturbation directions can influence the attention output through query gating. Perturbations orthogonal to this subspace produce no first-order query-gating change. Consequently, query gating is insensitive to at least d− dim(Ur) independent input directions. The three-dimensional projections provide a schematic visualization of the higher-dimensional geometry.

Figure 3: From self-attention decomposition to gating-induced regime switching. Self-attention induces three local mechanisms: value transport, query gating, and key gating, represented by their corresponding Jacobian components. These components jointly determine directional representation growth through the induced growth operator GM = J⊤MJ −M . The three-dimensional illustration shows how different perturbation directions can exhibit contraction or expansion. Interactions between value transport and attention gating can reverse transport contraction, causing a representation difference to grow under full attention.

Figure 4: Geometric support of query gating. (a) Schematic three-dimensional slice illustrating directions orthogonal to the query-gating support. (b) Analytical response versus support overlap, including near-null directions and the theoretical upper bound. (c) Finite-forward changes in attention weights under fixed-key query perturbations.

Figure 9: Search quality and amortized cost of spectral guidance. (a) Blind random search finds no switch within the tested budget, while oracle-assisted sampling in the transport-contractive subspace finds ordinary switches but misses severe reversals. (b) Spectral preprocessing incurs a one-time setup cost but becomes advantageous for sufficiently many directional evaluations. Total-cost curves are projected from measured setup and throughput timings.

Figure 1: Conceptual illustration of gating-induced regime switching. Two nearby representations initially differ by a small perturbation δzℓ. Under fixed attention weights, value transport contracts this difference. However, a small change in the query can redistribute attention among token representations, introducing an additional gating contribution. When this contribution is sufficiently strong, the full attention computation amplifies the same representation difference rather than suppressing it. The illustration motivates our analysis of how attention routing can reverse transport contraction.

Figure 11: Progressive classification of local switching regimes. Five columns reveal the conditions defining transport non-contraction (blue), persistent contraction (red), joint query–key necessity (cyan), query-only or key-only sufficiency (green or purple), and either-pathway sufficiency (orange). The top and bottom rows apply analytic and finite-forward tests to the same selected directional slice. The classifications concern counterfactual growth signs, not an additive partition of total growth.

Figure 14: Relative strength and absolute contraction severity. (a) Relative switching ratios for the relative optimum and a numerically identified severe switch (logarithmic axis; dashed line at Γ = 1). (b) Fractions of incoming squared magnitude removed by transport for the same directions. The green reference marks τcert ≈ 0.967. The two panels compare different objectives, not two estimates of the same quantity.

Figure 13: Switching spectrum and severity-restricted certification. (a) Ordered eigenvalues of W = C−1/2RC−1/2, shown for comparison with the severity test; the switching boundary is λ = 1. (b) Leading eigenvalue of Wτ0 on subspaces constrained to have transport severity at least τ0. The green reference line indicates a separately computed τcert ≈ 0.967; the displayed orange sweep does not reach that threshold and is not, on its own, the certificate.

Figure 12: Growth margins under pathway ablations. (a) Query gating alone crosses the zerogrowth boundary. (b) Neither query nor key gating alone produces expansion, whereas their joint inclusion does. Bars in each panel evaluate the same perturbation direction under different counterfactual dynamics; dashed lines mark zero growth.

Figure 5: Theory-predicted regime geometry and gating-pathway ablations. (a,b) Analytical and finite-forward regime maps on the same selected directional slice, with exact switching and mechanism-label agreement across the tested directions. (c) Growth-sign boundaries separating the observed regimes. (d) Directional growth under transport-only, single-gating-pathway, and fullattention counterfactuals for representative directions.
Figure 8: Spectral certification. (a) Switching spectrum; (b) relative/absolute reversal severity.

Nested orthonormal probe spaces of dimensions 32, 64, 128, and 256 are evaluated at matched model–prompt–depth operating points. (a) Median projected λmax(W ); (b) median normalized effective switching dimension; (c) median query-sufficient fraction among sampled switches. Shaded regions indicate interquartile ranges across operating points, not confidence intervals or convergence guarantees.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn LLM routing selects a model at every turn before its response is available, yet task success is revealed only when the interaction ends, leaving each intermediate choice without a label of its own. Logged trajectories, however, retain the response each call produced, which exposes what each turn required and how well the chosen model served it, evidence that outcomes alone hide. We introduce RIVET (Response-Informed Value Estimation for Turn-Level Routing), which exploits this post-call evidence during training while keeping routing strictly pre-call at deployment. RIVET jointly trains two value estimators over a shared state-model representation: a deployable Routing Value Estimator that scores candidate models from pre-call information, and a training-only Response-Informed Value Estimator that additionally observes the realized response. Conditioning on the response turns response-induced return variation from residual noise into an observed covariate, and we show that this reduces the leading asymptotic estimation error of the shared representation. On the MINT benchmark, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while using 74.7% less total call cost.
authors: Haotian Yan, Jiaqi Liu, Bingyi Jing, Tianjun Yao
bullets: Multi-turn routing lacks turn-level labels because task success is known only after the interaction ends.
RIVET uses logged responses as training-only evidence while keeping deployment routing strictly pre-call.
It jointly trains a deployable Routing Value Estimator and a response-informed training estimator over shared representations.
Response conditioning reduces estimation error by explaining return variation otherwise treated as noise.
On MINT, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while reducing total call cost by 74.7%.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RIVET separates pre-call deployment from post-call training. Both estimators read the same trainable state–model representation zθ(st,m). The Routing Value Estimator (RVE, deployed) scores every candidate model from pre-call information and makes the routing decision; the Response-Informed Value Estimator (RIVE, training only) additionally conditions on the executed response and shapes the shared representation through its own regression loss. Both estimators regress to the same scalar return target; deployment uses RVE alone.

Figure 1: Intermediate responses reveal what outcomes hide. Three candidate models on a four-turn recommendation task. Each turn demands a different ability (bottom labels), and the response exposes whether the model met it: check and cross mark acceptable and unacceptable responses, and the remaining icons mark responses that are vague, over-deliberated, or needlessly verbose. The green path is the cost-efficient route and switches models across turns. Illustrative; each logged turn observes only the selected model’s response.

Figure 4: Online adaptation on MINT Test-141. Accuracy (left axis) and total test model-call cost in dollars (right axis) after cumulatively adding 35, 70, 105, and 140 online trajectories in batches within a single training run.

Figure 3: Cost-coefficient sensitivity on MINT Test-141. Highlighted settings achieve the highest accuracy (λ = 0.05) and lowest cost (λ = 0.50) among evaluated configurations. Cost denotes total test model-call cost in dollars.

papers.abstract: Jointly reconstructing RGB and X-ray provides new insights by connecting external appearance with internal structure, enabling a more complete understanding of real-world objects than single modality. Yet existing methods train separate models per modality and suffer from redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and loose coupling that limits cross-modal insight discovery. We propose a unified representation in which all Gaussian primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, with only surface-proximal primitives additionally carrying appearance attributes. We perform cross-modal registration through clean multi-view stereo and X-ray geometric proxies instead of aligning two sets of optimized Gaussians, improving alignment stability. We then jointly optimize the unified representation via supervision from both modalities, complemented by a surface-depth consistency loss derived from X-ray geometry to guide RGB reconstruction. Experiments on the InsideOut dataset and our Flower & Insect dataset show that our framework achieves more robust cross-modal alignment, higher RGB rendering quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction, and a more compact representation than maintaining two independent geometries.
authors: Wangze Xu, Chu Zhou, Mae Yamaguchi, Linrui Dai, I-Chao Shen, Takashi Ijiri, Imari Sato
bullets: Addresses redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and weak coupling in separate RGB/X-ray models.
Uses shared geometric Gaussian parameters, with appearance attributes assigned only to surface-proximal primitives.
Registers modalities using multi-view stereo and X-ray geometric proxies rather than separately optimized Gaussian sets.
Jointly optimizes both modalities with an X-ray-derived surface-depth consistency loss guiding RGB reconstruction.
Experiments on InsideOut and Flower & Insect show more robust alignment, better RGB rendering, preserved X-ray reconstruction, and compactness.

papers.abstract: Making a conference poster is visual coding in miniature: an entire paper must be compressed onto a single page, which exercises summarization, visual design, and code implementation at once, using nothing beyond the paper itself. Yet benchmarks for this task in the context of visual coding remain scarce: existing resources are small and annotated only with layout boxes, so evaluation must fall back on VLM-as-judge or human checklists rather than objective render-and-compare, and the generation methods they support design layouts from scratch, leaving human-crafted posters unusable as either a retrievable design library or as verified supervision. We introduce RAP (Reconstruct A Poster), a dataset and benchmark for paper-to-poster generation as a visual coding task. RAP contains 25K+ verified paper-poster pairs from various machine learning conferences held between 2022 and 2026, annotated with a three-level content taxonomy, plus a held-out benchmark of 150 test papers each paired with its human poster. A fully automated derendering pipeline turns each poster into styled HTML/CSS of typed, refillable slots, so every sample is a paper-poster-markup triplet verifiable by rendering against the source poster. The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training-free multi-agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. An online demo is available at https://reconstruct-a-poster.github.io/.
authors: Haonan Han, Yukang Lin, Minliang Lin, Haoxian Tan, Jun-Yan He, Rui Yang, Zhi-Qi Cheng, Jie Hu, Guanglu Wan, Xiu Li

Uses automated derendering to convert posters into styled HTML/CSS with typed, refillable slots, enabling render-and-compare verification.
Supports both retrieval-based inference through PosterRAG and model training with an SFT+RL recipe.
Scope is centered on machine learning conference posters from 2022–2026 and human-crafted layouts.

papers.abstract: Drifting Models generate a sample with a single function evaluation, making them attractive for fast parallel language generation, but their one-step formulation does not support iterative refinement. We propose Recurrent Language Generation via Drifting (ReLaDrift), which uses a shared Drifting Model to generate an initial draft from noise and iteratively refine it in a continuous latent space. We train this recurrence by sampling the number of rounds and applying the drifting loss only at the final round, stopping gradients through preceding rounds so that only one round requires backpropagation. Unlike the one-step Drifting Model, whose accuracy does not improve when iterated, ReLaDrift enables a trade-off between test-time computation and generation quality, as diffusion and flow language models do. On Sudoku Hard and GSM8K, it achieves competitive or superior performance compared with these iterative-generation approaches across a range of inference budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yuki-Ots/ReLaDrift
authors: Yuki Otsuka, Daisuke Oba, Naoaki Okazaki
bullets: Drifting Models generate samples in one function evaluation but cannot benefit from iterative refinement.
ReLaDrift first creates a draft from noise, then repeatedly refines it using a shared model in continuous latent space.
Training samples different recurrence lengths and applies the drifting loss only at the final round, avoiding backpropagation through earlier rounds.
On Sudoku Hard and GSM8K, it performs competitively or better than iterative diffusion and flow language models across inference budgets.
The approach supports adjustable test-time computation while retaining the parallel-generation advantages of drifting models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Accuracy vs. the number of function evaluations (NFE) on Sudoku Hard (top) and GSM8K (bottom). Results use a single generation trajectory and EMA weights, with mean ± standard deviation over three seeds for Sudoku. Models are evaluated at 20,000 updates (Sudoku) and 250,000 updates (GSM8K); sampling settings are detailed in Tables 1 and 3.

Figure 3: GSM8K test accuracy versus the wall-clock time of generating the 1,319 test programs on one H200 (log scale; batches of 64 problems; settings of Table 3). The labels are the NFE; the time of ReLaDrift includes the encoder and the decoder.

papers.abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) play a central role in test-time scaling for large language model (LLM) reasoning. However, PRMs may provide inaccurate process rewards for test-time scaling, which we identify as arising from two sources of uncertainty: (1) \textit{PRM uncertainty} that arises from insufficient supervision data and imperfect PRM training; and (2) \textit{policy uncertainty} that results from the mismatch between the policy to collect supervision data and the policy for test-time scaling, leading to systematic reward overestimation. Previous studies fail to jointly consider both uncertainties. To bridge this gap, we propose BayesianPRM, which treats the process reward as a random variable within a reward hypothesis space and maintains a Bayesian belief over it. Since exact Bayesian inference over the continuous hypothesis space is generally intractable, we discretize the reward hypothesis space with a reward ensemble and introduce two complementary belief updates, each targeting one source of uncertainty: (1) to address PRM uncertainty, we introduce \textit{reliability-aware belief updating} that measures how well each ensemble member explains the supervision data and updates the belief with an amortized belief network optimized by the evidence lower bound (ELBO); and (2) to tackle policy uncertainty, we propose \textit{conservatism-aware belief calibration} which further reweights the belief toward lower rewards to suppress overestimation. These two updates yield a reliability- and conservatism-aware Bayesian belief, whose expectation determines the process reward. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks indicate that BayesianPRM consistently yields more accurate process reward estimates while enhancing test-time scaling performance.
authors: Zhongjian Qiao, Zhixiang Zhou, Jiafei Lyu, Peisong Wang, Qiaosheng Zhang, Siyang Gao, Shuang Qiu

papers.abstract: This paper presents the overview of the runs related to the Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS) and Video Question Answering (VQA) tracks of TRECVID 2025 on behalf of the CERTH-ITI team. For the AVS track, we introduce a two-stage framework built on foundation models. In the first stage, multiple vision-language models (VLMs) encode both the input query, augmented through LLM-generated rephrasings, and the candidate video shots, producing weighted similarity scores for initial retrieval. In the second stage, we utilize a Multimodal-LLM(MLLM)-based reranking module that evaluates the semantic alignment between each shot among the top-N highest-ranked ones and the original query, generating updated relevance scores for reordering these shots. This MLLM-driven reranking significantly improves contextual matching and produces more accurate final rankings without requiring any model training. Regarding the VQA track, we fine-tune an audio-visual MLLM model on the provided TRECVID training dataset and we implement an inference-time scaling technique to enhance the multimodal understanding capabilities of the MLLM. For the open-ended Answer Generation (AG) task, we aggregate multiple model responses per question via a majority vote. The responses are generated with greedy sampling from different random frame subsets of the video and they are ranked based on the number of votes. For the Multiple-Choice (MC) task, instead of voting, we use mean pooling on the logits assigned by the fine-tuned model to each candidate response. Through the combination of fine-tuning and frame subset ensembling we achieve the highest score across 3 metrics in the VQA AG task and the second highest in the VQA MC task.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? We present SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework developed through studies of navigation formulation, data construction, and optimization. At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global-local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation. For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7% and 80.1% success rates on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results show that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.

Trains progressively from imitation learning to DAgger and task-level reinforcement learning.
Achieves 76.7% success on R2R-CE and 80.1% on RxR-CE across multiple MLLM backbones and sizes.

papers.abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) rapidly produces high-quality solutions for problem structures encountered during training, but operational requirements may change after deployment and be communicated in natural language. We propose LangNCO, a framework that compiles instance-specific requirements into structured inference-time interventions for a frozen NCO solver, without changing the pretrained policy's architecture, learned input representation, or parameters. A pretrained LLM serves as a replaceable semantic front end, translating each requirement into a schema-validated domain-specific language (DSL) rule set. A deterministic Rule Executor applies the rules as nonexpansive hard action masks. Because local masking prevents immediate violations but does not ensure that a complete feasible continuation remains reachable, Critical-Offset Decoding extracts rule-referenced critical nodes and reallocates part of a fixed rollout budget to multi-strength biased rollouts. Using controlled task-specific language to isolate solver adaptation from open-ended language robustness, we evaluate a CVRP policy on road closures, time windows, vehicle assignments, visit-order requirements, all pairwise combinations, and twelve additional constraint types. LangNCO achieves 100% feasibility on the four primary datasets with mean reference gaps of 1.63--3.26%, 97.33--100% feasibility when separately generated rules are composed for pairwise constraints, and 98.67% feasibility across the additional constraints. These results demonstrate modular post-training adaptation of a frozen NCO solver through inspectable language-derived rules, without retraining.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, but its outcome-level rewards provide only sparse supervision. On-Policy Distillation offers dense token-level feedback, yet requires a stronger compatible teacher, while on-policy self-distillation relies on hand-designed privileged information. We observe that the MoE architecture itself offers a way to resolve this dilemma, as increasing the activation budget per token exposes latent expert capacity and yields a potentially stronger teacher within the model. However, naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together. We therefore propose MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework following a recovery-then-improvement strategy: we first restore the activation-expanded high-$k$ model and further strengthen it by exploiting its additional active capacity, then reverse the direction of distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back into the original low-$k$ configuration, retaining its inference-time activation budget. Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, MoEvolve improves the initial models by up to $22.2$ domain-average points and outperforms same-budget RLVR baselines by up to $6.5$ points. Notably, the final low-$k$ models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers.
authors: Haoyu Chen, Jun Bai, Yang Liu, Jianfei Zhang, Wenge Rong
bullets: RLVR provides sparse outcome-level supervision, while on-policy distillation offers denser token-level feedback but typically needs a stronger compatible teacher.
Activating more experts per token exposes additional capacity, yet naive expansion harms performance because the experts are not jointly optimized.
MoEvolve first recovers and improves the high-k expanded model, then reverses distillation to strengthen the original low-k model without increasing inference cost.
Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, it improves domain-average performance by up to 22.2 points and exceeds same-budget RLVR baselines by up to 6.5 points.
Final low-k models often outperform their activation-expanded teachers.

papers.abstract: Detecting faithfulness hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for their safe deployment in high-stakes domains. Recent approaches address this by contrasting contextual against parametric knowledge utilization, yet measuring context reliance typically demands noticeable overhead, such as materializing attention maps, running additional forward passes, or training auxiliary probes. In this work, we show that context reliance can be estimated by projecting hidden states onto the dark space - directions that compose weakly with the unembedding matrix. Beyond its recognized function as an initial-token attention sink, we show that this subspace actively mediates context processing, and that its share of hidden-state norm - termed the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR) - provides a direct score of context utilization. Pairing DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields DarkLens, a lightweight faithfulness detector operating strictly within a single forward pass. Evaluated across three QA and summarization benchmarks on six open-weight LLMs (4B-13B parameters), DarkLens matches or outperforms a wide range of baselines without requiring extra forward passes or probe training.
authors: Alexandra Kuleshova, Andrey Volodichev, Daria Kotova, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Context reliance is estimated from the hidden-state norm in weakly unembedded directions, called the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR).
The dark space is shown to mediate context processing, beyond its known role as an initial-token attention sink.
Combining DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields the lightweight DarkLens detector.
Across three QA and summarization benchmarks and six open-weight LLMs, DarkLens matches or outperforms many baselines without extra passes or probe training.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.
authors: Heming Zou, Qi Wang, Yixiu Mao, Yun Qu, Yuyi Guo, Zeyuan Liu, Chenglin Li, Weijie Liu, Saiyong Yang, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Addresses sparse, high-variance credit assignment from terminal-only rewards and policy drift during sequential updates.
Builds a tree of alternative continuations from shared interaction prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit.
Converts credit into a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution based on likelihood ratios to the frozen behavior policy.
Distillation matches policy-gradient behavior near the behavior policy while limiting overshooting toward a finite target.
Improves agentic performance across benchmarks and model scales, including a 4.97-point average accuracy gain over GRPO for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on Deep Research.
