papers.abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.
authors: Junyu Cao, Ruijiang Gao, Maytal Saar-Tsechansky, Mingzhang Yin
bullets: Reframes targeted AI deployment as multiple testing: select individuals whose policy-induced outcomes are unlikely to exceed a user-defined harm threshold.
Uses weighted conformal p-values to address distribution shift between observed behavior and the target policy.
Applies a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure with finite-sample FDR control.
Provides a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee when either the outcome or propensity model is correctly specified.
Synthetic and semi-synthetic studies support the guarantees and demonstrate use as a safety gate for high-risk subgroups.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Conformal Policy Selection, a method for safe AI deployment at inference time using conformal prediction to control false discovery rates for targeted interventions.
papers.title: Conformal Policy Selection: When to Deploy AI Decisions for Targeted Intervention
papers.tldr: Conformal Policy Selection identifies which individuals can safely receive an AI-driven intervention while controlling the false discovery rate of harmful deployments.

papers.abstract: The Levenberg-Marquardt (LMA) algorithm is a widely used nonlinear least-squares solver known for its rapid convergence. For small-scale neural networks, LMA provides better convergence and architectural robustness than first-order optimizers like Adam. However, LMA imposes prohibitive memory and computational costs. These costs are primarily from the Jacobian matrix, whose dimensions scale with both the number of samples and parameters. This bottleneck prevents its use in large-scale neural networks. Recent efforts scale LMA using preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) solvers to avoid materializing the Jacobian. However, PCG only approximates the solution, requiring many network propagations and a task-specific preconditioner. Other studies optimize LMA to reduce costs, but they restrict their methods to specific tasks or network architectures. As a result, LMA remains impractical for training general large-scale neural networks. In this paper, we propose LeMA, a distributed LMA algorithm for large-scale neural network training on multi-GPU platforms. Our contributions are twofold: First, an exact dual formulation of LMA removes the memory dependence on the parameter dimension. Second, a Jacobian sharding strategy computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel to avoid materializing the full Jacobian. For large-scale neural networks, LeMA reduces the memory footprint of LMA from quadratic in the number of parameters to quadratic in the batch size. This makes exact LMA steps feasible for billion-parameter models without approximate PCG solves. Furthermore, for a convolutional neural network with 1,000,022,632 parameters on an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves a 7.97x speedup over a single GPU, corresponding to a 99.7% strong scaling efficiency.
authors: Xianghao Wang, Johan Barth\'elemy, John Taylor
bullets: LMA can converge rapidly but is normally impractical at scale because storing and processing its Jacobian is prohibitively expensive.
LeMA uses an exact dual formulation to eliminate memory dependence on the number of parameters.
It computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel, avoiding materialization of the full Jacobian and approximate PCG solves.
The resulting memory footprint scales quadratically with batch size rather than parameter count.
On an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves 7.97× speedup and 99.7% strong-scaling efficiency for a 1-billion-parameter CNN.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. While implicit reasoning in continuous latent spaces offers a promising alternative, existing methods like Coconut and CODI often rely on fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. In this paper, we propose Sep-Latent, an adaptive implicit reasoning framework that utilizes separator tokens as structural semantic anchors. By introducing an Attention-Decay mechanism, we force the model to aggregate and compress reasoning logic into these anchors during training. We then align explicit and implicit pathways through multi-level distillation across all layers to ensure logical consistency. Crucially, Sep-Latent enables dynamic reasoning depth by adaptively terminating the latent thinking phase based on query complexity. Experimental results on the GSM8k-Aug benchmark show that Sep-Latent achieves an accuracy of 56.8\% with an average of only 5.4 tokens, significantly outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency while narrowing the performance gap with explicit CoT. Further analysis via PCA and symbolic variant testing confirms that our method ensures semantic grounding and exhibits superior robustness to perturbations.
authors: Yinlong Xu, Jianfeng Huang, Zhengdong Zhou, Mingjie Lin, Fuyu Lv, Dan Ou, Hongxia Xu, Jian Wu
bullets: Targets the verbosity and computational cost of explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning, while addressing collapse and fixed-length limitations in prior implicit methods.
Uses separator tokens as semantic anchors, with Attention-Decay to aggregate reasoning and multi-level distillation to align explicit and implicit pathways.
Adaptively terminates latent reasoning according to query complexity rather than using a fixed latent sequence length.
On GSM8k-Aug, reaches 56.8% accuracy using an average of 5.4 tokens, outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency.
PCA and symbolic-variant analyses support semantic grounding and robustness to perturbations; scope is primarily demonstrated on GSM8k-Aug.

papers.abstract: Token merging improves the efficiency of Vision Transformers by combining redundant tokens, but existing methods largely rely on feature similarity to determine which tokens to merge. This criterion is effective for semantic segmentation, yet can fail in instance segmentation, where adjacent objects of the same class often have highly similar features. We identify this failure mode as cross-instance token fusion. We introduce MaskMerge, an instance-aware token merging method that uses coarse intermediate mask predictions to constrain feature-based merging and preserve instance boundaries. We evaluate MaskMerge on two diverse instance segmentation domains characterized by high inter-instance visual similarity: PanNuke and iSAID. Against the SOTA token merging method ALGM, MaskMerge improves mAP from 30.1 to 32.1 on PanNuke while reducing computation from 229 to 153 GFLOPs and running 1.18x faster, and from 33.1 to 36.2 on iSAID while reducing computation from 198 to 182 GFLOPs and running 1.23x faster. Additionally, we also test it on Cityscapes and match ALGM's performance while using fewer FLOPs. The gains also transfer to an MAE pretrained backbone, demonstrating that instance-aware merging enables more aggressive compression when appearance similarity alone cannot reliably preserve object identity.
authors: Bavesh Balaji, Letian Jiang, Alexander Wong, David Clausi, Sirisha Rambhatla
bullets: Feature-similarity merging can blur boundaries between adjacent same-class instances, causing cross-instance token fusion.
MaskMerge constrains feature-based token merging with intermediate mask predictions to preserve instance identities.
On PanNuke and iSAID, it improves mAP while reducing computation and increasing speed relative to ALGM.
On Cityscapes, it matches ALGM’s performance with fewer FLOPs.
The approach also transfers to an MAE-pretrained backbone, supporting more aggressive compression when appearance similarity is ambiguous.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overall pipeline of MaskMerge. Given an input image I ∈ RH×W , the standard patch tokens X0 ∈ RN×D of the image are initially passed through L1 layers of the transformer encoder. After that, similar tokens within a small neighbourhood are merged together using the local merge module resulting in X′ L1 ∈ N′ × D where N ′ < N . After this, the model is passed through Lm transformer layers to get X′ Lm where our object-level adaptive token merging (OLAM) module further reduces tokens from N ′ to N ′′ while preserving instance identities. These reduced tokens are prcoessed by the rest of the transformer encoder layers and then unmerged back to the original dimensions before being fed to the segmentation head.

Figure 2. Cross-instance token fusion in similarity-based token merging. (a) ALGM frequently merges tokens across different nuclei instances, whereas MaskMerge constrains merges within predicted instances. (b) At the same merge budget, ALGM produces 5.7× and 2.9× more cross-instance merges than MaskMerge on PanNuke [17] and iSAID [62], respectively, demonstrating that instance-aware constraints enable safer token reduction.

Figure 1. Throughput–accuracy Pareto frontier on PanNuke [17] across ViT-S, ViT-B, and ViT-L backbones. MaskMerge consistently achieves a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off than ToMe [1] and ALGM [43] across model scales, indicating that instance-aware merging enables more aggressive token reduction while better preserving instance segmentation accuracy.

papers.abstract: Language models generalize beyond their training corpus to learn linguistic phenomena (Patil et al., 2024; Misra and Mahowald, 2024), showing that there exists indirect evidence driving learning. Prior work has inferred that indirect evidence exists without identifying its character or considered specific hypotheses about what it might be. We explore an alternative bottom-up method for identifying indirect evidence. We use influence functions (Koh and Liang, 2017) to measure how individual training sentences affect model predictions in 15 grammatical phenomena from BLiMP (Warstadt et al., 2020). We filter out a phenomenon's direct evidence using hand-constructed rules and take the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences as indirect evidence. This indirect evidence substantially affects learning: retraining without it lowers held-out accuracy more than removing a matched random group for every phenomenon across five models (by a median of 12 points). We characterize the indirect evidence by its similarity to our direct evidence filters: it (partially) meets the filters' structural conditions at a median of 4.7 times the rate of a matched random group. Finally, clustering phenomena by indirect-evidence overlap recovers three of the five BLiMP categories that include multiple phenomena, suggesting that this method can reveal linguistic relationships.
authors: William Dai, Zhenghao Herbert Zhou, Maya Viswanathan, Robert Frank
bullets: Studies indirect evidence for 15 grammatical phenomena from BLiMP across five language models.
Uses influence functions to rank training sentences, removes rule-defined direct evidence, and selects the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences.
Removing this indirect evidence reduces held-out accuracy more than removing matched random sentences for every phenomenon, with a median 12-point drop.
Indirect evidence partially shares structural properties with direct evidence, occurring at a median 4.7× the rate of matched random data.
Clustering phenomena by shared indirect evidence recovers three of five multi-phenomenon BLiMP categories.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates grammatical generalization in LLMs using influence functions to identify 'indirect evidence' driving learning, offering a methodological tool for analyzing LLM behavior.
papers.title: Where's the Indirect Evidence? Investigating Grammatical Generalization with Influence Functions
papers.tldr: Influence functions identify training sentences that indirectly support grammatical generalization, and removing them consistently harms language-model performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP retain zero-shot recognition ability, but their open-world use often requires task-agnostic continual learning: tasks arrive sequentially, past data are unavailable, task identity is unknown, and the backbone cannot be retrained. We argue that this setting fails VLMs through three coupled pressures beyond the stability-plasticity tradeoff: (1) modal-consistency drift, (2) representation-space interference, and (3) per-task capacity shortfall. We propose COMET (Collaborative Mixture-of-Expert Transfer) to resolve these three issues respectively as follows. A frozen teacher provides only a feature reference on a shared image-text pool; Tri-Affinity Distillation preserves image-image, text-text, and image-text geometry; and Student-Aware Cross-Expert Distillation aligns new experts with compatible prior experts so routing errors degrade gracefully. We design COMET to keep capacity and inference separate: a contextual bandit keeps or merges full per-task experts using post-training signals, while a reconstruction router selects sparse experts at test time without teacher semantics. On the X-TAIL benchmark, we show that each proposed component improves continual learning performance. COMET shows that continual vision-language adaptation can preserve multimodal geometry, coordinate accumulated experts, and allocate capacity jointly when feature reference, expert shaping, routing, and capacity control are separated by construction.
authors: Seungyoon Woo, Keonhee Park, Gunhee Kim
bullets: Addresses continual learning with sequential tasks, no past data, unknown task identity, and a frozen backbone.
Uses a frozen teacher and Tri-Affinity Distillation to preserve image-image, text-text, and image-text relationships.
Applies Student-Aware Cross-Expert Distillation so new experts align with compatible prior experts and routing mistakes are less harmful.
Separates capacity management from inference: a contextual bandit keeps or merges experts, while a reconstruction router selects sparse experts.
On X-TAIL, the abstract reports that each component improves continual-learning performance.

papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Massimo Piccardi, Mehran Abolhasan, Farzad Tofigh, Ian Zhou, Justin Lipman
bullets: Targets the computational and communication costs that hinder federated NLP and multimodal learning.
Processes text, images, and other modalities uniformly as byte sequences, without tokenization.
Uses lean linear attention to reduce memory and computational requirements.
Evaluated on multilingual and multimodal sentiment analysis using Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA.
The abstract reports higher accuracy than ByT5 and LSTM, alongside substantially lower memory and communication overheads.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The FederatedBytes Inference Pipeline. An illustrative walkthrough of the running example (“This product is amazing...”) as it passes through the three stages of the model architecture. Stage 1: Input text is patched and processed by the Hierarchical Encoder (Conv1d) to reduce sequence length. Stage 2: Patches are contextualized via Performer linear attention. Stage 3: Features are pooled for final classification.

Figure 1: End-to-end FederatedBytes Architecture. The pipeline operates in three sequential stages tailored for efficient federated learning: Stage 1 (Input Processing): Raw multilingual text is encoded into UTF-8 bytes. These bytes are compressed into patch embeddings using a Hierarchical Patch Encoder (1D Convolution→ ReLU→Adaptive Pooling) to reduce sequence length. Stage 2 (Memory-Efficient Processing): The patch sequence is processed by a Transformer Encoder utilizing the Performer mechanism. This approximates the full attention matrix using Orthogonal Random Features (ORFs) Yu et al. (2016), achieving linear O(L) time and space complexity. Stage 3 (Prediction & Classification): The encoded representations are aggregated via global mean pooling, normalized via BatchNorm, and passed through a linear classification head to generate final class logits.

Figure 3: FederatedBytes Scalability and Efficiency Analysis. Top: FederatedBytes maintains high AUC scores while ByT5 collapses as client counts increase. Bottom: FederatedBytes demonstrates significantly lower computational overhead, network traffic, and memory footprint compared to ByT5. Data points represent averages across Amazon (en), (zh), and (de) datasets.

papers.abstract: A robot swarm covers a building faster with more robots, but the map is only as complete as the space the robots have physically visited. We target the amount of an unknown building a decentralized swarm knows at each instant, ahead of physical coverage. SenseSwarm serves a lightweight learned map predictor on the swarm's shared occupancy map and folds the predicted structure back into a stigmergic guidance field. Its 709K-parameter predictor is fine-tuned on the swarm's own multi-front observations, which we show is necessary: a single-robot predictor collapses on such views. We build a benchmark of twelve real building floors from HouseExpo, HKUST, and KTH, up to 24,000 square meters, and run 1,620 simulations across nine coordination methods, swarm sizes 32 to 512, and three seeds. On physical coverage the swarm is near parity with a greedy frontier planner, as expected. On map reconstruction, every non-predictive baseline needs 1.3 to 1.9 times longer to reach an 80 percent known map, and SenseSwarm holds an equal-time area lead of about 670 square meters, up to 1,359. Folding the prediction into the shared field matters: the same predictor applied per robot matches our speed but suffers a 6.9 times higher inter-robot contact rate at 512 robots. The prediction is computed once per shared map, so its cost stayed flat from 32 to 512 robots.
authors: Haohua Que, Haojia Gao, Mingkai Liu, Hoiian Au, Qian Zhang, Jiayue Xie, Yule Cai, Bokui Chen, Xueqian Wang, Fei Qiao
bullets: Targets earlier knowledge of unknown building structure, beyond physical exploration coverage.
A lightweight 709K-parameter predictor is fine-tuned on multi-front swarm observations and integrated into a stigmergic guidance field.
Evaluated across 12 real building floors, 1,620 simulations, swarm sizes of 32–512, and nine coordination methods.
Non-predictive baselines took 1.3–1.9× longer to reach 80% map knowledge; SenseSwarm led equal-time mapped area by about 670 m², up to 1,359 m².
Shared-field integration maintained similar speed while reducing inter-robot contact versus per-robot prediction; prediction cost remained flat with swarm size.

papers.title: SenseSwarm: Swarm Exploration via Neural Structure Estimation with Shared World-Anticipation for Rapid Mapping

papers.abstract: Autonomously navigating off-road terrain at high speed demands accurate control, which often relies on dynamics models that capture complex interactions between the robot and terrain. In off-road regimes, terrain interaction is a major component of the vehicle's dynamics. Prior work attempts to capture this effect by training learned models of the vehicle's dynamics, conditioned on its perception of the local environment. However, said conditioning is often overly simplistic, ignoring the spatial structure of the dynamics problem. Our approach, SpatialBEV, exploits this spatial structure. At each step, we query the bird's-eye-view (BEV) features around the predicted state, conditioning the next prediction on current geometric and semantic cues. We additionally present a benchmarking approach that mines a dataset's most difficult scenarios. On datasets collected across seasons, SpatialBEV reduces prediction error by 17.1%, compared to physics-based and learned baselines. We further evaluate on hardware on high-speed ($\geq$10 m/s) and geometrically challenging courses with a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error. More details can be found at https://theairlab.org/spatial-bev-dynamics .
authors: Micah Nye, Samuel Triest, Matthew Sivaprakasam, Isaiah Adu, Sebastian Scherer, Wenshan Wang
bullets: Off-road terrain interactions create complex dynamics that simplistic perception conditioning may miss.
SpatialBEV queries BEV features around the predicted state at each step to capture local spatial structure.
The paper introduces a benchmark that mines the most difficult scenarios from datasets collected across seasons.
It reduces prediction error by 17.1% versus physics-based and learned baselines.
Hardware tests on high-speed (≥10 m/s), challenging courses show a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents learn from failure, but the value of a failure record can change as execution progresses. We study when retaining, compressing, or removing the same history block improves subsequent execution relative to full-history KEEP. We introduce RECAP, a framework that combines matched context interventions, execution-relational prediction, and independent policy certification. Matched environment states and rollout seeds measure success and continuation prompt-cost differences; prefix-only relations between a failure block and the current execution propose promising edits. Independent task bundles then select a policy subject to harmful-intervention and non-positive-benefit risk constraints under a fixed measurement protocol. A five-seed longitudinal case holds both the failure block and its summary fixed: compression fails at an early state and becomes a cost-saving intervention at a later state. Across five backbones, RECAP produces positive paired-success saving estimates with backbone-specific reliability-efficiency tradeoffs. On Hunyuan-A13B, it edits 43.24% of retained checkpoints while matching KEEP's observed 91.89% continuation success and reducing unconditional mean continuation prompt cost by 4,619.8 tokens (2.13%). The framework provides an execution-level reference for deciding when to forget: retain history by its value to what comes next.
authors: Chenle Chen, Yangbo Wei, Zhijie Zheng, Zhenyu Su, Qifan Wang, Junhong Qian, Chao Yao, Chen Wu, Lei He
bullets: Addresses the changing value of failure records during execution compared with always keeping full history.
Uses matched context interventions, execution-relative prediction, and independent policy certification under risk constraints.
A longitudinal case shows compression can fail early but save cost later, even with the same failure block and summary.
Across five backbones, RECAP finds positive paired-success savings with backbone-specific reliability–efficiency tradeoffs.
On Hunyuan-A13B, it reduced mean continuation prompt cost by 2.13% while matching observed KEEP success of 91.89%.

papers.abstract: Physical reasoning about humans in videos has largely focused on everyday interactions, where contact, pressure, pose, and motion support embodied perception and contact-aware applications. Still, short and forceful properties like impact events remain relatively underexplored, despite their relevance to broader understanding of how abrupt physical events affect the human body. To fill this gap, we introduce human-centric impact localization, a new task that localizes target physical impacts temporally within a video and spatially on the human body. We further present HAPACT, a HumAn-centric imPACT dataset and benchmark built from movie clips, containing over 2.8K video-query pairs with more than 20K fine-grained human-annotated frames. We built HAPACT around viewer-grounded annotation, text-conditioned localization, and supervision at frame-level temporal and SMPL-X-based spatial granularity. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our benchmark, we conduct extensive evaluations of existing methods, employing video moment retrieval models for temporal localization and human-scene contact models for spatial localization. For the spatial task, we propose a text-conditioned baseline by reformulating localization as query-guided body-region selection. Benchmark results show that physical impact localization remains challenging for existing methods, motivating HAPACT as a dedicated benchmark to support physical impact reasoning in videos.
authors: Youngrae Kim, Yejin Jang, Eunho Kim, Youjin Sung, Kun-Woo Song, Sangpil Kim, Sang Ho Yoon
bullets: Defines human-centric impact localization as joint temporal and spatial localization of abrupt physical impacts.
Provides over 2.8K video-query pairs and more than 20K fine-grained, human-annotated frames from movie clips.
Uses viewer-grounded, text-conditioned annotations with frame-level timing and SMPL-X-based body-region supervision.
Evaluates video moment retrieval and human-scene contact models, and introduces a text-conditioned body-region selection baseline.
Results indicate that existing methods face substantial challenges in physical impact reasoning.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.
authors: Jize Jiang, Chengxiang Zhai
bullets: Standard benchmarks may overstate reasoning ability because they measure performance on selected tasks rather than generalization across a problem family.
CBE uses parameterized generators to increase complexity while preserving the required competence, plus answer-preserving reformulations to test robustness.
Applied to elementary ordering tasks across six GPT and Qwen models, the evaluation found good performance within bounded ranges but failures of consistent competence across the tested family.
Chain-of-thought and GRPO improved or extended strong performance but did not eliminate all failures; supervised LoRA showed limited held-out transfer.
The protocol produces diagnostic competence profiles and is designed to scale with future models.

papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard component of conditional diffusion models, and guided generation performance has become the \textit{de facto} measure of state-of-the-art models. Recent work on latent diffusion models seeks to learn latent spaces that are easier to model with diffusion. However, under CFG, generation additionally depends on how conditions are arranged in the latent space. We study this arrangement under discrete class conditions, termed \emph{class geometry}, and investigate what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG. Under a Gaussian class model, we show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance makes classes more distinguishable under noise, and derive a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle CFG correction. Based on the analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the intractable noisy posterior objective, which applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents. With a controlled training budget (20 epochs for VAE, 80 epochs for DiT), adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID on ImageNet from 3.31 to 2.28, surpassing a DINOv3-aligned VA-VAE (2.44) with negligible overhead. We further demonstrate that PR generalizes to pseudo-labels derived from clustering, continuous text-embedding conditions, and video latents. Together, our findings highlight class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and take a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning. Our project page is available at: https://maps-research.github.io/cfg-geometry/.
authors: Haoming Liu, Junhao Zhu, Shaoyi Zheng, Yuanhe Guo, Jinnuo Liu, Shenji Wan, Hongyi Wen
bullets: Motivation: CFG performance depends not only on diffusion modeling but also on how conditions are arranged in latent space.
Analysis: Under a Gaussian class model, increasing inter-class variance relative to intra-class variance improves class distinguishability under noise.
Method: Prototype Regularization (PR) approximates a noisy-posterior objective using a cosine prototype classifier over spatially pooled latents.
Result: Adding PR reduces ImageNet guided gFID from 3.31 to 2.28 with negligible overhead under the stated training budget.
Scope: PR also works with clustering-based pseudo-labels, continuous text embeddings, and video latents.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Noisy marginals of zt at several t ∈ (0, 1) for toy Gaussian mixtures with fixed total variance but different allocations between inter-class and intra-class variance. With larger inter-class variance, classes become separable at smaller t, i.e., at noisier levels, and the confident MAP regions align more closely with the true class supports.

With clearer class geometry, the conditional and correction velocities point more consistently toward the target class mean, and the correction vanishes where the posterior concentrates on the target class. All variants use the default PR setting (cosine prototype classifier on clean-only latents) and differ only in the output shape of spatial average pooling applied before the classifier, where 16×16 corresponds to no pooling. Overall, prototypes with lower resolutions perform best: 1×1 prototypes (i.e., global average pooling) achieve the best rFID and gFID without CFG, and 2×2 prototypes achieve the best gFID with CFG, while further increasing prototype resolution consistently degrades generation quality. This suggests that reducing the spatial resolution of prototypes benefits generation, likely because it avoids imposing class-level layout constraints on the latent space.

Table 10: Ablation on DINO pseudo-label granularity (reduced compute budget). All PR variants improve over LDM both with and without CFG, and the differences among τ values are small compared with the gain from adding PR, indicating that τ = 0.1 is a reasonable default. Adjusting τ (e.g., τ = 0.3 here) may bring further improvements, though the best value is likely setting-dependent.

The cosine head on clean-only latents achieves the best rFID and gFID, both with and without CFG. Applying PR on uniform-time noisy latents over-regularizes the latent space: the top PCA component degenerates into a near-constant channel that fails to capture spatial variations (i.e., over-smoothed latents). The linear head, optimized with additional weight decay, collapses to a trivial solution that arbitrarily inflates the latent norm to enlarge the logits.

papers.abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a prevalent strategy for adapting large pre-trained models. Among PEFT techniques, reparameterization-based methods, particularly those that employ low-rank or sparsity structures, have attracted significant attention. However, these approaches often underperform full fine-tuning. Specifically, low-rank methods constrain the update rank, which is misaligned with the inherently high-rank nature of full fine-tuning. In contrast, sparsity-based techniques limit the flexibility of the parameter space and compromise connectivity across weights. To overcome these limitations, we explore the use of Toeplitz matrices, whose entries are constant along each diagonal, therefore providing a compact parameterization without imposing explicit rank or sparsity constraints. A straightforward approach is to update weights via a product of Toeplitz matrices. However, similar to RNNs, long multiplicative chains often lead to gradient instability. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{ToPA}, a more refined version of this idea that replaces standard Toeplitz matrices with block-wise Toeplitz, greatly increasing each factor's capacity and shortening the chain, thereby stabilizing training and improving expressiveness. We theoretically show that products of block-wise Toeplitz matrices can approximate arbitrary matrices under shorter chain length, justifying the structural design of ToPA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ToPA offers greater expressivity than existing low-rank and sparse parameterizations. Empirical evaluations across 21 NLP and CV datasets, spanning 5 model architectures, consistently validate the effectiveness of ToPA.
authors: Sicong Li, Qianqian Xu, Zhiyong Yang, Zitai Wang, Longtao Huang, Xiaochun Cao, Qingming Huang
bullets: Low-rank PEFT restricts update rank, while sparse methods limit connectivity and flexibility.
ToPA replaces long products of standard Toeplitz matrices with shorter products of higher-capacity block-wise Toeplitz factors.
Theoretical analysis shows these products can approximate arbitrary matrices with shorter chains.
Experiments across 21 NLP and computer-vision datasets and 5 model architectures consistently support ToPA’s effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. Critically, we find that the semantic dispersion of sibling actions predicts the redundancy of their downstream continuations, permitting a subtree's budget to be fixed before expansion. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this: treating the per-step budget as the Monte Carlo sample size for estimating a step's residual answer entropy, we derive a sufficient budget that shrinks with sibling dispersion. We accordingly propose $\textbf{Uncertainty-Aware Allocation}$ (UAA), a training-free framework that decouples value from uncertainty: values determine which candidates are promising, while uncertainty, estimated from sibling dispersion at no additional model cost, determines how many merit expansion, via uncertainty-aware pruning and uncertainty-aware budgeting. Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token usage by up to $90\%$ and latency by up to $9\times$ at comparable accuracy, generalizing across four tree search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.
authors: Jianguo Huang, Zhiyi Lyu, Fuxiang Zhang, Yanchen Deng, Deheng Ye, Bo An
bullets: Sibling continuations from the same intermediate state are often redundant and collapse to a few distinct answers.
Semantic dispersion among sibling actions predicts downstream redundancy and can estimate uncertainty before subtree expansion.
UAA is training-free and separates candidate value from uncertainty: value selects promising candidates, while uncertainty controls pruning and expansion budgets.
Across reasoning and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token use by up to 90% and latency by up to 9× at comparable accuracy.
The framework generalizes across four tree-search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies offer strong behavioral priors, but achieving deployment-level reliability and throughput remains difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these policies, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the cost of online interaction. Existing methods adapt frozen flow-matching policies by treating noise space as a continuous action space. We show that this behaviorally unstructured space makes exploration inefficient, often preventing these methods from extracting meaningful learning signals on challenging tasks. We introduce AnchorQ, which enables coarse-to-fine policy improvement through a structured, refinable latent action representation. At each decision step, AnchorQ uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, samples local particles around those anchors, and applies value-guided sampling to explore promising refinements. Our analysis shows that anchors reduce identification complexity at the cost of support bias; particle refinement trades this bias against action-class complexity; and critic accuracy determines the reliability of KL-regularized, value-guided selection. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, AnchorQ outperforms state-of-the-art post-training baselines in sample efficiency, delivering a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput under the same interaction budget. Additional visualizations are available on our website https://anchorq-rl.com/.
authors: Carl Qi, Weijun Dong, Xiaojie Wang, Peiyi Chen, Rahul Sajnani, Mingyuan Zhang, Amy Zhang, Jose Barreiros, Manikatan Nambi, Lillian J. Ratliff, Dylan Randle
bullets: Addresses the high online-interaction cost of reinforcement-learning-based policy improvement for generalist robot policies.
Uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, then refines local particle samples with value-guided selection.
Provides a coarse-to-fine, KL-regularized exploration strategy whose effectiveness depends on anchor support bias, action-class complexity, and critic accuracy.

Outperforms post-training baselines across simulated and real manipulation tasks, with reported gains of 37% in real-world success rate and 97% in simulated throughput under the same interaction budget.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering (VQA) models are known to suffer from the bias issue, which refers to overfitting the regularities of frequent patterns. Previously, researchers only consider the language bias. Recently, the multimodal bias is noticed. However, what multimodal bias is remains unclear. In this paper, we investigate the multimodal bias in counting and non-counting questions. We find that they have distinct underlying mechanism, so their biases come from distinct reasons. We provide valuable interpretations of VQA counting mechanism: \textbf{quantity information stems from the magnitude of the multimodal features in specific dimensions.} Thus, counting bias stems from the vision side and propagates to multimodal features through modality fusion, while the non-counting bias stems from primarily language bias and slightly vision bias. Thus, we propose a method to deal with them differently: Variational and Decomposed method for mitigating Bimodal Bias (VDB). It extracts bimodal bias affected by different proportion of vision and language sides. We introduce variational bias models utilizing the principle of Variational Auto-Encoder to learn mainly language bias with slight vision effect, and a bimodal bias model for bimodal bias combining language and vision sides. Extensive experiments on VQACPv2, VQACPv1, and GQAOOD datasets demonstrate the rationality of our claim and the effectiveness of our method. We also provide explanation for the compromised performance on VQAv2.
authors: Yihan Zhao, Yuncheng Jiang
bullets: Analyzes multimodal bias in counting versus non-counting VQA questions.
Finds that counting information is encoded in the magnitude of specific multimodal feature dimensions, linking counting bias to vision and modality fusion.
Attributes non-counting bias mainly to language, with a smaller visual contribution.
Introduces VDB, combining variational language-dominant bias models with a bimodal bias model.
Experiments on VQACPv1/v2 and GQAOOD support the bias analysis and method’s effectiveness; the paper also explains compromised VQAv2 performance.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained alignment between text and video object trajectories is a core challenge in multimodal understanding. Existing embedding models excel at global retrieval, yet their single global representation entangles multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics, limiting direct object-level grounding. To address this issue, we propose VTrajEmbed, an embedding model that decomposes a video into object trajectories and aligns each trajectory embedding with text for object-level grounding through retrieval. Our main contributions: (1)Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding, a dual-branch architecture that establishes trajectory representations by densely sampling low-resolution frames for high-frequency motion cues and sparsely selecting high-resolution frames for scene context, aggregated by a shared LLM backbone; (2)Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning, a training objective built upon these representations that couples an intra-group loss and a batch-level bidirectional loss under a relation mask, excluding unverified relations and preventing confirmed matches from becoming false negatives; (3)Text2Traj-Bench, a trajectory-level text-video benchmark with model-assisted construction and human-verified query--trajectory relations. Experimental results show that VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively, and achieves 49.48% average R@1 across five global retrieval benchmarks, compared with 42.86% for Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B.
authors: Ruizhi Chen, Zining Fan, Yudi Guo, Jiang Liu, Zhiyu Lin, Zhongjiang He, Shouqian Shi, Hao Sun
bullets: Addresses global embeddings’ tendency to entangle multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics.
Uses Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding to combine dense low-resolution motion cues with sparse high-resolution scene context.
Introduces Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning with relation masking to handle verified matches and unknown relationships.
Provides Text2Traj-Bench, a human-verified trajectory-level text–video benchmark.
VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively.

(c) Data. papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type (knowledge- or reasoning-intensive). On parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU) in eight languages, faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across four models and several faithfulness measures. We propose, and find support for, the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks. Model confidence partly explains the effect of resource level, but not the knowledge-reasoning gap. Languages in which models are less confident rely more on reasoning, yet less confident answers within a language do not, a Simpson's paradox. In lower-resource languages, models rely on their reasoning for more answers, not more strongly for each. CoT monitoring may therefore be most informative in lower-resource languages, where it is least often validated.
authors: Lucas Resck, Jingyi Sun, Qianli Wang, Isabelle Augenstein, Anna Korhonen
bullets: Studies CoT faithfulness across eight languages, four models, and multiple measures using parallel MMMLU questions.
Faithfulness rises as language resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks, but not on reasoning-intensive tasks.
Findings support the Reliance Hypothesis: limited knowledge access increases reliance on stated reasoning.
Model confidence partly explains the resource-level effect, but not the gap between knowledge- and reasoning-intensive tasks.
Lower-resource languages may be especially valuable for CoT monitoring, despite receiving less validation.

papers.abstract: Manipulating deformable objects toward desired 3D configurations is a fundamental capability for robots operating in unstructured physical environments. However, as the range of possible initial and target configurations grows, goal-conditioned deformable manipulation requires a robot to infer increasingly diverse manipulation behaviors in addition to precise continuous actions. We introduce DefFlow, a framework for goal-conditioned manipulation of deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations. DefFlow learns from demonstrations by jointly predicting the goal-conditioned 3D point flow of the robot and deformable object. We show that this formulation better captures both the manipulation decisions, such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp, and the precise continuous motions required for goal reaching, rather than predicting only the robot flow. Across rope, granular-media, and cloth manipulation settings with diverse initial and target configurations, DefFlow substantially outperforms goal-conditioned action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines on success rates and goal-distance metrics. We further demonstrate deployment of our framework on a real robot using real point-cloud observations and unseen goal configurations.
authors: Gaurav Singh, Sergio Orozco, Ryan Duong, Mete Tuluhan Akbulut, George Konidaris, Srinath Sridhar
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing varied manipulation behaviors and precise motions for deformable objects.
Learns goal-conditioned 3D point flows for both the robot and deformable object from demonstrations.
Captures decisions such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp alongside continuous motion.
Outperforms action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines across rope, granular-media, and cloth settings.
Demonstrates real-robot deployment using point-cloud observations and unseen goal configurations.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: DefFlow architecture. Given the scene (including the robot) and a goal point cloud, DefFlow processes all points in a unified 3D space using a PTv3 backbone with learned typeembeddings, which is passed through an MLP to get 3D scene flow. The robot flows are then used to recover executable robot actions.

Fig. 3: Simulation benchmarking environments. This figure shows the distribution of tasks in each environment. As can be seen in (a), each task differs not only in the deformed shape, orientation, and position of both start and goal configurations, but also in the action trajectory required to reach the goal. Some require grasping the middle of the rope, others an end or a point in between. Some require only one grasp, while others require multiple grasps; some may require dragging forward, to the left, or in a zigzag pattern, or swishing. For (b), each task involves a different target shape and requires a different combination of paddle sweeps, varying in number, angle, and extent. Some target shapes require the sweeps to be performed in a specific order. In (c), tasks differ not only in the cloth’s starting position and orientation and its goal configuration, but also significantly in the actions required, as some might require grasping the middle of an edge and simply draping the cloth over the bunny, while others require a corner grasp, a slight swish, and then draping. All three environments share large scene configuration spaces and combinatorial action spaces, much broader than those explored previously [4]–[6], [18].

As can be seen, DefFlow predicts the precise grasp+swishing, while the baselines either get the grasp incorrect and collide with the rope, or do not predict the precise swish resulting in the rope not reaching the exact shape. In (b) we showcase two settings with the same goal but different initial configurations, one from the same demo as the goal and the other from a separate demo, while in (c) we show settings with the same starting state but another goal from a separate demo. As can be seen, DefFlow also generalizes to these unseen settings by predicting different action trajectories as in (c) and taking different decisions in (b) where for one it grasps and lifts while for the second it first grasps and moves the rope to align it and then re-grasps and lifts.

papers.abstract: Blindness and low vision limit many people's ability to complete daily tasks, motivating AI assistants that provide useful guidance. Yet, existing benchmarks do not adequately test whether vision models can provide effective everyday assistance. In particular, i) existing benchmarks primarily rely on visual and textual inputs, with limited support for other modalities that are increasingly available in egocentric wearable devices such as gaze, inertial measurements, spatial trajectories, and others; and ii) existing evaluations emphasize scene understanding and question answering, with limited coverage of goal-conditioned guidance for blind and low-vision users across everyday tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce VISTA (Visually Impaired Scene and Task Annotations), a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal-oriented assistance for blind and low-vision users. VISTA contains $\sim$1,000 egocentric recordings captured with Project Aria glasses; each recording provides synchronized sensor streams, six of which serve as model inputs, and three different types of annotation, covering ten task categories (TC), from object localization to hazard detection. We evaluate 14 representative vision-language models zero-shot on VISTA and design a lightweight multimodal model baseline that integrates all six modalities. Experimental results show that, although existing models can often describe egocentric scenes, they remain limited in generating goal-directed assistive guidance. VISTA thus provides a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models that could improve everyday accessibility.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive language models generate text sequentially, but revision requires referring back to tokens in the input context or those already generated. Causal Edit Serialization (CES) is introduced as a framework for expressing such revisions within the same causal token stream. Special pointer tokens are paired with predicted source addresses, allowing insertion, deletion, replacement, copying and movement to be localized explicitly. A lightweight localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding support both address prediction and conditioning on previously emitted pointers, while retaining a standard causal attention mask. A pretraining procedure combines ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model-generated edits and repeated text. Across model scales and editing baselines, CES models demonstrate complete applied edits with modestly higher clean-text bits per byte than clean autoregressive models. Supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training provide a grammatical-error-correction proof of concept, producing more beneficial than harmful changes under reference-blind model judging. Correct repair programs also improve subsequent text prediction while the original context and its cached states are retained. CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer-addressed transformations.
authors: Louis Robinson
bullets: Supports insertion, deletion, replacement, copying, and movement through explicit source-address pointers.
Uses a localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding while preserving standard causal attention.
Pretraining combines language modeling with repairs from random corruptions, generated edits, and repeated text.
Across scales and baselines, models complete edits with only modestly worse clean-text bits per byte than standard models.
A grammatical-error-correction proof of concept shows more beneficial than harmful edits, and correct repairs improve later prediction while cached context is retained.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces causal edit serialization with pointer tokens for autoregressive language models; a novel architecture and training contribution to language foundation models.
papers.title: Causal Edit Serialization
papers.tldr: Causal Edit Serialization lets autoregressive language models perform localized text revisions by encoding edits as pointer-addressed operations in the causal token stream.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires not only understanding instructions but also determining whether and how a robot can physically execute them. However, existing VLN benchmarks typically assume executable instructions and focus on long-horizon tasks. This leaves body-dependent local execution, including passability and collision-free execution, largely unexamined. Evaluating these factors within long-horizon tasks would entangle local physical execution with task planning and long-term spatial memory, making navigation failures difficult to attribute. We therefore focus on grounding local navigation commands in executable motion under environmental and robot body constraints. We present PASS-VLN, a passability-aware local-command VLN benchmark and model. The benchmark holds the scene, instruction, start pose, and reference route fixed while varying robot body width, requiring target completion when the instructed passage is feasible and stopping before blockage otherwise. Our model encodes body width through obstacle inflation in a depth-derived local bird's-eye view, fuses geometry with visual and linguistic context, and predicts discrete latent action codes for continuous closed-loop execution. Experiments show that PASS-VLN improves collision-free success by approximately 12 percentage points over a strong VLN model fine-tuned on our benchmark, while adapting reach-versus-stop behavior to body constraints and generalizing to unseen body widths. When integrated with a high-level planner, PASS-VLN achieves higher success with fewer local commands, while real-world deployment further demonstrates its effectiveness as a low-level executor. The benchmark and model will be released.
authors: Cong Zou, Xiangsheng Shi, Xuanhui Wang, Fubin Wang, Guangjun Ge, Chao Wang, Yu Wang
bullets: Targets the underexplored problem of body-dependent, collision-free local execution in VLN, separate from long-horizon planning.
Keeps the scene, instruction, start pose, and route fixed while varying robot width to test passability-aware behavior.
Encodes body width via obstacle inflation in a depth-based local bird’s-eye view, fusing geometry, vision, and language to predict closed-loop actions.
Improves collision-free success by approximately 12 percentage points over a fine-tuned strong VLN baseline and generalizes to unseen widths.
Integration with a high-level planner yields higher success with fewer local commands; real-world deployment demonstrates low-level execution effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Speed-limit sign recognition on an automotive camera system-on-chip (SoC) must fit a detector and a classifier (the reader) into the memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets of the device. In our two-stage recognizer, the detector, a YOLO-family network with ReLU and hard-sigmoid operators, is compressed by channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade identifies the channels to remove, the recorded deletions are replayed on the original task-trained network, the parent, and one continuous knowledge-distillation recovery follows. On a YOLOv5n, replay removes 60.3% of the parameters at the accuracy of the parent and, in validation mAP50-95 over five matched seeds, outperforms iterative pruning and training from scratch, and its per-step variant (per-step replay) is the most accurate pruning method. On a YOLOv8n, replay and per-step replay outperform every other method and the unpruned parent. The reader, a five-layer CNN with 18k parameters, and the post-processing of the YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n heads use integer arithmetic only. With 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W4A8), the reader matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory, and an executable streaming model reproduces the INT8 class predictions of its runtime on all 9,850 test crops. On a Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only in the implicit formulation of TensorRT, and the replay detector runs fastest on the deep-learning accelerator (DLA). Trained on public data only, the combined system of 0.72 M parameters recognizes 95.2% of the signs of a held-out automotive camera at 90% precision and 94 frames per second.
authors: Se Un Park, Kyungkeon Chung, Huigeol Kim, Junyoung Park
bullets: Channel replay removes 60.3% of YOLOv5n parameters while maintaining parent accuracy; replay variants outperform competing pruning methods on YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n.
A five-layer, 18k-parameter reader achieves FP32-equivalent accuracy with 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory.
Integer-only post-processing and reader inference support executable streaming deployment, reproducing runtime INT8 predictions on all 9,850 test crops.
The combined 0.72M-parameter system reaches 95.2% sign recognition at 90% precision and 94 frames per second on a held-out automotive camera.
On Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only for TensorRT’s implicit formulation; replay detection runs fastest on the DLA.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.
authors: Yining Li, Huayang Li, Lemao Liu, Taro Watanabe
bullets: Studies position bias in multiple-choice and multi-document tasks across five languages.
Covers models ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameter scales.
Finds position bias remains noticeable in small models and non-English languages.
Reports that larger models and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate the issue.

papers.abstract: Reusing a Transformer block across depth increases computation without replicating its parameters, but successive passes have no dedicated state through which positions can exchange compact summaries of their causal prefix. We introduce the causal latent workspace Transformer: an anchored, four-round shared-depth architecture in which each position writes gated vectors into prefix-specific latent slots and retrieves a content-addressed summary before the next shared block application. This path complements causal self-attention while the original input embedding remains accessible at every round. Across three byte-level corpora, three seeds, and two matched parameter budgets, the proposed model achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings against five Transformer controls. At 101.71M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories, reaching perplexities 2.7820, 2.7843, and 1.6823; these improve upon the strongest non-workspace control on each corpus by 1.06%, 0.73%, and 1.01%. All nine seed-labelled comparisons at this budget favor the workspace. At 0.918M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories, whereas a conditioned loop is stronger on enwik8. Architectural ablations show that adding the workspace improves upon the anchored loop in all six settings and support refreshing its causal summaries at each round. Together, these results identify a causal, content-addressable prefix workspace as an effective structural augmentation of looped Transformers.
authors: Ilia Zaznov
bullets: Addresses the lack of dedicated state for causal prefix information in parameter-shared Transformer loops.
Uses an anchored four-round architecture with gated writes to causal latent slots and content-addressed retrieval before each shared block pass.
The workspace achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings across three byte-level corpora and two parameter budgets.
At 101.71M parameters, it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories; at 0.918M, it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories.
Ablations show consistent gains over the anchored loop and support refreshing causal summaries each round; a conditioned loop remains stronger on small-budget enwik8.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
authors: Lieqi Liu, Rui gao, Jia-Chen Gu, Wenbo Hu, Zhaobin Mo, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar, Wei Wang, Nanyun Peng

papers.abstract: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3\% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132.
authors: Xinyu Luo, Jincheng Zhou, Mengbo Wang, Zilin Shen, Nadia Atallah Lanman, Petros Drineas, Bruno Ribeiro, Brian Bullins
bullets: Targets the stale-subspace problem in gradient-projecting low-rank optimizers such as GaLore.
Uses an Oja++-inspired streaming $k$-PCA algorithm for frequent, on-the-fly tracking of principal gradient directions.
Reduces the performance gap to full-rank optimization by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task.
Achieves the best performance in 10 of 16 RoBERTa-Base fine-tuning scenarios.
Designed for stringent low-rank constraints with low per-step tracking cost.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on proprietary records enables domain adaptation but introduces two challenges: (i) privacy leakage of memorized private data, such as personally identifiable information (PII), and (ii) balancing private data removal with utility preservation. Existing defenses, including data sanitization and differential privacy, often degrade performance, while privacy-neuron editing lacks a PII-free reference to distinguish identity-specific neurons from those supporting useful text. We propose JEPA-Prune, a post-hoc neuron pruning framework guided by a model trained exclusively on PII-free views. Alongside the fine-tuned private model, JEPA-Prune, trains a public model on surrogate and masked views of the same records using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), capturing domain knowledge without identifiers. A cross-model representation probe quantifies deviations between private representations of leaked records and this PII-free reference. Integrated gradients and a scale-invariant specificity score then identify PII-responsive neurons, which are pruned without retraining. Experiments show that pruning just 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4x and PII extraction recall by up to 13.9x, while keeping unseen-text perplexity within 16% of that of the unpruned model for most LLMs. In contrast, privacy-neuron editing increases perplexity by at least 26x.
authors: Mohamed Shaaban, Mohamed Elmahallawy
bullets: Fine-tuning on proprietary records can memorize PII, creating a privacy–utility trade-off.
JEPA-Prune trains a PII-free public reference model on surrogate and masked views of the same records.
Cross-model representation probing, integrated gradients, and a scale-invariant specificity score identify neurons associated with PII.
Pruning 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4× and extraction recall by up to 13.9×.
Unseen-text perplexity generally remains within 16% of the unpruned model, outperforming privacy-neuron editing in utility preservation.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive decoding advances one token at a time, even when several upcoming tokens can be predicted together. We propose CADENCE (Context-Adaptive DEcoding), a generation method that learns both what to draft and how far to draft. Gaussian prediction heads represent future spans as continuous latent vectors, and a shared decoder converts the selected vector into token predictions in parallel. A learned router selects the prediction length from the model's own hidden states and predicted Gaussian parameters, adapting generation granularity to the current context with single-token generation as a fallback. The backbone verifies each proposed continuation and retains the prefix that matches its greedy predictions. Experiments with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval show that router-selected positions yield higher draft acceptance than applying the corresponding prediction length everywhere. CADENCE achieves up to 1.3x higher generation throughput than standard greedy decoding.
authors: Sai Sreenivas Chintha, Chidera Biringa, Rishab Sharma, Anusha Agrawal, Prachi Badarayani, Gemma Zhang, Nigel Boachie Kumankumah, Marco Ayala, Sulaiman Vesal
bullets: Standard decoding generates one token at a time despite predictable multi-token continuations.
Gaussian prediction heads encode future spans as continuous latent vectors, which a shared decoder converts into parallel token predictions.
A learned router selects the draft length from hidden states and Gaussian parameters, with single-token decoding as a fallback.
The backbone verifies drafts and keeps the prefix matching its greedy predictions.
On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval, CADENCE achieves up to 1.3× higher throughput than greedy decoding; adaptive routing also improves draft acceptance over fixed lengths.

A shared decoder generates token predictions, while a router selects the prediction horizon using the context and Gaussian parameters. papers.abstract: N-dimensional splatting extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with view direction and time to model view-dependent and dynamic effects. Each primitive is lifted into a joint distribution over position and conditioning variables, then conditionally sliced at each rendering query. N-DGS and UBS share this step across Gaussian and Beta kernels: recovering the conditional mean, opacity, and covariance requires per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products in every forward pass. We introduce direct conditional parameterization, replacing this covariance-derived readout with explicit per-effect parameters: a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query-to-position regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling. Unrestricted conditional coordinates recover a valid joint covariance; our factorization adds spatial-scale and coupling priors. Applied to both kernels, the parameterization yields dGS (Gaussian) and dBS (Beta). Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, they match or exceed their covariance-derived counterparts on quality, with gains up to +1.26 dB in the main MCMC evaluation. Production slicing is 6.9-7.7 times faster than on-the-fly covariance-derived conditioning; complete-render profiling gives 1.25-1.91 times speedups on four trained scenes. Direct conditioning provides a structured, kernel-agnostic alternative for N-dimensional splatting. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/dgs/.
authors: Zhongpai Gao, Benjamin Planche, Van Nguyen Nguyen, Meng Zheng, Anwesa Choudhuri, Arun Innanje, Terrence Chen, Ziyan Wu
bullets: N-dimensional splatting models view-dependent and dynamic effects by conditioning primitives on query variables.
The method replaces per-query covariance inversions and regression products with explicit Cholesky precision and factorized query-to-position parameters.
Applied to Gaussian and Beta kernels, it produces dGS and dBS with structured spatial-scale and coupling priors.
Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, quality matches or exceeds covariance-derived methods, with gains up to 1.26 dB.
Production slicing is 6.9–7.7× faster, while complete rendering is 1.25–1.91× faster on four trained scenes.

papers.abstract: Scale calibration learns an update for one model representation. We study how much of that update can be reused by another representation of the same pretrained model. Our transfer procedure extracts positive group-wise gains and installs them in the recipient's weights or native quantization scales without recipient-side optimization. On a quantized recipient, it preserves integer codes, zero points and storage layout. For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, bidirectional transfer retains 76.9-90.5% of the text-loss improvement from recipient-specific calibration on fresh WikiText and C4 cohorts excluded from project development. Shuffling the same gain values within each projection worsens both recipients, showing that their learned group assignment matters after transfer. A Llama-3.2-3B control keeps the initial native tensors at all four calibrated projections identical and changes nine projections elsewhere. Cross-installation retains 98.6-99.3% of the text-calibration benefit, alongside a small, resolved preference for each recipient's own gain. These results quantify both the adaptation carried by a reusable calibration update and the remaining benefit of recipient-specific training.
authors: Xu Cao, Wenxuan Xiao
bullets: Problem: Determine whether calibration updates learned for one model representation can be reused by another representation.
Method: Extract positive group-wise gains and install them into recipient weights or native quantization scales while preserving quantized codes, zero points, and storage layout.
Main result: For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, transfer retained 76.9–90.5% of recipient-specific text-loss improvement on held-out WikiText and C4 cohorts.
Shuffling gain values within projections degraded both recipients, indicating that learned group assignments are important.
A Llama-3.2-3B control retained 98.6–99.3% of text-calibration benefit after cross-installation, with a small remaining preference for recipient-specific gains.

papers.abstract: Precise pedicel-targeted grasping in strawberry harvesting remains a critical bottleneck due to the pedicel's small diameter (1.3-3 mm), color similarity with surrounding foliage, and precise force control required for clean abscission zone detachment. As a market-grade crop, strawberry aesthetic value makes bruise-free pedicel detachment essential over direct fruit grasping. Classical approaches struggle to unify vision models, motion planning, and contact manipulation into a robust framework, particularly in occluded canopy environments. Therefore, this work presents a visuomotor imitation learning pipeline for pedicel-targeted strawberry harvesting that unifies perception, motion planning, and contact manipulation from collecting human teleoperation demonstrations, training an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy with a ResNet-50 visual backbone, and deploying the learned policy autonomously on a Jetson AGX Orin edge platform at 15 Hz. The trained policy achieved consistent loss convergence from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100K gradient steps on 130 demonstrations. We have also established a reproducible open-source pipeline with publicly released dataset and model weights for the agricultural robotics community. Full dataset is available at, https://huggingface.co/datasets/nitindominicrai/strawberry_pedicel_grasp_teleoperation and trained policy at, https://huggingface.co/nitindominicrai/act_strawberry_pedicel. To replicate this work, all code, configurations, and deployment instructions are publicly available at, https://github.com/nitin-dominic/autonomous_strawberry_pedicel_harvesting.
authors: Nitin Rai, Won Suk Lee, Hongyoung Leon, Heping Zhu
bullets: Addresses precise, bruise-free pedicel detachment in visually challenging strawberry canopies.
Learns from human teleoperation demonstrations using an ACT policy with a ResNet-50 visual backbone.
Runs autonomously at 15 Hz on a Jetson AGX Orin edge platform.
Training loss decreased from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100K steps using 130 demonstrations.
Reproducible code, dataset, model weights, and deployment instructions are publicly released.

(b) Each episode is stored as synchronized wrist-camera frames and 6-DOF joint positions (130 episodes, 250k frames); joint trajectories are shown with mean (dashed) (c) An ACT policy with ResNet-50 backbone is trained via behavioral cloning over 150K steps. (d) The policy runs autonomously on a Jetson AGX Orin at 15 Hz from live wrist-camera input.
