The task demands gripper alignment to a 1.3-3 mm pedicel under foliage occlusion and color ambiguity, addressed here as a unified visuomotor imitation learning problem via policy trained on human teleoperation demonstrations.

papers.tldr: An imitation-learning pipeline enables a low-cost robotic arm to target strawberry pedicels by combining visual perception, motion planning, and contact manipulation.

papers.abstract: Rigid-body motion planning is fundamental to robotic transport and manipulation, where both object position and orientation determine whether a body can move through cluttered environments. This coupling makes planning chal- lenging because translation and rotation can be constrained very differently by surrounding geometry. We propose Shape- Aware Neural Time Fields, a physics-informed neural motion planning framework that learns a reusable travel-time, or cost- to-go, representation for rigid-body motion while explicitly accounting for these distinct geometric restrictions. The learned field captures local motion difficulty in translation and rotation and is paired with a sampling-based planner that balances progress toward the goal with the cost of reaching nearby poses. We evaluate the framework across 2D and 3D rigid- body planning tasks and non-prehensile manipulation through object pushing in diverse environments. Results show substantial improvements in planning success and inference efficiency over physics-informed neural planning baselines, while remaining competitive with classical sampling-based planners at significantly lower planning times. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of both the learned representation and the proposed planning strategy. Finally, closed-loop pushing experiments under execution deviations and external disturbances demonstrate that fast replanning enables reactive and adaptive task execution.
authors: Yanming Zhou, Yuchen Liu, Ahmed H. Qureshi
bullets: Targets rigid-body planning where position and orientation face different geometric constraints in cluttered environments.
Learns a reusable physics-informed travel-time/cost-to-go field capturing local difficulty in translation and rotation.
Combines the learned field with a sampling-based planner that balances goal progress against nearby-pose reachability costs.

Evaluated on 2D/3D planning and non-prehensile pushing, with improved success and inference efficiency over physics-informed neural baselines and competitiveness with classical planners at lower planning times.
Closed-loop pushing experiments show that fast replanning supports adaptation to execution deviations and external disturbances.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Method overview. (1) Start and goal poses share an encoder with separate translation and rotation branches followed by fusion. Comparing their embeddings gives the approximate travel time T (qs, qg). (2) Geometry supplies speed targets S⋆ c and normals nc for translation and rotation (c). Gradients of T give network-implied speeds Sc. Blockwise Eikonal regularization aligns them with the targets using inverse-speed weighting; Relative Normal Loss encourages speed decrease along nc with the goal fixed. Both losses train the same field. (3) The trained field scores candidates using remaining time T (qi,h, q̄) and local slowness T (q, qi,h)/ℓi,h, the predicted time per displacement from the current pose. Scores weight first steps, while inverse slowness supplies speeds for fitting a steering direction. The planner corrects the weighted step and repeats, extending both endpoints until their paths connect.

Fig. 3. Qualitative path comparison across six planners. Rows show A-shaped planar navigation and T-shaped spatial navigation. Columns show Ours, TDM, PC-Planner, LazyPRM, RRTConnect, and STOMP. Overlaid object poses show translation and rotation along each path; red poses indicate collisions. TDM fails to converge in the A-shaped tasks and collides in the T-shaped task. PC-Planner and STOMP produce collisions in both tasks.

Fig. 4. Real-world Push-T with an external perturbation. (a) Initial planned path. (b) Perturbation during execution. (c) Updated path from the measured block pose. (d) Final observed pose. The planner reuses the learned traveltime field within the repeated loop of perception, planning, and pushing.

papers.title: Shape-Aware Neural Time Fields for Rigid-Body Motion and Manipulation Planning
papers.tldr: A shape-aware neural time field enables faster, reactive rigid-body motion and pushing plans by modeling translation and rotation constraints separately.

papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are trained predominantly on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images but are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for immunohistochemistry (IHC), where cross-hospital differences can impair grading. However, systematic comparisons of correction methods for cross-hospital IHC grading remain limited. To address this gap, we benchmark label-free transformations applied to input images before frozen-FM encoding and to features after frozen-FM encoding using UNI and Virchow2, three IHC markers, and six directed cross-hospital transfers, yielding 12 settings. Among the evaluated input-space methods, our proposed method FIX achieved the largest macro-F1 improvement over no correction, outperforming well-known stain normalization techniques. Among feature-space methods, a simple feature-wise standardization achieved the best improvement over no correction, outperforming CORAL. Under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation, combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) by 0.181 and 0.208, respectively, and reduced ordinal error by 0.209 relative to no correction. These results show that input- and feature-space transformations can provide complementary benefits for cross-hospital IHC grading with frozen pathology FMs.
authors: Jongwoon Lee, Jhair Gallardo, Christopher Kanan
bullets: Cross-hospital variation can impair IHC grading when H&E-trained foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors.
The study benchmarks input-space corrections and feature-space corrections with UNI and Virchow2 across three IHC markers and six directed hospital transfers.
FIX achieved the strongest improvement among input-space methods, while feature-wise standardization outperformed CORAL in feature space.
Combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and QWK and reduced ordinal error under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) for visual question answering (VQA) often pass long visual-token sequences to the language model, making visual-token pruning attractive but risky for medical images, where answers may depend on localized boundary and texture evidence. We study training free pre-decoding pruning and treat pruning as a subspace stable evidence preservation problem. The retained tokens should remain close to the dominant visual evidence subspace induced by the full token set. To this end, we propose \emph{Subspace-Transition Token Pruning} (\method{}), which estimates each token's spectral support from principal component space and constructs a compact representation subspace. To better reflect medical image structure, \method{} further uses a bounded token-grid transition prior to promote boundary and texture sensitive tokens. We evaluate \method{} on the closed-ended SLAKE and OmniMedVQA benchmarks and on RadImageNet-VQA, which provides both closed-ended and open-ended evaluations, using Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones. \method{} delivers consistently strong performance on both the closed-ended and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations. These results show that \method{} is an effective training free pruning framework for medical domain VQA.
authors: Mengchen Fan, Qizhen Lan, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Liang He, Tianyang Wang, Xiaoqian Jiang, Pulin Che, Baocheng Geng
bullets: Medical VQA often uses long visual-token sequences, but pruning can remove localized evidence needed for accurate answers.
MedSTP estimates tokens’ support in principal-component space to preserve the dominant visual evidence subspace.
A bounded token-grid transition prior promotes tokens capturing medical-image boundaries and textures.
Evaluated on SLAKE, OmniMedVQA, and RadImageNet-VQA with Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B.
It shows consistently strong performance on both closed- and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations.

papers.abstract: Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce $R^2$-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.
authors: Xiaoyan Cong, Tianyu Wang, Hyeonho Jeong, Zhifei Zhang, Yuqian Zhou, Yijun Li, Shaoteng Liu, Zhe Lin, Srinath Sridhar, Soo Ye Kim

Uses a reference-bank interface, R²-RoPE for reference scalability, and a single-stream diffusion transformer with MLLM-derived context.

Introduces OmniXRef-Bench for evaluating video-reference attribute transfer across camera, motion, content, style, and VFX.
Reports better performance than task-specific baselines and commercial models in comprehensive evaluations.

papers.abstract: Spatial memory enables robots to reuse past observations for localization, navigation, and question answering. Designing such memory involves jointly deciding what to retain and how to retrieve it for diverse semantic, metric, and temporal needs. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent. The resulting implementations are frozen before building memories from held-out observation histories, without access to downstream questions, and evaluated across five complementary task tracks using the same Query Agent. Across three independent design searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra averages 44.23 on the equally weighted five-track score, versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, the strongest evaluated baseline supporting all five tracks, a 50.9% relative improvement. Qualitative analysis relates performance differences to evidence retention and retrieval, while identifying grounding and evidence-use failures. These results demonstrate the potential of coding agents to automate spatial memory design, while revealing task-dependent trade-offs in performance and computational cost. Project page: https://ba-fa-3344.github.io/.
authors: Qianwei Wang, Ce Zhang, Zhanpeng Luo, Pengpeng Su, Shuo Yang, Hao Xu
bullets: Spatial memory must retain and retrieve observations for semantic, metric, and temporal tasks.

papers.abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.
authors: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Zixiao Chen, Jeevana Priya Inala, Charlotte Siska, Acar Tamersoy, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: Evaluates agents on continuous, multi-task development and maintenance workflows rather than isolated tasks.
Uses an external black-box controller to inject useful operational micro-skills, prune persistently irrelevant tools, and interrupt unproductive failure loops.
Reduces average token costs by 18.4–30.9% across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI with frontier models, with savings reported for every tested repository and agent-model setting.
Generalizes to sequential web development and security auditing, yielding cost reductions of 6.4–21.2% depending on task structure.
The approach targets environment-dependent recurring costs and is evaluated within the tested agents, repositories, and domains.

papers.abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attacker, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here, it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
authors: Georgios Politis, Evangelos Pappas
bullets: Addresses inconsistent evaluations caused by differing attacker access, model knowledge, datasets, and recovery metrics.
Records messages and attack settings so compatible attacks can be reused, independently scored, and compared.
Requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass and separates implementation checks from attack effectiveness.
In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding training-time gradients increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%.
Supports further analysis of corpus choice, compression defences, attack implementations, and measurement code; claims should state controls and untested attacks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces LLM-Attacker, a framework for evaluating privacy in split and distributed LLM systems. It provides a unified approach to red-teaming LLM architectures.
papers.title: The LLM-Attacker: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
papers.tldr: LLM-Attacker standardizes and audits privacy evaluations for split and distributed LLMs by tracking attacker assumptions, enabling reproducible comparisons, and exposing untested attacks.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning aims to forget certain information while preserving others, without retraining from scratch. SoTA methods such as NPO, SimNPO, and SatImp balance forgetting and retain through whole model fine-tuning, while FOM-UL explores selective layer updates. Prior works show that suppressing target information can damage retained knowledge. This trade-off can vary across layers even under the same unlearning loss. In this work, we propose Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning (CoLU), which combines a novel confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating a single selected transformer layer, rather than the whole model for unlearning. To reduce CoLU compute cost, we further propose Brief Layer Screening (BLS), which uses a newly defined normalized forgetting-retention (NFR) score to first rank layers through a brief unlearning trials using a subset of forgetting dataset and fewer epochs. BLS pre-selects top-k ranked layer candidates, which will then be fully profiled using full data analysis. BLS is proven to reduce the runtime of CoLU by 60.2-79.7% with almost the same performance. On TOFU dataset, CoLU improves both forgetting and retention over NPO, SatImp, and GA-based FOM-UL in all six TOFU settings, and over SimNPO in five of the six settings. On MUSE Books and News datasets, CoLU achieves the highest retained KnowMem and the PrivLeak closest to zero among the compared SOTA unlearning methods. CoLU presents a new record performance in both unlearning and retain in most settings up to date. Moreover, across the measured settings, average CoLU GPU memory usage is 77.4% to 79.5% lower than full-model unlearning.
authors: Jingkai Guo, Ziyi Zhao, Chaitali Chakrabarti, Deliang Fan
bullets: Addresses the risk that suppressing target information damages retained knowledge, with trade-offs varying across layers.
Uses confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating only a selected layer.
Brief Layer Screening (BLS) ranks candidate layers using a normalized forgetting-retention score before full profiling.
BLS reduces CoLU runtime by 60.2–79.7% with nearly unchanged performance.
Across TOFU, MUSE Books, and News, CoLU generally improves forgetting and retention while using 77.4–79.5% less GPU memory than full-model unlearning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes CoLU, a layerwise unlearning method for LLMs. It balances forgetting and retention by updating specific layers, contributing to the understanding of LLM memory and adaptation.
papers.title: CoLU: Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning for Large Language Models

papers.abstract: High-fidelity 3D generative modeling underpins game asset creation, medical imaging, and VR/AR environmental design, where geometric structure directly influences perception and decision-making. Diffusion models represent a powerful paradigm for point cloud generation. However, existing approaches rely heavily on local voxel or patch features and often miss global structural organization, and much less work has studied how global conditioning can be used to improve generation quality. In this paper, we introduce HilbertGen-3D, a novel topology-aware conditional diffusion framework based on Hilbert-Multifractal Conditioning (HMC). HMC computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them via a 3D Hilbert curve to expose structured spatial dependencies, and estimates the generalized fractal dimensions from scale-dependent partition functions. We encode these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, and inject them into a diffusion denoiser through an efficient bottleneck fusion module. Across the Chair, Airplane, and Car categories of ShapeNet, our two conditioning variants reduce the absolute deviation of 1-Nearest Neighbor Accuracy (1-NNA) from 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and increase coverage by up to 5.88 percentage points relative to TopoDiT-3D. This shows that combining local density cues with global Hilbert-multifractal structure provides a simple and effective recipe for high-fidelity and diverse 3D generation.
authors: Ziyi Zhang, Shixuan Li, Yorie Nakahira, Paul Bogdan, Guannan Qu
bullets: Addresses the inability of local voxel or patch features to capture global geometric organization in 3D generation.
Computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them with a 3D Hilbert curve, and estimates generalized fractal dimensions.
Encodes these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, fused into the diffusion denoiser through a bottleneck module.
On ShapeNet Chair, Airplane, and Car categories, it improves 1-NNA closeness to 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and coverage by up to 5.88 points versus TopoDiT-3D.
Scope is limited to the reported ShapeNet categories and two proposed conditioning variants.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HilbertGen-3D. Multi-scale voxel measures are serialized along 3D Hilbert curves to construct Hilbert-ordered sequences, while generalized fractal dimensions form the global descriptor D. Separate encoders produce HMC tokens C and a global HMC embedding gHMC, respectively. The noisy point cloud Xt is embedded into geometry tokens Ht, which are fused with the projected HMC tokens through bottleneck latents B. Successive DiT blocks update B, with adaptive layer normalization conditioned on the timestep embedding Etime(t) and the projected global embedding Pg(gHMC). The processed latents update the geometry tokens, and the output head unpatchifies and devoxelizes the predicted features to obtain the noise estimate εθ(Xt, t, C) for DDPM training and reverse-diffusion sampling.

papers.abstract: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at $8\times$ the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about $25\%$.
authors: Yuxuan Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of monotonic decay mechanisms that cannot erase intermediate tokens selectively.
Uses path extrema: logits are penalized according to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field across the key–query span.
Includes the Forgetting Transformer as a special case; under a shared learned walk, unpenalized keys form a stack.
A constant-dimensional FPA head can realize arbitrary subsets of surviving keys, unlike comparable softmax-based mechanisms requiring dimension linear in key count.
In experiments, FPA converges to target key sets, matches FoX perplexity, and achieves perfect passkey retrieval at 8× training length with a cache compressed to about 25%.

papers.abstract: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.
authors: Nicholas Saban, Charvi Bannur, Mariya Vasileva, Darshan Deshpande
bullets: Covers five domains and 19 simulation skills, evaluating state-transition prediction from full agent trajectories.
Compares model predictions with execution-derived references using deterministic checks and a semantic judge.
Across 20 general-purpose and specialized models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest reported success rate at 49.57%.
Performance drops sharply when actions affect dependent objects, with average success of 5.1% on such tasks.
631 tasks remain unsolved by every evaluated model, highlighting substantial world-modeling gaps.

papers.abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.
authors: Faizan Siddiqui, Nirav Savaliya, Sahith Reddy Chada, Enna Sachdeva
bullets: Addresses the lack of stable spatial context in video MLLMs that primarily organize observations over time.
Back-projects visual patch features using depth and camera pose into shared BEV coordinates, averaging features within spatial cells.
Compresses 128 frames and roughly 100K patch features into 729 BEV tokens without architectural changes beyond tokenization.
Reduces LLM prefill time by 2.9× and peak memory by 3.6×.
Outperforms the matched frame-token control on VSI-Bench and ReVSI, with especially strong VSI-Bench gains in room-size and relative-direction reasoning.

The BEV projection (green) is introduced only in the final fine-tuning stage (stage 5, Tab. papers.abstract: We study personalized LLM routing, where a router selects among heterogeneous models with different costs and capabilities. The router must minimize cumulative inference cost while ensuring reliable realized response quality, even though user preferences are unknown and must be learned from feedback during deployment. We formulate this problem as a constrained contextual bandit and develop an algorithm that learns preferences while balancing cost and quality. Under a logistic preference model and a strict-feasibility condition, we establish sublinear expected cost regret relative to an optimal stationary randomized contextual oracle and a high-probability guarantee on realized cumulative satisfaction. The framework extends beyond LLM routing to broader online model-selection problems with reliability requirements.

bullets: Addresses personalized routing across heterogeneous LLMs with different costs and capabilities.
Models routing as a constrained contextual bandit with unknown preferences learned from deployment feedback.
Uses chance constraints to control realized cumulative user satisfaction, not just expected quality.
Under a logistic preference model and strict feasibility, proves sublinear expected cost regret and high-probability satisfaction guarantees.
Applies more broadly to online model selection with reliability requirements.

papers.abstract: Agents operating over long horizons need an effective memory that allows them to reuse their experience throughout long interactions. If the entire history of an interaction is retained, it becomes difficult to find the relevant experience, while compressing it into summaries may result in the loss of visual and spatial details that are required later on. We present \textbf{MFM}, a multimodal filesystem memory architecture that keeps complementary types of agent memory. \textbf{Episodic memory} stores the observations, actions, and outcomes, and \textbf{spatial memory} associates experiences with locations. \textbf{Semantic and procedural memory} build up general knowledge and reusable methods of acting, and \textbf{working memory} holds the current plans. MFM makes use of searchable textual records to connect these different representations to the underlying multimodal episodes. The agents are able to find previous experiences by means of contextual cues and to examine the original observations in order to recover details that are missing from their textual descriptions. Through consolidation, the agents convert experience into higher-level knowledge and procedures while still keeping references to the original episodes. In the case of long-horizon Minecraft and computer-use tasks, MFM leads to improved performance with three base models. With GPT-6-Astra, MFM completes \emph{Mine Diamond from Scratch} and reaches 16 out of 24 milestones on the \emph{Ender Dragon} task, as against 12.7 for the best baseline. On CUABench-KiCad it attains a mean reward of 0.440, as compared to 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 in the case of no persistent memory.
authors: Chloe Su, Jiahan Li, Zhenting Qi, Chaoran Cheng, Haoyu Chen, Sejoon Jun, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of retrieving relevant history while preserving visual and spatial details over long interactions.
Combines episodic, spatial, semantic, procedural, and working memory in a filesystem-based architecture.
Uses searchable textual records to retrieve experiences and inspect their underlying multimodal observations.
Consolidates experiences into reusable knowledge and procedures while retaining links to source episodes.
Improves results across three base models, including stronger performance on long-horizon Minecraft and CUABench-KiCad tasks.

The agent retrieves by searching cues and inspecting original evidence (Sec. 3.3), and consolidates experience into knowledge, procedures, and plans without modifying episodic records (Sec. 3.4).

papers.abstract: Answering complex spatial reasoning questions from egocentric video requires determining what evidence is needed, acquiring targeted observations, and combining them through multiple reasoning steps. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to perform this process reliably. Agentic systems address this challenge by querying external vision and geometry tools, but training their reasoning leaves these tools unchanged, so inaccurate observations can still lead to incorrect answers. We introduce EgoP$^{2}$C, a framework that internalizes a plan-perceive-compose process within a single VLM. To this end, we first train specialized Planner and Perception teachers using separate adapters (Dual-LoRA), then fine-tune the corresponding experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) student under their supervision. We subsequently train the student on trajectories generated by its current policy using a segment-level extension of multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), assigning different trajectory segments to different supervisors. The Planner teacher supervises which evidence-seeking questions to ask, when to stop gathering evidence, and how to compose the final answer. The Perception teacher supervises the video-grounded answers to those questions. At inference, the student executes this adaptive workflow end-to-end, without external spatial tools. Across three spatial reasoning benchmarks, EgoP$^{2}$C students built from Qwen3-VL-8B and SenseNova-SI-1.3-8B outperform their base models by an average of 9.2 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. Across both backbones, EgoP$^{2}$C reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8-66.3% and achieves $1.29$-$1.49\times$ speedups over their shared Dual-LoRA teacher.
authors: Chaoyu Li, Arka Sadhu, Yuliang Li, Hyo Jin Kim, Yuning Chai, Pooyan Fazli
bullets: Addresses unreliable multi-step spatial reasoning caused by inaccurate external tool observations.
Uses Planner and Perception teachers with Dual-LoRA to supervise a mixture-of-experts student.
Applies segment-level multi-teacher on-policy distillation to train the student on its own trajectories.
The resulting workflow adaptively asks evidence-seeking questions, stops gathering evidence, and composes final answers.
Across three benchmarks, it improves base-model accuracy by 9.2 and 7.5 points, reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8–66.3%, and achieves 1.29–1.49× speedups over the teachers.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of the segment-level MOPD pipeline. Each training iteration (i) selects a training sample, (ii) generates a rollout with the MoE student model, (iii) assigns each segment to the corresponding frozen teacher, (iv) obtains teacher log probabilities for the sampled tokens, and (v) updates the student with a reverse-KL policy gradient. The example follows the PLAN path. Orange bars indicate the probabilities of the same sampled token under the student (top) and its assigned teacher (bottom).

Figure 2 Overview of EgoP2C. The framework integrates planning, perception, and composition into a single VLM. (a) Planner (PC) and Perception (V) teachers share a frozen backbone and use separate LoRA adapters trained with SFT followed by GRPO. (b) Teacher-generated sequences initialize corresponding MoE experts through separate role training followed by joint SFT. zt denotes the t-th token. (c) Segment-level MOPD trains the student on its own interactions, with PC supervising subquestions and composition and V supervising observations. (d) At inference, the Planner expert either answers directly using the General expert (DIRECT) or iteratively requests subquestion answers from Perception before composing the final answer (PLAN).

papers.abstract: As assistants move from reactive answering toward proactive intervention, memory changes role: it no longer only supplies the answer to a query, it determines whether and when to speak at all. Prior work in this setting hands the system the relevant fact in context; we study the regime that makes the problem hard, where the evidence justifying an intervention must be mined from a long-horizon personal memory. We introduce ProPerMem, a benchmark for memory-driven proactive assistance (MPA), pairing egocentric video with year-long, distractor-rich user memories (~618K tokens on average), human-verified trigger windows, and a protocol that scores content and timing jointly. Every baseline we evaluate performs poorly (at most 15%), including frontier models given summarized or retrieval-augmented memory. A controlled study explains why: with oracle evidence delivered inside the trigger window GPT-5.3-Chat reaches 96%; letting it choose the timing drops it to 38%, and replacing oracle evidence with retrieval drops it to 15%. Content and timing are separately necessary, and missing either is catastrophic. Guided by this, we build ProPerAgent (Proactive Personalized Agent) with a plug-and-play harness that surfaces memory from a graph-organized store and gates it down to what is worth interrupting for, plus a lightweight RL stage that curbs early and repeated firing. Without any training, ProPerAgent lifts strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5% on Qwen3.8-27B and 38% on GPT-5.3-Chat; RL post-training reaches 42.4%.
authors: Shenglai Zeng, Xiao Yang, Tiffany Ma, Xinyuan Zhang, Nanshu Wang, Deren Lei, Kai Sun, Xilun Chen, Tammy Stark, Xianhui Zhu, Yuetai Li, Rulin Shao, Tianxin Wei, Rakesh Wanga, Anuj Kumar, Jiliang Tang, Wen-tau Yih, Xin Luna Dong

papers.abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.
authors: Zihao Zhao, Avi Schwarzschild, Casey Meehan, Katherine Lee, Zhili Feng, Dylan Sam
bullets: Direct finetuning achieves the strongest capabilities but causes the most privacy leakage.

papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Surprisingly, we find little evidence of a meaningful optimizer mismatch penalty: final performance is largely explained by the independent effects of the pretraining and post-training optimizers, with downstream performance generally improving as the proportion of Muon updates during SFT increases. Although matching the pretraining optimizer can reduce forgetting during SFT, this does not translate into improved final benchmark performance. We further evaluate AdamW and Muon for task-general SFT of open-weight models, across the Llama and Qwen families up to 14B parameters, where Muon remains competitive with AdamW, despite these models having been pretrained with AdamW. Together, our results suggest that the choice of optimizer for post-training can be made largely independently of the optimizer used during pretraining.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly serve as judges in training and evaluation pipelines, often assessing answers together with explanations. Although AI judges are sensitive to textual factors, it remains unclear whether ordinary plausible explanations can sway judgments requiring visual verification. We introduce JUPE, a visual-question-answering (VQA)-style benchmark that fixes answers while varying explanations. Across 14 MLLM judges, ordinary explanations that sound plausible mislead judges, with effects comparable on average to deliberately persuasive arguments. Plain justifications and chain-of-thought rationales reduce rejection of incorrect answers by 12.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively. We call this failure plausibility capture. Using signal detection theory, we find a significant mean shift in decision criterion toward acceptance, without a clear change in mean discriminability. Explanations sway judgments across domains, explanation generators, and judging protocols, while tested mitigations offer limited, model-dependent protection. Such shifts can inflate performance estimates when judges evaluate answers with explanations.
authors: Anglin Cai, Zhiqi Wang, Xiaozhi Yang, Yurun Lin, Dongwon Lee, Yuchen Yang

The vulnerability persisted across domains, explanation generators, and judging protocols; mitigations were limited and model-dependent.

papers.abstract: The training loss of binary and ternary neural networks, expanded as a multilinear polynomial over the discrete weights, is structurally equivalent to the energy of a hierarchical high-order Ising model. We exploit this equivalence to apply Ising solvers to discrete-weight network training, while accounting for a fundamental difference in objectives: an Ising solver seeks the ground state of a fixed energy function, whereas training seeks solutions that generalize to unseen data. Our key contribution is $\Sigma\Delta$-Sampler, an optimizer that reconciles these objectives by embedding a stochastic sampling-and-annealing step as a noisy quantizer inside a first-order $\Sigma\Delta$ noise-shaping loop. The loop pushes noise from weight quantization, high-order frustration, and mini-batch sampling out of the low-frequency adaptation band, so that discrete weight updates follow the smooth descent trajectories embedded in the rugged loss landscape. We validate the framework on a planted quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) benchmark with a known minimizer; on CIFAR-10, where a $13$M-parameter ternary model comes within $1\%$ of full-precision accuracy; on ImageNet-1k, where a ternary ResNet-18 comes within $0.4\%$ Top-5 accuracy of a ternary baseline; on class-incremental continual learning, where prior-task accuracy is preserved; and on MatMul-free language models up to $2.7$B parameters, where it outperforms a straight-through-estimator baseline under matched continued pre-training. Compared with standard quantization-aware training, $\Sigma\Delta$-Sampler reduces the training memory footprint by over $50\%$, delivers an order-of-magnitude speed-up, and reduces weight-update memory traffic by four orders of magnitude, making it attractive for on-device training and fine-tuning of large binary and ternary models.
authors: Zihao Chen, Zhili Xiao, Rui-Jie Zhu, Yipeng Wang, Jason Eshraghian, Shantanu Chakrabartty
bullets: Recasts discrete-weight training as hierarchical high-order Ising optimization while accounting for the need to generalize beyond a fixed ground state.
Uses a noisy stochastic quantizer within a first-order ΣΔ loop to suppress quantization, frustration, and mini-batch noise from the adaptation band.
Validated on QUBO, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1k, continual learning, and MatMul-free language models up to 2.7B parameters.
Reports competitive accuracy, including near-full-precision CIFAR-10 performance and close ImageNet-1k ternary-baseline performance.
Compared with standard quantization-aware training, reduces training memory by over 50%, speeds training by 10×, and cuts weight-update traffic by 10,000×.

papers.title: Noise-shaped Sampling and Annealing for Scalable On-the-edge Training of Binary and Ternary AI Models

papers.abstract: Quadruped parkour policies handle canonical obstacles well, but their training curricula often miss the irregular, compound geometry of industrial and disaster-response sites, where agile locomotion matters most. Such environments pose a hard generalization problem: even training directly on reconstructed geometry from the target site does not reliably yield policies that traverse it. Hand-designed curricula span only a few terrain families, and recent LLM-generated curricula offer little control over which policy weaknesses they target. We propose FCTS, a failure-conditioned terrain curriculum framework that uses localized traversal failures to automatically generate the terrains a policy should train on next. Each failure's location, termination mode, robot state, and surrounding terrain geometry condition this generation, and Monte Carlo Tree Search explores alternative curriculum trajectories under a fixed training budget. On terrains built from scanned real-world construction sites, FCTS raises success rate from 28.4% to 85.8% on a medium-difficulty course and from 14.9% to 44.7% on a hard course relative to the strongest parkour or LLM-curriculum baselines, and maintains higher progress on extreme terrains where full traversal is rare. Hardware experiments on a quadruped robot confirm that the learned FCTS policies transfer to the real world.
authors: Narayanan Palghat Parameswaran (Carnegie Mellon University), Dong-Ki Kim (FieldAI), Jay Patrikar (FieldAI), Santiago Gutierrez (FieldAI), Harshad Zade (FieldAI), Shayegan Omidshafiei (FieldAI), Harmish Khambhaita (FieldAI)
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training policies for irregular, compound terrain in industrial and disaster-response settings.
Conditions generated terrains on failure location, termination mode, robot state, and surrounding geometry.
Uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to select curriculum trajectories under a fixed training budget.
On scanned construction-site terrains, improves success from 28.4% to 85.8% on medium courses and 14.9% to 44.7% on hard courses versus the strongest baselines.
Policies maintain better progress on extreme terrains and transfer successfully to a real quadruped robot.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are usually chosen from leaderboards, which give one ranking for every application. On questions about objects that a scene suggests but does not contain, however, the model with the lowest error on the POPE hallucination benchmark is not the one with the lowest error on such questions. For yes/no questions about object presence, we show that the best model for a target domain can be predicted without running any candidate on that domain, given 650 to 1,200 labeled target items that calibrate a detector. We measure each model's reliance on a cue, a feature such as scene context or text in the image, by editing 100 labeled source images so that the cue suggests the wrong answer, and comparing with a matched control edit. Reliance predicts which VLMs are misled by physical sticker attacks (Spearman .93 on nine models not used to design the score) and which hallucinate on unedited COCO photographs, beyond what their tendency to answer yes explains. Shift-Reliance Alignment (SRA) scores a model by its source error on the labeled source questions plus its reliance multiplied by the shift. The shift is the proportion of target questions on which the cue misleads, and a detector estimates it on the unlabeled target images. SRA selects the model with the lowest score. In pre-registered tests on new images where most questions mislead, it lowered the error of the selected model from 30.4% under selection by source error to 18.8% on Objects365 and OpenImages but, against its prediction, not on COCO. On CueDial, a benchmark we release that varies how often a cue misleads, selection by model confidence falls more than 40 percentage points behind the best model when overlaid text denies a visible object, and SRA stays within 3 points.
authors: Faisal Mohammad, Mohamed Younis
bullets: Leaderboard rankings can fail when target questions rely on misleading scene context or image text.
SRA measures each model’s cue reliance using edited labeled source images and estimates how often that cue misleads in unlabeled target images.
With 650–1,200 labeled target items for detector calibration, SRA predicts target model errors without evaluating every candidate on the target domain.
Cue reliance strongly predicted vulnerability to sticker attacks and hallucinations on COCO images beyond models’ general tendency to answer yes.

In preregistered tests, SRA reduced selected-model error from 30.4% to 18.8% on Objects365 and OpenImages; it did not improve selection on COCO and stayed within 3 points of the best model on CueDial.

papers.selection_reason: Ranks and selects VLMs by cue reliance for hallucination robustness, contributing to multimodal foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: Shift-Reliance Alignment: Ranking Vision-Language Models by the Cues They Trust
papers.tldr: Shift-Reliance Alignment selects vision-language models for a target domain by estimating which visual cues mislead them, often outperforming selection by standard source-domain error.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation let users create high-quality videos from natural language descriptions, yet obtaining results that match user intent remains time-consuming: individual generations are computationally expensive, and underspecified prompts force repeated cycles of generation, inspection, and revision. Existing video prompt optimization methods improve generation through automatic rewriting, but cannot supply the ideas and preferences that were not in the initial description. We propose ProactGen, a video generation framework that learns proactive clarification, eliciting user intent through questions grounded in generated video drafts. Specifically, we train a vision-language model as a questioning policy with reinforcement learning: observing the initial prompt and a video draft, it learns to ask the questions most valuable to downstream generation, rewarded by the alignment between the final generated video and a target reference. We further find that effective questioning does not require drafts of final-output quality, and exploit this property by generating drafts with fewer denoising steps, keeping the added cost of clarification low. Experiments show that ProactGen improves target alignment over direct generation by at least 1.8x the gain of the strongest baselines. Moreover, a single round of ProactGen already exceeds the alignment that the strongest baseline reaches after four refinement rounds, in 29% of its time.
authors: Zhixiao Wang, Yang Chen, Yifan Xu, Chenbin Li, Yue Chang, Kai Long, Fengming Dong, Limin Wang
bullets: Addresses underspecified prompts that otherwise require costly generate–inspect–revise cycles.
Uses a vision-language model trained with reinforcement learning to ask questions based on the initial prompt and a video draft.
Questions are optimized for their value to downstream generation, using final-video alignment to a target reference as the reward.
Low-cost drafts with fewer denoising steps keep clarification overhead small.
A single round outperforms the strongest baseline’s four-round refinement alignment in 29% of the time, and achieves at least 1.8× its alignment gain over direct generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ProactGen. The questioning policy asks scoped questions conditioned on the initial prompt and a low-cost video draft; a simulated user answers from the reference video; the answers are merged into a refined prompt from which the final video is generated at full budget. During training, the alignment between the final video and the reference is the reward for updating the questioning policy; all other components are frozen.
Figure 3: Per-sample time versus target alignment (InstanceCap, DS-DTW). The horizontal axis is linear up to 50 s and logarithmic beyond.

Figure 1: A user’s initial prompt often omits preferences the user already has in mind (here, the hand gesture, the boy’s posture, the table’s material, and the framing). (a) Automatic prompt optimization rewrites the prompt from the prompt alone, so missing preferences can only be guessed. (b) Uncertainty-based clarification asks the user, but derives its questions from the prompt text without knowing what the generator will actually produce. (c) ProactGen first observes what the generator produces for the prompt through a low-cost draft, asks the user targeted questions grounded in it, and learns what to ask from the alignment of the final video.

Each row shows the reference video, the initial prompt, the draft, three question–answer pairs, and the final video, with the refined prompt below and answers highlighted. papers.selection_reason: Learns proactive clarification for text-to-video generation with RL-trained questioning policies, directly relevant to video diffusion and prompt refinement.
papers.title: ProactGen: Learning Proactive Clarification for Video Generation
papers.tldr: ProactGen improves text-to-video alignment by proactively asking users targeted questions about draft videos before final generation.

papers.abstract: FOR-species20K is the largest public LiDAR benchmark for tree-species classification, pooling 25 independently collected terrestrial, mobile, and airborne laser-scanning datasets across 33 species. We introduce a multi-resolution, multi-view ConvNeXtV2 model that improves official hidden-test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%, ranking first at the time of submission. We then examine what this score measures. Because the hidden test is species-balanced, its overall accuracy is more comparable to a macro metric than to accuracy under the public set's long-tailed distribution. Moreover, the official random split places every source dataset in both training and evaluation. A logistic probe recovers source identity from out-of-fold model probabilities with 69% accuracy, while geometric features identify the source above 90% within two widely shared species; 18 of the 33 species occur in only one source. Under a source-species-cell holdout, evaluated on 5,566 trees from eight eligible species that retain the same LiDAR-type training support in other sources, the unweighted species mean falls from 82% to 36%, and tree-weighted accuracy falls from 95% to 60%. Count-matched retraining and experiments with two alternative backbones indicate that this gap is not explained by reduced training support alone, while an external PureForest experiment shows a smaller but consistent grouped-split effect. These results establish the 85% leaderboard score as strong in-distribution performance, but not as an estimate of source-disjoint generalization, motivating balanced metrics and source-aware evaluation. The code is available at: https://github.com/JaeLee18/FOR20K-lidar-tree-species
authors: Jae Joong Lee, Bedrich Benes
bullets: FOR-species20K combines 25 terrestrial, mobile, and airborne LiDAR datasets covering 33 tree species.
A multi-resolution, multi-view ConvNeXtV2 model raises hidden-test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%.
The official random split mixes source datasets across training and evaluation, enabling substantial source-identity cues.
Under source-species-cell holdout, performance drops to 36% unweighted species mean and 60% tree-weighted accuracy.
The study recommends balanced metrics and source-aware splits for evaluating LiDAR tree-species recognition.

papers.abstract: Retrieval is a fundamental task in multimodal systems: given an image or text query, the goal is to find the most relevant images or texts in a collection, often using a shared embedding space. Reliable retrieval requires these embeddings to capture not only which concepts are present, but also how they are composed. One key compositional challenge is attribute--object binding: encoding which attributes belong to which objects. Existing benchmarks provide a limited view of this capability, typically covering a subset of modality pairings, simple two-object swaps, or small attribute sets. Consequently, it remains unclear how robustly current models preserve attribute--object bindings across different modality pairings and more complex settings. We therefore introduce SABER, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute--object binding across all four image and text modality pairings, spanning diverse attribute types and scenes with up to ten objects. Evaluating models on SABER reveals substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and recent MLLM-based embedders. These findings motivate us to ask how binding can be improved efficiently. While multimodal supervision may be effective, collecting suitable images is difficult and costly. Text, on the other hand, is well suited to binding supervision: it is cheap to generate, supports a broader range of attributes and enables precisely controlled hard negatives. We thus finetune an MLLM-based embedder exclusively on synthetic attribute-binding text. Despite the absence of image supervision, the gains transfer to cross-modal and image--image retrieval while preserving general multimodal embedding performance. Our model achieves SOTA results on SABER while also improving on negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks, demonstrating broader benefits of our binding-focused supervision.
authors: Netanel Y. Tamir, Michael Green, Issar Tzachor, Or Shimshi, Dvir Samuel, Or Patashnik, Rami Ben-Ari
bullets: Introduces SABER, a controlled benchmark covering all four image/text retrieval pairings, diverse attributes, and scenes with up to ten objects.
Finds substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and MLLM-based embedders.
Fine-tunes an MLLM-based embedder exclusively with synthetic text designed to teach attribute–object binding and hard negatives.
Improvements transfer to cross-modal and image–image retrieval despite no image supervision, while preserving general embedding performance.
The approach achieves state-of-the-art SABER results and also improves negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and improves attribute-object binding in vision-language and MLLM-based embedders, relevant to multimodal foundation model capabilities.
papers.title: Stuck on Shuffle: On Attribute-Object Binding in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: SABER exposes widespread attribute–object binding failures in vision-language embedders and shows that synthetic text-only supervision can improve binding across retrieval modalities.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI make Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) increasingly plausible. Large Language Models (LLMs) can already propose, select, and run Machine Learning (ML) experiments. However, the space of possible design choices in ML is vast. An LLM that proposes an experiment needs a reliable intuition of whether it is worth running given the timing constraints of long training runs. In this work, we measure such intuition in current frontier LLMs by evaluating how accurately they predict the impact of self-generated ML experiment ideas before these are put into training runs. To this end, we construct a dataset of 288 LLM-proposed ideas on eight MLE-bench tasks. We then prompt five frontier LLMs (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3) to predict the impact of each idea and compare their predictions with the actual outcomes after training. We report four main findings. First, LLM predictions are substantially better than random chance but far from accurate: even the best model, Claude Opus 5.5, explains only half of the variance in outcomes (R^2 = 0.49). Second, we notice that all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes. Third, prediction quality varies widely across tasks. Finally, the choice of the coding harness that actually implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, and we find no evidence of self-preference. Higher reasoning settings and additional context lead to modest gains. Overall, our results show that current LLMs have useful but limited intuition about which ML ideas will work. We release our dataset to support further study.
authors: Ayush Bansal, Aldo Pareja, Sean Klein, Serge Didenko, Artem Lukoianov
bullets: Evaluates predictions for 288 LLM-generated ideas across eight MLE-bench tasks using five frontier LLMs.
The best model explains 49% of outcome variance, indicating useful but imperfect predictive ability.
All tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of experimental effects.
Prediction quality varies substantially by task; more reasoning and context provide modest improvements.
Coding-harness choice has little impact on outcomes, with no evidence of self-preference; the dataset is released.

figures.caption: Figure 1. We prompt LLMs to predict how much an ML experiment idea will change the final training outcome. Left: predicted versus actual change for each idea, for the best model (Opus 5.5) and the worst model (Kimi K3), with each model’s line of best fit. A perfect predictor would lie on the dashed line. Points beyond ±3σ are not shown. Right: R2 and slope for all five models. Even the best model explains only half of the variance, and every fitted line is flatter than the diagonal, so all models underestimate large changes.

Figure 2. Left: starting from the baseline, a model proposes four ideas and then two follow-up ideas for each. Each node is a working solution and each edge is an idea. Right: a real example from our dataset, showing the idea, its code diff, and the predicted versus actual score after training. Here, Opus 5.5 predicts the right direction but underestimates the size of the improvement.

Figure 4. Each point is one idea, for the best model (Opus 5.5) and the worst model (Kimi K3). Points in the shaded quadrants have the correct predicted direction, and crosses mark ideas where the model predicted the wrong direction. Most ideas cluster near zero, so most have only a modest effect on the score. The table shows how often each model predicts the right direction, for all ideas and for ideas that changed the score by at least 0.25σ. Points beyond ±3σ are not shown. Every model predicts the direction of most changes correctly, and accuracy rises once small changes are excluded.

Figure 6. From left to right, the model sees only the idea, the idea and its code diff, or the idea, its code diff, a data card describing the data, and the first 20 rows of the data. Error bars are 95% intervals from bootstrapping over the ideas. Removing the code diff lowers R2 for the three strongest models, while the data card helps only Opus 5.5.

Figure 5. R2 of each model as a function of reasoning level, from low to max. GLM-5.3 only has three reasoning levels, while all others have five. Error bars are 95% intervals from bootstrapping over the ideas. R2 rises with reasoning level for the three strongest models, but not for Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3.

Figure 9. Each dot is one idea at its real change in score, split by whether the model was prompted to improve or to worsen the score. The black line marks the median, and the numbers on the right show how often the score went up or down. Points beyond ±3σ and failed runs are not shown, but they are still counted.

Figure 7. Each point is one idea, plotted at its change in score when implemented by Fable 5.1 (x-axis) and by Kimi K3 (y-axis). Points on the dashed line scored identically under both implementations. The four circled ideas are examples where the implementer does and does not matter. Most ideas score nearly the same regardless of the implementer, with 58 of 66 within 0.25σ.

Figure 3. R2 per task. Each row is one MLE-bench task and each marker one model. The same model can be highly accurate on one task and poor on another, and Opus 5.5 beats Kimi K3 on every task. The two image tasks, dog breeds and document denoising, are the hardest for the best model.

Figure 8. Each cell shows how far one model’s predictions (rows) lie above its own line of best fit, relative to the other four models on the same ideas, averaged over the ideas written by each model (columns). The outlined diagonal shows each model predicting its own ideas, where self-preference would appear as positive values. All diagonal values are close to zero, so we find no self-preference.

Table 1. Each row is one idea, where we specify the model that wrote it and whether it was asked to improve or worsen the score. In the dog breed identification and denoising dirty documents examples, the ideas were intended to worsen the score but improved it, whereas Opus 5.5 predicted a decrease. The full text of the dog breed idea is shown below the table.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates frontier LLMs' ability to predict ML experiment outcomes, relevant to LLM reasoning and self-improvement.
papers.title: Can LLMs predict the outcomes of machine learning experiments?
papers.tldr: Current frontier LLMs can predict the outcomes of ML experiments better than chance, but their intuition remains limited and task-dependent.

papers.abstract: Flow-based policies such as $\pi_0$ are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem. To adapt a frozen $\pi_0$ to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks. On transfer tasks that $\pi_0$ saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of $\pi_0$ with the classifier's gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body. On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises $\pi_0$'s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction). In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly. Guidance is mixed on weak wrists and harmful on a locked wrist, when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions. Collecting more target-body data with guided $\pi_0$ can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided $\pi_0$ solved a task on which unguided $\pi_0$ had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.
authors: Devin Han, Hershraj Niranjani
bullets: Motivation: Transfer frozen VLAs such as π₀ across robot embodiments without collecting demonstrations or changing policy parameters.
Method: Train a classifier on successful source- and target-body action chunks from a few calibration tasks, then use its gradient during each denoising step to guide π₀.

Result: On LIBERO with four modified controllers, average target-body success increased from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs; 11 of 12 improved, with 5 statistically significant after Holm correction.
Scope: Guidance is data-efficient in simulation and may support sim-to-real transfer where target rollouts are costly.
Limitation: It can be ineffective or harmful for weak or locked wrists when classifier data are insufficient or favor infeasible motions; guided data and retraining can partially address this.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the transfer of frozen VLA policies (like $	extit{$ ackslash$pi$_0$}) to new robot embodiments. It uses a lightweight classifier to guide the denoising process, a transferable technique for embodied AI.
papers.title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
papers.tldr: A lightweight embodiment classifier can guide a frozen flow-based policy toward successful actions for a new robot body without demonstrations or policy updates, improving simulated transfer but struggling with poorly represented or infeasible dynamics.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as formalizers: given a reasoning problem expressed in natural language, they produce a formal specification that a symbolic solver can then solve, with guarantees relative to that specification. Many specifications are runnable yet semantically wrong, encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals, and solver-error feedback dries up once execution succeeds. Purely LLM-based diagnosis, lacking a formal ground truth, often fails to spot these errors, and its ungrounded critiques cause regressions in 11.8% of initially correct specifications in our experiments. We propose DRAGO, a repair framework that replaces this ungrounded critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis, and retains a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases under a reference-free acceptance predicate. Across five benchmarks spanning logical reasoning (SMT-LIB2), constraint programming (MiniZinc), and planning (PDDL), DRAGO cuts regressions by nearly an order of magnitude, to 1.3%, while improving answer accuracy by 12.9 percentage points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 percentage points over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged across benchmarks. We also uncover two rendering defects in Planetarium that cause 50% (3,086 instances) of its floor-tile split to be inconsistent with the reference formalizations, and release a corrected split.
authors: Giovanni Vaccarino, Emanuele La Malfa, Dehai Min, Hanrong Zhang, Pier Luca Lanzi, Lu Cheng, Michael J. Wooldridge, Philip S. Yu, Sara Bernardini
bullets: LLM-generated specifications can execute successfully while encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals.
DRAGO uses formalism-specific deterministic diagnosis instead of ungrounded LLM critique.
A rewrite is accepted only when a reference-free error-weight measure strictly decreases.
Across five SMT-LIB2, MiniZinc, and PDDL benchmarks, regressions fell from initially correct specifications to 1.3%, while accuracy improved by 12.9 and 8.7 percentage points over two baselines.
The work identifies and corrects rendering defects affecting 3,086 Planetarium floor-tile instances.
