papers.selection_reason: Proposes DRAGO, a framework for repairing LLM-generated formal specifications using deterministic diagnosis. This addresses the issue of semantic errors in LLM formalization outputs.
papers.title: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis
papers.tldr: DRAGO repairs runnable-but-semantically-wrong LLM-generated formal specifications using deterministic diagnosis, substantially reducing regressions and improving answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: Manual annotation of synchronized video and EEG recordings is a bottleneck in preclinical seizure research. We present an empirical study of seizure detection and behavioral severity grading using 24,131 paired clips from 601 sessions across 20 rats in a soman-induced epilepsy model. Ten video architectures and seven single-channel EEG models are evaluated independently on binary detection and three- and five-class severity tasks. In the session-exclusive reference comparison, R(2+1)D-18 and GRU achieve detection macro-F1 scores of 0.968 and 0.974, respectively; for five-class grading, the corresponding scores are 0.657 and 0.560. Subject-exclusive evaluation reduces five-class macro-F1 to 0.475 for video and 0.404 for EEG, highlighting the difficulty of grading unseen animals. Temporal-sampling experiments demonstrate the value of multiple frames, while detection performance varies relatively little across the evaluated video architectures. A separate video-only binary-detection evaluation on RodEpil achieves a mean seizure-class F1 of 0.979 after uniform re-encoding to reduce identified class-correlated encoding cues. The study characterizes existing models for behavior-defined severity labels under the evaluated protocol, motivating further investigation of expert-assisted annotation workflows. Our code and github page is available here.
authors: Alloy Das, Shreyan Ganguly, Nyzil Massey, Hung Phi Doan, Zhanhong Jiang, Thimmasettappa Thippeswamy, Soumik Sarkar
bullets: Evaluates 10 video architectures and 7 EEG models on 24,131 synchronized clips from 601 sessions involving 20 rats.
Detection is strong under session-exclusive evaluation, with best reported macro-F1 of 0.968 for video and 0.974 for EEG.
Five-class severity grading is more difficult, reaching 0.657 for video and 0.560 for EEG in session-exclusive evaluation.
Subject-exclusive testing lowers five-class macro-F1 to 0.475 for video and 0.404 for EEG, emphasizing limited generalization to unseen rats.
Multiple-frame temporal sampling helps; detection varies little across video architectures, and a re-encoded RodEpil evaluation reports seizure-class F1 of 0.979.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Grad-CAM [48] for R(2+1)D-18. Four of eight frames are shown, with input frames above activation maps. Activations concentrate on the animal in the Stage 4 example and are more diffuse in the non-seizure example. These observations do not establish causal reliance on behavior or exclude shortcuts. Full sequences appear in App. D.2, Fig. 14. Identifying tags are blurred.

Figure 3. Binary-detection macro-F1 versus video model size under the evaluated training budget. Scores range from 0.945 to 0.974. X3D-M (4M parameters) achieves 0.969, compared with 0.971 for R(2+1)D-18 (33M). This comparison concerns detection, not equivalence across severity tasks (Tables 2 and 9).

Figure 14. A full-width, extended version of Fig. 5. This layout shows all eight sample frames from the exact same pair of clips. For each sequence, the raw video frames sit on top, with the model’s attention heatmaps (seizure-class activation) directly underneath. While this sharp contrast strongly supports the idea that the model is genuinely focusing on the animal to make its predictions, it does not act as definitive proof against hidden visual shortcuts. (All clips have been completely de-identified, and any specific cage identifying bands have been redacted.)

Figure 15. Grad-CAM heatmaps for the R(2+1)D video model across different severity stages. The network’s attention consistently locks onto the animal across the illustrated Stages 2, 3, and 5, showing similar activation patterns in these selected examples. Still, we must treat these visualizations as descriptive rather than causal they show us where the model is looking, but they do not serve as absolute proof of how it makes its final decisions. (All clips have been de-identified, and any identifying cage bands have been completely redacted.)

Figure 11. A visual breakdown of the clip counts for each animal across the entire dataset, representing the stacked totals from Table 10. The distribution of seizures is incredibly lopsided: the four most heavily affected rats (R1-R4) completely overshadow the rest of the group, with individual contributions ranging drastically from just 11 clips up to 3,091. More importantly, the most violent seizures (Stage 4 in dark shading, Stage 5 in the darkest) barely register as a thin sliver on any animal’s bar graph, yielding only 193 Stage 5 clips in the whole study. This extreme rarity is exactly why teaching models to perform detailed severity grading is such a difficult challenge.

Figure 16. Row-normalized confusion matrices comparing both modalities across all three evaluation tasks (drawn from a representative seed-42 diagnostic run; displaying true-class fractions with raw counts in parentheses). On the granular 5-class task, the video model’s mistakes cluster tightly along the diagonal, meaning its errors are almost entirely limited to adjacent severity levels. In stark contrast, the EEG baseline not only misses active seizures completely, but also frequently commits erratic, non-adjacent grading errors.

Figure 4. A paired Stage 3 seizure from rat R7. Top: Four sample video frames. Bottom: The corresponding single-channel EEG trace (∼64 s), with the active seizure period highlighted. Watching these streams side-by-side provides a complete view of both the physical symptoms and the electrical brain activity. Identifying markers have been masked.

Figure 7. Macro-F1 across task granularities for the results displayed in this plot. Video decreases from 0.970 for binary detection to 0.662 for five-class classification; EEG decreases from 0.966 to 0.534. Both modalities perform less well as the label set becomes more detailed. The plotted values differ from the runaveraged values in Table 1.

Figure 8. Per-class F1 for the five-class results displayed in this plot. Video/EEG values are 0.97/0.78 for non-seizure, 0.67/0.45 for Stage 2, 0.90/0.38 for Stage 3, 0.36/0.10 for Stage 4, and 0.42/0.03 for Stage 5. Rare severe stages remain difficult for both modalities.

Figure 6. Per-fold binary-detection macro-F1 for unseen animals, as displayed in the plot: video 0.948 ± 0.016 and EEG 0.849 ± 0.055. The plotted video results have a higher mean and lower fold-to-fold variability than the plotted EEG results.

Figure 9. A visual breakdown of our basic yes/no detection task. We show four sample frames from a normal, non-seizure period (top) alongside four frames from an active seizure (bottom). Because both examples feature the same rat during the same recording session, the animal’s appearance, the camera angle, and the overall background perfectly match. This careful pairing drastically reduces the chance that the model can cheat by memorizing static visual shortcuts in the scene. (All clips have been de-identified).

Figure 10. Visual filmstrips for each seizure stage: Each row (S2-S5) shows five sequential frames taken from a typical seizure clip, with time moving from left to right. As the severity stage increases, the physical symptoms become much more obvious escalating from mild movements in Stage 2 to extreme rearing and violent convulsions in Stages 4 and 5. Crucially, these behavioral shifts are plainly visible on camera, whereas the recorded EEG signal only captures them indirectly through shifting brain waves. (All frames are pulled from de-identified clips and tightly cropped to hide any specific cage labels.)

Figure 12. Visual examples of variation across different subjects: a single frame taken from six different animals (where ’R’ simply indicates a de-identified subject). The exact cage placement, camera angle, lighting conditions (which alternate between natural daylight and infrared), and even the animal’s coat vary drastically from rat to rat. This massive visual inconsistency is exactly why forcing a model to generalize to entirely unseen animals is so much harder than simply testing it on new recording sessions from familiar ones. It also highlights exactly why the video model’s consistent stability across different subjects (Fig. 6) is such a crucial finding.

Figure 2. Recording setup: each rat is recorded in its home cage using a fixed overhead camera and implanted EEG sensors. Cage cropping reduces variation in the field of view but does not remove all differences in camera geometry. Identifying details are masked.

Figure 13. Examples of where the video model struggles the most. (a) A very mild Stage 2 seizure featuring only subtle movements, making it incredibly easy to confuse with normal, everyday behavior. (b) An animal that rarely experienced seizures (found at the bottom of Table 10, App. C), leaving the model with very few validation clips captured under poor, grainy infrared lighting. Ultimately, extremely mild symptoms and data-starved animals drive almost all of the network’s remaining errors. (All clips have been de-identified.)

Figure 17. Error diagnostics for the 5-class severity grading task. (a) Numeric label-distance histogram. Because baseline non-seizure behavior falls completely outside the standard Racine scale, this panel remains purely descriptive and should not be treated as a strict ordinal metric. (b) Per-class recall annotated with absolute support counts, distinctly highlighting the Stage 2 performance reversal. (c) Direct head-to-head outcomes across the strictly shared intersection of 2,830 test clips evaluated by both modalities.
Table 8. Representative human video-EEG systems. Animal fusion remains sparse and has concentrated almost entirely on simple yes-orno seizure detection [35, 42].

Table 11. R(2+1)D binary-detection data-size and pretraining experiments under session-exclusive evaluation. The validation set is fixed as the training-subject subset grows. Macro-F1 rises from 0.957 with ten animals to 0.970 with twenty; intermediate results are non-monotonic. Kinetics pretraining improves macro-F1 by 0.018. These experiments do not establish data saturation for other architectures or tasks.

Table 3. Temporal-sampling ablation for R(2+1)D (seed 42). Single-frame performance is poor, while performance peaks around 32 frames. Using 64 frames gives no detection gain and lowers 5-class F1. AUROC results are reported in App. E.5, Table 17.

Table 2. We tested ten video models using the exact same data splits and a strict 12-epoch training limit. Scores show the mean± std over five test runs (SlowFast detection uses n=4). Basic detection scores barely changed, shifting by only 0.03 across all the models. You can find the AUROC scores and exact model setups in App. E.5 and App. B.1. We bolded the best results and underlined the second-best.
Table 7. The research landscape for automated seizure analysis broken down by data type and subject. The clearest open gap is multi-level severity grading using paired animal video-EEG data.

Table 10. A complete, animal-by-animal breakdown of our combined video and EEG dataset across all 20 rats. For every subject, we track the number of recording sessions, total clips, the split between non-seizure and seizure clips, and the exact breakdown of seizure severity (Stages 2 through 5). As the numbers show, the frequency of seizures is drastically uneven across the cohort. Just four heavily affected animals (R1, R2, R3, and R4) provide nearly half of the entire dataset, with individual totals swinging wildly from as few as 11 to as many as 3,091 clips. Across the board, the most violent events (Stage 5) remain extremely rare, yielding only 193 clips. It is worth noting that these counts represent the final, human-labeled dataset; a small handful of clips might still be dropped later when we format the data specifically for the video or EEG models. Finally, all true animal identities have been hidden, and the subjects are simply listed in order from highest to lowest clip count (R1 to R20).

Table 9. Video backbones evaluated in Table 2, outlining their core design paradigms and overall parameter counts. Network capacities range broadly from 4M to 121M parameters. The smallest model is marked in bold, while the second-smallest is underlined.

Table 12. Performance breakdown for all ten video models on the thoroughly sanitized RodEpil dataset [44], evaluated under strict subject-exclusive five-fold cross-validation. F1 and AUROC scores represent the average across all five folds, while MCC includes the standard deviation (mean± std). Notice how drastically the model rankings shuffle compared to our native dataset a clear reminder that a network’s success is deeply tied to the specific visual quirks of its training data. †We have explicitly flagged the SlowFast model; its perfect score warrants further investigation for residual shortcuts, without establishing their presence. The highest non-flagged score is highlighted in bold.

Table 13. Ablation experiment evaluating spatial resolution for the R(2+1)D detection model across three input image sizes (16 frames, session-exclusive split, seed 42, 10 epochs; batch sizes scaled to 16, 8, and 4, respectively). Because the native source footage is only ∼300 to 480 px, both of the higher resolution settings force the network to upsample the video. Consequently, performance drops steadily across all three metrics. In terms of AUROC, the gap between the top two settings only emerges past the third decimal place (0.9934 vs. 0.9926). Note that the 448 px run suffered an out-of-memory crash after completing 8 of its 10 epochs; we report metrics from its best saved checkpoint, meaning this row represents an optimistic upper bound for the largest resolution setting. The best score in each column is highlighted in bold.

Table 18. Direct head-to-head evaluation across the 2,830 heldout test clips shared between both modalities for 5-class severity grading. To ensure a strictly fair comparison, this analysis is restricted to the exact intersection of clips evaluated by both models. Per-class rows highlight “solo victories” instances where precisely one model correctly predicted the severity stage while the other failed. Notably, Stage 2 represents the sole category where the EEG model outperforms the video network in solo correct predictions.

Table 4. Seven EEG baselines use the same 6 s windows, 3 s stride, 125 Hz sampling, and log-mean aggregation (App. B.5). TCN performs best for detection and 3-class grading, while GRU and TCN are similar at 5 classes. Two LSTM runs failed to converge, so its 3- and 5-class results use n=4. Best results are in bold; second-best are underlined.

Table 16. AUROC scores for all ten video and seven EEG backbones, following the exact same row order as Tables 2 and 4 for easy comparison. We use binary AUROC for the basic detection task and a macro one-vs-rest approach for multi-class severity grading.

Table 17. AUROC scores for both the video frame-count sweep and the rigorously re-encoded RodEpil cross-validation folds. For the sake of clarity, we have broken out the specific RodEpil AUROC results into their own dedicated section immediately below the frame-count data.

Table 19. Recall evaluated across the low- and high-motion halves of each severity class, partitioned strictly at the class-specific median motion energy (900 clips sampled from the paired evaluation set). We define motion energy as the mean absolute frame difference across 24 evenly spaced 96 × 96 grayscale frames. Because this metric is computed over the entire duration of the clip including its 10 s pre- and post-event buffers it serves as a coarse but objective proxy for the overall physical intensity of the seizure.

Table 5. Testing new sessions versus new animals. Testing unseen animals keeps basic detection high but hurts exact grading. Video’s 5-class lead shrinks from 0.097 to 0.071. Scores show the mean± std over five tests.
Table 6. RodEpil [44] subject-wise five-fold evaluation. Uniform re-encoding removes the identified class-correlated encoding cues; R(2+1)D then reaches 0.979 mean F1 and 0.972 MCC.

Table 14. Per-class diagnostic precision (P), recall (R), and F1 for five-class classification, with modality-specific support counts (n). These tabulated results expose differences between common and rare classes. They should not be conflated with the values displayed in Fig. 8.

Table 15. AUROC scores comparing the standard sessionexclusive evaluation against the strictly segregated subjectexclusive cross-validation. We use binary AUROC for basic detection and a macro one-vs-rest approach for multi-class severity grading. All values represent the mean± std across five independent runs.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of video and EEG models for seizure detection and severity grading, fitting video understanding and temporal representation learning.
papers.title: Seeing Seizures: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Video and EEG Deep Learning for Automated Rodent Seizure Detection and Severity Grading
papers.tldr: This study benchmarks video and single-channel EEG deep-learning models for automated rodent seizure detection and behavioral severity grading, finding strong detection but substantially harder generalization to unseen animals and severity classes.

papers.abstract: We demonstrate high-precision global localization using natural ground texture viewed through microscope optics, achieving localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime. For the planar ground texture localization problem considered here, we relate optical magnification and image-space localization uncertainty to physical localization precision. Leveraging this relationship, we then develop a microscope-based localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification imaging. We evaluate this system across several surface textures using a calibrated precision gantry. Across 1,007 held-out queries per surface, the system localizes every query and achieves translation RMSEs of 28$-$73 $\mu$m. Independent photometric registration agrees with the feature-based localization estimates to within approximately 9 $\mu$m RMSE. We further demonstrate localization on a low-cost mobile robot using the gantry-collected maps, and also show that the system can resolve micrometer-scale displacement caused by thermal expansion. These results show that microscopic natural surface texture can bring mobile localization into a precision regime typically associated with fixed positioning systems.
authors: Aaron Wilhelm, Marina de Albuquerque Marcon, Emith Uyanwatte, Nils Napp
bullets: Targets high-precision planar localization using naturally occurring surface texture rather than fixed positioning infrastructure.
Relates optical magnification and image-space uncertainty to achievable physical localization precision.
Develops a microscope-based system addressing high-magnification calibration, camera modeling, and focus challenges.
Across several textures, all 1,007 held-out queries per surface were localized, with 28–73 μm translation RMSE; independent photometric registration agreed within about 9 μm RMSE.
Demonstrates operation on a low-cost mobile robot and detection of micrometer-scale thermal-expansion displacement.

(D) Spatial localization performance over the mapped workspace, showing gantry query errors and mobile-robot trajectories colored by translational error.

Macroscopic views (top) and corresponding microscopic views (bottom) of printed wood grain (left), concrete (middle), and terrazzo (right). papers.selection_reason: High-precision mobile robot localization from ground texture; relevant to embodied perception and robot navigation.
papers.title: Micro-Localization: High-Precision Mobile Robot Localization Using Microscopic Ground Texture
papers.tldr: Microscopic views of natural ground texture enable mobile robots to localize globally with tens-of-micrometers precision.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy's own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of 0.981-0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.
authors: Victoria Smelova, Daniil Kazachkov, Georgiy Kazantsev, Iuliia Tsvetkova, Egor Cherepanov, Nikita Kachaev, Artem Latyshev, Aleksandr I. Panov, Alexey K. Kovalev
bullets: Addresses the cost and redundancy of retaining complete visual observation histories in long-horizon, multi-stage tasks.
Compares 35 plan-disagreement measures across autoregressive and flow-matching VLA policies, then validates selected signals on pretrained policies.
Uses plan-revision signals to trigger bounded visual-memory updates, with a robot-masked filter to suppress redundant frames.
Event detectors achieve ROC-AUC values of 0.981–0.997 in the reported evaluations.
The method preserved task-relevant observations until later decision points in 100% of evaluated episodes and showed transfer to real-robot replay data.

figures.caption: Figure 4: RePlanMem-VLA overview. At replanning step q, the VLA first predicts a chunk C− q from the current observation, instruction, and existing memory. The temporally aligned overlap with the preceding plan is converted into a task-calibrated surprise percentile pq. If pq > τ , a selected observation is written to FIFO memory and the policy performs a second forward pass with the updated memory, yielding Cfinal

Figure 2: Real-robot delayed-cue setup. The robot observes the target object’s color. The cue then leaves the observation, and the robot must later select the matching object among distractors using stored visual information.

Figure 6: Real-robot replay of the surprise-based event detector and redundancy-aware memoryselection pipeline. White highlights indicate memory updates, while red crosses mark detector activations for which the redundancy filter prevents overwriting existing memory frames.

Figure 7: Correlation structure of the disagreement measures. Pairwise within-episode Spearman correlations are aggregated across eight tasks with equal task weights. The top row shows autoregressive policies and the bottom row shows Flow-Matching policies. Columns correspond to full-context and current-only conditioning.

Figure 1: RePlanMem-VLA. Task-relevant cues may disappear from the current observation before they are needed. When consecutive replans disagree on their overlapping actions, the important observation is stored in memory and remains available after the cue is no longer visible.

Figure 8: Within-episode keyframe detection on RememberColor5. Each panel shows example observations, selected disagreement features standardized within the episode, and keyframe probabilities predicted by XGBoost, CatBoost, and LSTM. Horizontal dotted lines indicate detector decision thresholds.

Figure 3: Surprise-gated memory updates on the RememberColor task. The surprise score Sq and task-calibrated percentile pq identify candidate update times near transitions between the cue, empty, and action phases.
Table 4: Best-performing disagreement metrics across the eight RQ1 tasks.
Table 2: Keyframe detection under RH1 and EXEC4.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces RePlanMem-VLA, a method for selective visual memory in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. It uses replanning signals to trigger memory updates, directly addressing VLA policy limitations.
papers.title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: RePlanMem-VLA uses unusually large changes in a VLA policy’s rolling action predictions to selectively store task-relevant visual keyframes.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at 92-100% of positions, but not which position comes next. Based on this observation, we introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), which learns to predict this order. A 0.62M-parameter model reads only the target's output distributions and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, and the target verifies all of them in a single pass by checking whether each equals its own next state. On the verification side, our analysis shows that prior block-diffusion verification approaches either assume $T=0$ or a sequential proposal interface. To support tree-based speculation at any temperature, we propose using coupled-noise match verification for diffusion blocks, following shared-Gumbel-noise coupling approaches. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to 6.8x and reaches up to 3.2x the throughput of standard decoding, beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that the learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT-dLLM/
authors: Eliezer Shlomi, Eliron Rahimi, Avi Mendelson, Chaim Baskin
bullets: DLMs must decide both what token to generate and which position to commit, limiting direct transfer of autoregressive speculative decoding.
SPOT uses a 0.62M-parameter drafter that reads target output distributions and predicts candidate commit-order trajectories.
A single target pass verifies the proposed tree using coupled-noise matching, supporting diffusion blocks at arbitrary temperatures.
Experiments report up to 6.8× fewer target passes and up to 3.2× higher throughput than standard decoding.
The learned drafter transfers across six different diffusion language models and outperforms calibrated and training-free baselines across tested tasks and budgets.

papers.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
papers.tldr: SPOT accelerates diffusion language model decoding by predicting the order in which positions should be committed, enabling lossless tree-based speculation and up to 3.2× higher throughput.

papers.abstract: While LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in English Relation Extraction (RE) tasks, a significant gap remains in assessing their RE performance in low-resource languages, due to a lack of standardized benchmarks. Creating native, language-specific annotated RE benchmarks is expensive and requires human expertise, while relying on translation yields suboptimal, inaccurate datasets that introduce English-centric biases. To tackle this, we propose a scalable, language-agnostic methodology to create RE data by denoising naturally occurring yet noisy alignments of knowledge bases and corresponding texts. We define a proper alignment via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, where a relation triplet is entailed by an input text. We empirically assess five denoising strategies, and demonstrate that multilingual models outperform language-specific models in the few-shot LLM setting, while Hebrew-specific encoders remain competitive under NLI fine-tuning and are strongest in the label-free cross-training setting. We further find that prompting in the native language achieves performance on par with or slightly exceeding English prompts, confirming that the pipeline operates naturally in the target language. The best open-weights model, Gemma-4-31B-it (F1\,=\,0.915), matches the best API model, GPT-5.4 (0.921), and reaches F1\,=\,0.844 on a fully held-out, dual-annotated test set. Applying the optimized pipeline, we release HeRE: a novel, massive, 1.5-million-instance silver dataset for Hebrew RE, designed to support data-intensive experimentation and model fine-tuning. HeRE bridges a critical gap in standard Hebrew RE evaluation, while providing the NLP community with a reproducible, language-agnostic pipeline for RE dataset construction in other low-resource settings.
authors: Ron Keinan, Amir David Nissan Cohen, Reut Tsarfaty
bullets: Addresses the lack of standardized Hebrew and other low-resource-language RE benchmarks.
Frames alignment validation as an NLI task: whether a relation triplet is entailed by the text.
Evaluates five denoising strategies and compares multilingual, Hebrew-specific, and general LLM approaches.
Releases HeRE, a 1.5-million-instance silver Hebrew RE dataset, plus a reproducible construction pipeline.
The best open-weights and API models achieve F1 scores of 0.915 and 0.921, respectively; the dual-annotated held-out test reaches F1=0.844.

papers.title: HeRE: A Novel Benchmark for Hebrew Relation Extraction via LLM-Guided Denoising of Knowledge Graph Alignments
papers.tldr: HeRE introduces a scalable, language-agnostic pipeline that denoises knowledge-graph–text alignments to create a large Hebrew relation-extraction benchmark without relying on costly native annotation or biased translation.

papers.abstract: The web is not static or uniform. Websites that serve the same purpose can look and navigate very differently. Even within a single site, successive redesigns can change how familiar features are presented and accessed. Humans adapt to this by recognizing familiar interaction patterns and reusing what they already know. We give web agents a similar ability with WebMix, a mixture hypernetwork that adapts them to unseen interfaces by composing previously trained low-rank adapters. WebMix begins with a bank of adapters trained on source interfaces. At deployment, a scout agent explores the target interface and summarizes its observations into a compact manual. A lightweight router uses this manual to predict mixing coefficients over the adapter bank, which combine the existing adapters into a new one for inference. Adapting to a new interface takes only a scouting run and a forward pass, without gradient updates on the target. With Qwen and Llama models, we evaluate domain transfer on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2, and version transfer on TimeWarp. In all three settings, WebMix matches or outperforms in-context learning and LoRA baselines, often matching the average success of specialists trained directly on those interfaces. On TimeWarp domain transfer, it gains about 8 percentage points on average over the best baseline with both models. These gains do not come at the cost of seen interfaces, where WebMix keeps its lead, and extend to version transfer. Adapting to a new interface can therefore rely on exploration and composition instead of retraining.
authors: Md Farhan Ishmam, Minh Pham Dinh, Kenneth Marino
bullets: Web interfaces vary across sites and redesigns, motivating reusable adaptation mechanisms.
A scout agent creates a compact manual of the target interface, and a router selects adapter-mixture weights.
The resulting adapter is composed from previously trained adapters and used in a single forward pass without gradient updates.
Evaluated with Qwen and Llama on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2 for domain and version transfer.
WebMix matches or exceeds in-context learning and LoRA baselines, with about an 8-point average gain over the best baseline on TimeWarp domain transfer.

Their weighted sum is a site-specific adapter ∆W , added to the base weights Wθ of the agent πθ, which reads the accessibility tree and emits grounded actions (e.g., click [31]). Websites vary across versions (v1–v5) and domains.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their ability to perform \textit{everyday logical reasoning}, which often departs from textbook formal logic, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate how well reasoning models align with everyday reasoning patterns by introducing a benchmark based on linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena. We also compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting conditions. We find that, in many cases, (1) reasoning models show degraded performance in everyday reasoning when such reasoning deviates from formal logical rules, (2) some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models in everyday reasoning, and (3) prompting with additional instructions provides limited control over reasoning behavior. These findings suggest that current reasoning models do not reliably capture everyday reasoning and point to limitations in post-training, motivating improved training objectives and evaluation across diverse forms of reasoning.
authors: Kentaro Ozeki, Risako Ando, Takanobu Morishita, Hirohiko Abe, Koji Mineshima, Mitsuhiro Okada
bullets: Introduces a benchmark targeting linguistic and pragmatic phenomena in everyday reasoning.
Systematically compares reasoning and non-reasoning models under controlled prompting.
Reasoning models frequently perform worse when everyday reasoning conflicts with formal logical rules.
Some non-reasoning models using chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models.
Additional instructions provide limited control, highlighting gaps in post-training and evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) on 'everyday logical reasoning' tasks, comparing them to non-reasoning models. This provides insights into the limitations and capabilities of LLMs in pragmatic reasoning.
papers.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks
papers.tldr: Current large reasoning models often struggle with everyday logical reasoning, especially when it departs from formal logic, and may be outperformed by prompted non-reasoning models.

papers.abstract: Inferring dynamics from real-world experimental data is inherently ambiguous, as many plausible dynamical systems can explain the same positional observations at measurement times. For higher fidelity modeling of applications ranging from single-cell RNA to vortex dynamics and even flocking of birds, scientific observables increasingly also include velocity estimates that serve to resolve this issue. However, incorporating this rich information in a scalable manner, free of simulation or unnecessary approximations, has remained a difficult challenge. In this paper, we introduce Kinematic Interpolants (KI), a novel framework that extends the seminal methodology of stochastic interpolants to infer nonlinear dynamics across multiple snapshots in phase space, i.e., observables with position and velocity measurements. Empirically, we demonstrate that across several scientific datasets, KI achieves superior reconstruction of the underlying dynamics compared to existing baselines while requiring only a fraction of the training time.
authors: Yiheng (Roger), Jiang, Youssef Marzouk, Avishek Joey Bose, Aram-Alexandre Pooladian
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in recovering dynamics from positional observations alone.
Extends stochastic interpolants to phase-space data containing positions and velocities.
Designed to scale across scientific applications with richer kinematic measurements.
Experiments on several scientific datasets show improved reconstruction over existing baselines with substantially shorter training time.

papers.abstract: Internet-scale photo collections of real-world landmarks have driven progress in 3D computer vision yet remain highly challenging for modern 3D foundation models (3DFMs) that estimate scene structure in a single feed-forward pass. In this work, we introduce ArchWorld, a benchmark of 3D architectural landmarks with high geographic coverage and rich metadata. We use this benchmark to conduct a thorough error analysis of current 3DFMs to understand where they fall short and how they can be improved. We examine socially relevant disparities in model error and find that model performance varies by geographic region; however, unlike typical fairness regimes, the trends only partially match training data representation. Our investigation reveals that the observed geographic disparities reflect not only differences in data representation and scene size but also differences in region-specific architectural features and background distractors that make scenes from different regions inherently vary in difficulty. Leveraging insights from these model failings, we introduce an intervention scheme that improves 3DFM performance while simultaneously reducing geographic disparities.
authors: Nicky Kriplani, Yiwen Zhang, Angelina Wang, Hadar Averbuch-Elor
bullets: Introduces ArchWorld, a landmark benchmark with broad geographic coverage and rich metadata.
Analyzes errors in single-pass 3D foundation models and identifies region-dependent performance differences.
Finds that disparities reflect data representation, scene size, architectural features, and background distractors.
Shows that geographic error trends only partially align with training-data representation.
Develops an intervention scheme that improves model performance and reduces geographic disparities.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies 3D foundation models, analyzing geographic disparities and proposing an intervention to improve reconstruction performance.
papers.title: Towards Reconstructing Geographically Diverse Architecture with 3D Foundation Models
papers.tldr: ArchWorld benchmarks geographically diverse architectural landmarks, diagnoses regional disparities in 3D foundation models, and presents an intervention that improves performance while reducing those disparities.

papers.abstract: Q-learning is premised on learning a function to predict the value of a state-action pair, with the goal of using such a function to guide policy improvement. Most approaches learn this function from scratch using scalar or distributional return targets. This discriminative approach leaves another source of supervision for learning representations unused: the actions themselves. Rather than directly predict the return of a state-action pair, we ask the reverse question: how likely is the action under each possible return? This perspective provides a critic whose generative component is a return-conditioned policy, which can share the actor's architecture. Training this policy supervises the critic with every action rather than with returns alone, and a squared-error loss anchors the critic's Q-value to the bootstrapped target. We evaluate our approach on both offline and online RL tasks and show gains over leading discriminative methods, including distributional RL methods.
authors: Alexander Swerdlow, Perry Dong, Chelsea Finn
bullets: Reframes value estimation as asking how likely an action is under each possible return.
Uses a return-conditioned policy as the critic’s generative component, potentially sharing the actor’s architecture.
Supervises the critic with actions in addition to return targets, while squared error anchors Q-values to bootstrapped targets.
Evaluated on offline and online reinforcement-learning tasks, with reported gains over leading discriminative and distributional methods.

papers.selection_reason: General Q-learning critic with a return-conditioned generative policy; transferable to robot policy learning and RL-based manipulation.
papers.title: Generative Value Classifier
papers.tldr: Generative Value Classifier improves Q-learning by modeling actions conditioned on possible returns, using action information to train a stronger critic.

papers.abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.
authors: Runhan Huang, Xiangcheng Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Yitong Li, Yen-Jen Wang, Bohan Lyu, Haotian Ye, Chuye Hong, Yixuan Wang, Chloe Su, Haoyu Xiong, Yangzhen Wu, Enze Xie, Travis Manderson, Stefano Ermon, Pieter Abbeel, Antonio Torralba, Dawn Song, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the need for new teleoperation datasets when adapting robot policies to new embodiments or tasks.
Uses a coding agent to generate executable robot-control programs and discover goal-achieving decision sequences through exploration.
Compiles successful experiences into modular perception-planning-control programs that can be reused and composed.
Evaluated across multiple simulated and real robot embodiments and manipulation tasks, with generalization improving as exploration scales.
Reports emergent active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration capabilities.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | System architecture and self-improving loop of RAX. The coding agent, powered by a frozen LLM, interacts with physical hardware across an isolation boundary using multimodal perception and control SDK interfaces. By reflecting on execution outcomes, the agent continually updates a persistent memory system containing working context, task notes, and a versioned repository of verified skills. During exploration, the agent compiles its perception and planning logic into standalone Python control programs that execute high-frequency loops directly on the robot. When encountering perception or planning failures due to environment variations, the program raises an exception (raise Unsure()), delegating control back to the agent to make adjustments and refine the codebase.

Figure 5 | A long-horizon task on the real RB-Y1. The agent composes six sub-tasks from skills learned in earlier sessions. It finds the cups from Gemini’s rim points and depth, measures the desk edge by picking points in the head image, and plans the base routes on a model of the scene.

papers.abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., {\pi}0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

Key open challenges include generalizable in-context learning, execution cost and time, state verification, recovery from irreversible failures, and preserving progress over long horizons.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have increased the demand for reliable watermarking for copyright protection, yet the robustness of video watermarks against removal attacks remains underexplored. Most watermark-removal methods originate from the image domain: signal optimization injects imperceptible pixel-domain perturbations, whereas generative resynthesis produces a visually similar instance through diffusion synthesis. When extended to videos, the former introduces temporally varying noise that causes visible flickering, while the latter regenerates fine-grained structures inconsistently across frames, leading to structural motion inconsistency. To evaluate video watermark robustness, we propose PoseRegen, a pose-consistent reconstruction framework that removes watermarks while preserving the original content and motion. PoseRegen first applies a temporally shared viewpoint transformation to disrupt watermark-bearing spatial patterns and then jointly reconstructs the transformed sequence with a pose-conditioned video model. A frozen video DiT processes the complete sequence with its reference-video latent, and full-sequence Flow Matching supervision keeps identity and background consistent across frames. To further preserve motion structure, we introduce a lightweight Pose-Conditioned Motion Consistency Adapter that adapts the frozen backbone to temporally ordered pose guidance and constrains body-part trajectories throughout reconstruction. Experiments on eleven video watermarking schemes show that PoseRegen reduces the average bit accuracy to 0.505, near random guessing, while outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.34% on motion-related VBench metrics. These results reveal a practical vulnerability of current video watermarks and highlight the need to evaluate robustness jointly with temporal and motion quality.

Across 11 watermarking schemes, watermark bit accuracy falls to 0.505—near random guessing—and motion-related VBench scores improve by 9.34% over the strongest baseline.
The work emphasizes evaluating watermark robustness together with temporal and motion quality.

papers.abstract: Three dimensional modeling for autonomous driving must continuously estimate road geometry, obstacle occupancy, traffic participant behavior, and observational uncertainty under limited computational resources. Existing reconstruction methods can synthesize realistic novel views, but visual fidelity does not sufficiently characterize the geometric reliability required for driving. Generative world models can expand scenarios and predict future observations, yet may introduce content unsupported by measurements. We propose DriveWorld3D, a framework combining temporal video learning, measurement constraints from multiple sensors, and offline generative simulation. Its online component maintains a unified world state comprising road surfaces, volumetric occupancy, dynamic entities, and road relations, while separately representing physical occupancy, observability, and evidence provenance. Action conditioned future prediction and risk sensitive planning connect this representation to driving decisions. Its offline component reconstructs recorded scenes using neural radiance fields or 3D Gaussian Splatting, then expands long tail conditions using generative models while restricting the use of generated content as geometric ground truth. We specify data partitioning, sensor ablations, fault injection, paired closed loop testing, and real to simulation consistency assessment. The central hypothesis is that explicit evidence management can reduce dangerous false free space predictions and occlusion risk within a matched computational budget while retaining acceptable driving efficiency. All performance claims remain subject to experimental validation. Keywords: autonomous driving; 3D occupancy; sensor fusion; uncertainty; generative world models; NeRF; 3D Gaussian Splatting; closed loop simulation

papers.abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to jointly localize a target in space and time given a natural-language query. Despite continued advances, existing STVG benchmarks remain largely centered on localizing targets through instance-specific descriptions, leaving them largely decoupled from long-form reasoning increasingly emphasized in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In this paper, we introduce Event-STVG, a task that shifts STVG from locating what is described toward event-level reasoning by unifying long-form context, repeated-event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi-target grounding. To facilitate research on Event-STVG, we construct a large-scale benchmark comprising 4,016 annotated event occurrences across soccer and seven additional domains. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal substantial difficulty, with the strongest model achieving only 5.4% m-vIoU at the 10-minute horizon. Across domains, we consistently observe confusion among repeated same-type events, spatial grounding bottlenecks, and rare success in jointly grounding all required roles. Event-STVG establishes a new challenge for visual understanding in MLLMs, calling for future models that can jointly reason about complex events across space and time. Code and annotations are available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/EventSTVG

State-of-the-art MLLMs perform poorly, with the strongest model reaching 5.4% m-vIoU at a 10-minute horizon.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a challenge in supervised continual learning, as adapting to new tasks causes representation drift and loss of previously learned information. This raises the question of which representational changes should be constrained while preserving plasticity. We therefore introduce Sparse Autoencoder Geometric Anchoring (SAGA), which converts a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained at each task boundary into local, low-rank constraints on representation drift. Replay examples specify where the constraints apply, while leading right singular directions of the encoder Jacobian specify which changes are penalized. The resulting geometry is input dependent and can be retained without keeping the SAE for subsequent tasks' training. We establish its local relation to latent code matching, define its spectral truncation error, and derive a conditional bound on frozen-readout drift. With replay and snapshot history, the method achieves the highest mean Class-IL accuracy and lowest mean forgetting among the evaluated ER, DER++, ER-ACE, and SGD baselines on three pretrained ViT-B/16 benchmarks, with accuracy gains of 12.15, 4.79, and 3.22 percentage points over the strongest conventional baseline on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R, respectively. From scratch results are more mixed, while rank ablations and geometry controls show that SAE-induced low-rank geometry offers useful stability-plasticity trade-offs.
authors: Kamil Faber, Katarzyna Filus, {\L}ukasz Pawela
bullets: Addresses representation drift and loss of prior-task knowledge during supervised continual learning.
Converts task-boundary SAEs into input-dependent constraints, using replay examples and leading encoder-Jacobian directions.

papers.abstract: Automated fundus-based diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading can substantially expand screening capacity, but source-trained models degrade sharply across different cameras, clinics, and patient populations. Existing test-time adaptation methods depend on entropy minimization or target information accumulated from image batches and streams. These mechanisms can reinforce confidently incorrect predictions and break down when clinical images arrive independently. We introduce CF-NODE, a novel counterfactual test-time adaptation framework for cross- domain DR grading. Instead of trusting prediction confidence or estimating a target distribution, CF-NODE asks how each prediction responds under a controlled intervention on the evidence supporting it. CF-NODE ranks internal spatial nodes using model-derived attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, progressively attenuates the highest-ranked nodes, and uses the stability of the resulting expected-grade response to apply a bounded calibration of the predicted grade distribution. The framework is fully frozen and adapts every image independently using only geometric views and a fixed source-derived prior, requiring no target-derived information or model updates. We evaluate CF-NODE on five external DR datasets under repeated-seed evaluation against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A. CF-NODE outperforms all four methods with statistically significant improvements over the second-best method, improves AUC on every target domain, and attains the highest average AUC and macro-F1, delivering stronger grade discrimination together with more balanced recognition across DR severity levels. These results demonstrate that counterfactual intervention sensitivity provides consistent and deployment-ready domain robustness for single-image clinical inference.
authors: Sabarish G, Deepak Parashar
bullets: Addresses performance degradation across cameras, clinics, and patient populations, where batch- or confidence-based adaptation can reinforce errors.
Ranks internal spatial nodes using attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, then attenuates selected nodes to measure prediction stability.
Calibrates each image’s predicted grade distribution using intervention sensitivity, geometric views, and a fixed source-derived prior.
Evaluated across five external DR datasets against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A; it achieved the highest average AUC and macro-F1 and improved AUC on every target domain.
Supports independent, deployment-oriented inference, but its scope is limited to the evaluated DR cross-domain settings.

papers.abstract: Distributed Transformer inference across co-located edge devices is fundamentally communication-bound, as exchanging activations between sequence-parallel partitions dominates inference latency under commodity edge bandwidths. Existing compression schemes reduce this cost but retain a structural bottleneck: the received data must still undergo key/value projection before attention can proceed, serializing computation behind communication. This paper presents Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding (Trace), a framework that addresses these limitations. Trace places a Vector Quantizer (VQ) at the post-attention residual of every Transformer layer and precomputes codebook-indexed key/value representations. During inference, exchanged activations are encoded into compact codebook indices, allowing receivers to directly recover keys and values through table lookup instead of executing the downstream computations required to derive them. By eliminating the received data downstream computation, Trace enables communication--computation overlap and reduces a key latency bottleneck in distributed Transformer inference. A hierarchical clustering further structures the learned codebook into a multi-resolution hierarchy, enabling runtime adaptation of the communication bitrate without retraining. The framework supports two operating variants: one prioritizing accuracy and the other balancing accuracy and efficiency through buffer-compatible quantization. Experiments on ViT-Base (ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100) and ViViT-B (UCF-101) show that Trace achieves up to 1.89% higher accuracy and up to 1.27x end-to-end inference speedup compared with the state-of-the-art VQ-based distributed inference framework. Compared with uncompressed sequence-parallel inference, Trace reduces communication overhead by up to 22,624x.
authors: Muhammad Azlan Qazi, Alexandros Iosifidis, Qi Zhang
bullets: Targets communication-bound inference across sequence-parallel edge devices, where activation exchange dominates latency.
Places a vector quantizer after attention and precomputes codebook-indexed key/value representations for direct receiver-side lookup.
Enables communication–computation overlap and runtime bitrate adaptation through a hierarchical multi-resolution codebook.
Offers accuracy-focused and buffer-compatible accuracy–efficiency variants without retraining for bitrate changes.
Experiments report up to 1.27× end-to-end speedup, 1.89% higher accuracy than a VQ-based baseline, and 22,624× lower communication overhead than uncompressed inference.

papers.selection_reason: Codebook-based activation compression and communication-computation overlap for distributed transformer inference, reducing latency and communication overhead in efficient AI.
papers.title: TRACE: Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding for Communication-efficient Distributed Edge Inference
papers.tldr: TRACE accelerates distributed Transformer inference by encoding residual activations into codebook indices that directly reconstruct attention keys/values, reducing communication and avoiding downstream computation bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: In a small language model the vocabulary is the single largest part. In Gemma 3 270M the embedding table holds 168M of 268M parameters, and because quantisation methods leave the embedding in 16-bit, it is also most of the file once the rest of the model is compressed. We ask what that table actually buys. We replace it with one frozen table of 512-bit codes, 16 MB, with no trainable parameters, derived once from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarisation, and we train the same Gemma-shaped body from scratch on the same 2.05B tokens with and without it. The learned table buys 0.20 nats of validation loss for 2.6 times the trainable parameters, but on LAMBADA, HellaSwag and PIQA the frozen-table model is better or tied; only ARC-Easy favours the learned table. With a ternary BitNet b1.58 body the whole model is a 46 MB file, still ties the float model on LAMBADA and PIQA, and on a laptop CPU generates 615 to 740 tokens per second in 62 MB of memory, five to six times the speed of the float model's 8-bit GGUF in llama.cpp at a seventh of the memory. The frozen table wins by 1.7 to 2.3 nats on rare words, accepts 10,000 new words after training with a 3% cost where the learned table collapses by 43%, and all of it is released with the weights, the data and every evaluation answer.
authors: Sai Kiran Bathula
bullets: Learned embeddings improve validation loss by 0.20 nats but require 2.6× more trainable parameters.
The frozen-table model is better or tied on LAMBADA, HellaSwag, and PIQA; ARC-Easy favors learned embeddings.
Combined with a ternary BitNet b1.58 body, the model is 46 MB and generates 615–740 tokens/s on a laptop CPU.
The frozen table performs 1.7–2.3 nats better on rare words and supports 10,000 new words with only a 3% cost.
Scope: results target small Gemma-shaped and ternary models, with the table derived from a pretrained embedding via PCA and sign binarization.

papers.title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
papers.tldr: A frozen 16 MB binary vocabulary can replace a large learned embedding table in small and ternary language models with competitive evaluation performance and much lower memory use.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.
authors: Hamed Khosravi, Xiaoming Huo
bullets: Targets agents that accept failed checks or stop at weaker conclusions without exploring valid alternatives.
Precommits rules for how each conclusion can be justified before evidence is checked.
A separate program records check outcomes, blocks unsupported conclusions, and guides or performs checks for stronger ones.
On 480 public-record tasks, PRIME eliminated the unjustified conclusions observed in 26.7% of baseline-agent cases.
Its guidance and additional checks improved justified-conclusion scores from 30.1 to 59.2/100; guarantees depend on correct requirements, exact check locations, and sufficient budget.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PRIME, a framework for verifiable evidence-grounded reasoning in LLM agents using precommitted rules. It focuses on constraint-based verification of agent conclusions.
papers.title: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: PRIME makes LLM-agent decisions verifiable by predefining evidence routes and enforcing conclusions through a programmatic evidence ledger.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon GUI agents rely on visual history to maintain task states, but retaining historical screenshots increases visual-token usage and inference costs, while textual summaries can discard critical state information, undermining long-horizon reliability. We propose ECHOES, which leverages training-time privileged information to guide textual history compression and strengthen long-horizon reasoning. Specifically, ECHOES adopts a Compression-Think-Action (CTA) format to recursively update a textual history state and reason. The same model, given privileged multi-image inputs, serves as a teacher that provides dense token-level on-policy distillation on student-generated CTA rollouts. Our Perception-Memory Fidelity (PMF) Gap-guided OPD-RL framework dynamically balances privileged distillation and task-reward optimization, with periodic teacher updates supporting continued improvement. We further introduce ECHOESBMK, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark derived from real GUI agent failure trajectories to jointly evaluate visual perception and cross-modal state retention. Experiments on four GUI benchmarks and ECHOESBMK demonstrate substantial gains in task performance and memory fidelity. Without retaining historical screenshots at deployment, ECHOES achieves competitive performance with a favorable performance-inference-cost trade-off and exhibits positive zero-shot transfer to unseen visual planning tasks.
authors: Tengda Guo (Tsinghua University), Jiawang Hu (StepFun), Yifei Tao (Nanyang Technological University), Yin Wang (StepFun), Haotian Hu (Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology Co., Ltd), Fanyi Wang (Honor), Liujuan Tang (StepFun)
bullets: Addresses the tension between retaining costly historical screenshots and losing critical information through textual summaries.
Uses a recursive Compression-Think-Action format to update textual history and guide reasoning.
Applies privileged multi-image teacher guidance through token-level on-policy distillation, balanced with task rewards by PMF Gap-guided OPD-RL.
Introduces ECHOESBMK, a diagnostic benchmark for visual perception and cross-modal state retention based on GUI failure trajectories.
Shows gains across four GUI benchmarks and ECHOESBMK, with favorable performance–inference-cost trade-offs and zero-shot transfer to unseen visual planning tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes recursive textual history compression and memory-fidelity distillation for GUI agents, fitting persistent agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: ECHOES: Seeing Beyond the Current Image via Recursive History Compression and Privileged On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: ECHOES enables long-horizon GUI agents to compress visual history into text while preserving task-relevant state, reducing inference costs without retaining screenshots at deployment.

papers.abstract: LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.
authors: Mowafak Allaham, Aditya Vempaty, Ashish Jagmohan, Prasenjit Dey, Ravi Kokku
bullets: Underspecified task descriptions can omit verifier-relevant edge cases, motivating clarification before formalization.
An elicitation agent decomposes tasks, asks up to 3 or 10 bounded questions to a reference-grounded simulated developer, and refines the natural-language specification before Lean translation.
Across 189 Verina Lean 4 tasks, same-model elicitation reduced strict pass@1 estimates, while several cross-model pipelines improved them.
The largest reported strict improvement was +6.3 percentage points in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline; effects also varied between basic and advanced tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Studies an elicitation agent that uses clarification questions to improve the quality of Lean specifications generated by LLMs. This explores interactive prompting and agent-based formalization.
papers.title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
papers.tldr: Interactive clarification can improve Lean specification generation in some cross-model setups, but its benefits are inconsistent and depend on the models, question budget, and task type.

papers.abstract: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter-updating test-time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation-valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot-matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre-relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never-seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning-savings
authors: Zhe Zhou
bullets: Tests whether later relearning reflects the specific fact previously learned, rather than familiarity with its components or query format.
Compares matched histories: correct binding (LEARNED), exposure without the binding (CONTROL), and a competing answer in the same slot (WRONG).
In Qwen2.5-1.5B, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL after rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning and partial forgetting.
WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, supporting binding-specific savings, though competitor interference may affect this comparison.
A secondary descriptive analysis estimates roughly 18% fewer optimizer updates for restoration after prior learning, using an unpaired never-seen pool.

papers.selection_reason: Relearning savings in test-time continual learning for language models fits adaptation and memory.
papers.title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Prior learning of a specific fact leaves a measurable relearning advantage even after partial forgetting, indicating that current accuracy can underestimate retained knowledge.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems communicate in text, which is lossy and wasteful: the sender throws away the reading it already did. A growing literature instead transmits the KV cache, the natural carrier of that reading. We study the most appealing form of the idea: both models stay frozen and the sender's cache is substituted for the reader's with nothing trained. It does not work, and the obstruction belongs to the reader. A frozen transformer reads only caches close to the one it would have written itself, a region we call its tolerable set. We show that geometric similarity to that cache does not predict whether the reader can use it, and the failure is not gradual, so a more faithful substitute is not the remedy it appears to be. We explain this phenomenon with competitive attention. Experimentally, we test eight diverse substitution methods against two measured anchors: an uninformative cache baseline and the reader's own accuracy from having read the passage. All sit at the baseline. That turns a long tail of separate negative results into one outcome with a stated condition for overturning it. A different design does work: if the reader keeps its own cache and attends over the sender's as extra context, adapting only its queries, it beats its own baseline, and also clears the baseline with eight senders pooled where undirected attention over the same union falls below it. We offer this as a characterization on one probe, not a leaderboard claim. Our central contribution is a redirection: pursuing faithful substitute caches is the wrong target; adding a cache to what the reader already has is the promising one.
authors: Adam Deng
Shicheng Liu
Yada Zhu
bullets: The study examines training-free KV-cache substitution between frozen LLMs as a less lossy alternative to text communication.
Readers only tolerate caches near those they would have produced themselves, but geometric similarity does not predict usability and failure is abrupt rather than gradual.
Competitive attention is offered as an explanation for why more faithful cache substitutes do not solve the problem.
Eight substitution methods perform at the uninformative-cache baseline, while a query-adaptation design that preserves the reader’s cache exceeds its own baseline in the reported probe.
The authors characterize this as a redirection from replacing reader caches to augmenting them with sender caches, not as a broad leaderboard claim.

papers.selection_reason: Studies KV cache substitution and cache-augmented inference in LLM systems, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Close Enough is Nowhere Near: Fidelity-Consumability Decoupling in KV Caches
papers.tldr: Frozen readers cannot reliably use substituted sender KV caches, even when those caches are geometrically similar; retaining the reader’s cache and adding the sender’s as context is more promising.

papers.abstract: Tiny robots have limited computation and memory, yet visual navigation systems often maintain more state than a task requires. We ask whether persistent memory can instead be shaped by the task. We present \textbf{RingNav}, a \(10.6\)k--parameter visual heading estimator that constrains its memory to the circular manifold \(S^1\). RingNav learns only the turn between consecutive images, while heading is composed directly on the circle. On the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge, RingNav reduces mean absolute turn error by \(27\%\) and accumulated heading error over $4$ sec by \(15\%\) relative to a similarly sized learned-memory model. The structured update also gives exactly zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal. Without fine-tuning, RingNav transfers to real-world drone experiments and continues estimating heading under severe visual degradation. RingNav runs at $27.3$Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and can be deployed on an ultra-low power GAP8 processor at $33.4$Hz.

Provides exact zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal.
Transfers without fine-tuning to real-world drone experiments and runs at 27.3 Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and 33.4 Hz on GAP8.

papers.abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.

Xinyi Wang

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for vision-language-action robot policies under hardware perturbations, directly fitting VLA and robot learning/manipulation.
papers.title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
